title: 721 Exchange Pros and Cons for Real Estate Investors
lead: A 721 exchange offers compelling pros — tax deferral, diversification, liquidity, passive income, and estate planning — but also real cons: the one-way nature, loss of control, the tax on converting units, dependence on the REIT, and fees. This guide gives a balanced look at the pros and cons, who they favor, and how to make the decision.

Like any significant financial strategy, the 721 exchange has both compelling advantages and real drawbacks, and a clear-eyed look at both is essential before deciding. On the pro side, it offers tax deferral (avoiding the substantial tax a sale would trigger), diversification (a stake in the REIT's portfolio instead of one property), liquidity (convertible units), passive income (distributions without management), and powerful estate planning (the step-up and divisibility). On the con side, it's generally a one-way move (you lose 1031 eligibility), you give up control (the REIT manages the portfolio), converting units to shares triggers tax, you depend on the REIT's performance, and there are fees and complexity. Whether the pros outweigh the cons depends on your goals. This guide gives a balanced look at the 721 exchange's pros and cons, who they favor, and how to decide.
takeaways: Pros: tax deferral, diversification, liquidity, passive income, and estate planning — a comprehensive set of benefits.
Cons: the one-way nature (lost 1031 eligibility), loss of control, the conversion tax, REIT dependence, and fees/complexity.
The pros favor owners ready to transition into passive, diversified, more liquid REIT ownership (especially for estate planning).
Investors who value control or flexibility, or aren't ready to commit to REIT ownership, should be cautious.

sections.heading: The pros
paras: The 721 exchange 's pros are substantial and center on five benefits. Tax deferral: under Section 721, contributing property for OP units defers the capital gains tax (the four-layer tax often totaling a third or more of the gain), preserving your full capital. Diversification: your single property becomes a stake in the REIT's diversified portfolio (many properties, types, markets), reducing concentration risk. These two — deferral and diversification — are foundational pros.

Liquidity: OP units are convertible into REIT shares, which (for public REITs) are liquid and tradable, giving a path to liquidity that direct real estate lacks. Passive income: the units pay distributions (comparable to REIT dividends) without any management work, providing hands-off real estate income. So the 721 adds liquidity and passive income to the deferral and diversification — valuable for owners wanting flexibility and hands-off income.

Estate planning: the units receive a step-up at death (erasing the deferred gain for heirs) and divide cleanly among multiple heirs — making the 721 a powerful wealth-transfer tool. This fifth pro is often decisive for older owners. Together, the five pros — deferral, diversification, liquidity, passive income, and estate planning — make the 721 exchange a comprehensive solution. The pros — tax deferral, diversification, liquidity, passive income, and estate planning — are the compelling advantages of the 721 exchange, addressing tax, risk, flexibility, income, and wealth transfer in one transition. Understanding the pros shows why the 721 exchange is attractive for the right owner. These benefits, working together, are the case for the 721 exchange, to be weighed against the cons.

sections.heading: The cons
paras: The 721 exchange's cons are real and must be weighed honestly. The one-way nature: it's generally an irreversible move into REIT ownership — you lose 1031 eligibility (OP units aren't real property), so you can't potentially tax-free return to direct real estate. This is the most significant con for investors who value flexibility. Loss of control: you become a passive investor, with the REIT managing the portfolio; you give up control over the real estate decisions.

The conversion tax: converting OP units to REIT shares (for liquidity) triggers the deferred gain (a taxable event), so accessing liquidity beyond the deferral has a tax cost. REIT dependence: your returns and the value of your holding depend on the REIT's management and performance (and, for public REITs, the share price's market volatility) — you're reliant on the REIT, not your own decisions. So you trade control and self-determination for dependence on the REIT.

Fees and complexity: the 721 exchange involves costs (the transaction, the REIT's fees and expenses) and complexity (the securities nature, the tax mechanics, the documentation), requiring professional guidance. And the investment is subject to the REIT's risks (real estate market, management, etc.). So the cons — one-way nature, loss of control, conversion tax, REIT dependence, fees, and complexity — are meaningful drawbacks. Then assess whether the cons (one-way nature, loss of control, conversion tax, REIT dependence, fees) are acceptable given your goals. Weigh the pros' alignment with your goals against the cons' acceptability — with professional guidance, given the significant, generally irreversible nature.

faq.q: Is the 721 better or worse than a 1031?
a: Neither universally — they suit different goals. The 1031 is better for staying in direct real estate (control, flexibility, continued exchanging); the 721 is better for transitioning into REIT ownership (diversification, liquidity, passivity, estate planning). The 721's pros are advantages the 1031 lacks (diversification, liquidity), but the 721's cons (one-way, loss of control) are things the 1031 avoids. So whether the 721 is better depends on whether you want its pros (and accept its cons) or prefer the 1031's flexibility. They're different tools for different goals.

faq.q: Should I get professional advice before deciding?
a: Yes — the 721 exchange is significant (generally irreversible), involves securities (OP units) and complex tax mechanics, and has major consequences, so you should decide with professional guidance: a financial advisor (suitability and fit), your CPA (the tax aspects), and your estate attorney (the estate-planning role). The complexity, securities nature, and irreversibility make professional advice essential. Don't make the 721 exchange decision without these professionals — their guidance ensures you weigh the pros and cons properly and decide deliberately based on your situation.

faq.q: Can I do a partial 721 exchange to balance the pros and cons?
a: In some cases — you don't necessarily have to commit all your real estate to a 721 exchange. You could contribute some assets (gaining the pros — diversification, passivity, estate benefits — for those, accepting the cons) while keeping other property in direct real estate (retaining control and 1031 flexibility for those). This hedged approach lets you capture some of the 721's pros while keeping some direct-real-estate flexibility, balancing the trade-offs. Whether this is feasible depends on the REIT's willingness to accept your contribution and your overall plan, which you'd discuss with your advisors.

faq.q: How do fees compare to a 1031 exchange?
a: Both have costs, but of different kinds. A 1031 has transaction costs (the sale and purchase of real estate, qualified intermediary fees) and the ongoing costs of owning and managing the property yourself. A 721 exchange has the transaction costs of the contribution plus the REIT's ongoing fees and expenses (management, etc.), which are built into the REIT's structure. So with a 721 you're paying for professional management (via the REIT's fees), whereas with a 1031 you manage yourself (saving management fees but doing the work). Weigh the REIT's fees against the value of professional management and the other 721 benefits.

title: 721 Exchange Risks and Drawbacks to Know
lead: The 721 exchange offers compelling benefits, but it also carries real risks and drawbacks that every investor should understand before proceeding. This guide candidly covers the key risks: the one-way commitment, loss of control, REIT performance and management risk, liquidity and conversion-tax risk, market and valuation risk, and fees and sponsor risk.

The 721 exchange's benefits — deferral, diversification, liquidity, passive income, and estate planning — are genuinely compelling, but a responsible decision requires understanding the risks and drawbacks just as clearly. The 721 exchange is a significant, generally irreversible move into REIT ownership, and it carries risks: you commit to REIT ownership (losing 1031 flexibility), you give up control to the REIT, your returns depend on the REIT's performance and management, accessing liquidity triggers tax, the REIT's value (or share price) can fluctuate, and there are fees and sponsor-related risks. None of these necessarily outweighs the benefits — but you should know them before committing. This guide candidly covers the 721 exchange's risks and drawbacks, so you can make an informed decision with eyes open.
takeaways: The one-way commitment risk (generally irreversible loss of 1031 eligibility) is the most significant drawback — it can lock you in.
Loss of control (becoming a passive investor) and REIT performance/management risk (your returns depend on the REIT) are key risks.
Liquidity has a tax cost (conversion triggers gain) and limitations (holding period, non-traded constraints).
Your holding's value is subject to market/share-price risk (traded) or valuation risk (non-traded), plus fees and sponsor risk.

sections.heading: The one-way commitment risk
paras: The most significant risk of a 721 exchange is its one-way nature — it's generally an irreversible commitment to REIT ownership. Once you contribute your property for OP units, you lose 1031 eligibility (OP units aren't real property), so you can't potentially tax-free return to direct real estate. This means you're committing to REIT ownership as a (generally) permanent endpoint, without the ability to reverse the move potentially tax-free.

The risk in this is that your circumstances or preferences might change after the irreversible commitment. If you later wish you'd stayed in direct real estate (to control properties, keep exchanging, or for other reasons), you can't get back potentially tax-free — you'd have to convert your units (triggering the gain) and buy real estate with the after-tax proceeds. So the one-way commitment risks 'locking you in' to REIT ownership even if your preferences change.

This risk is why being certain before committing is essential — because the move is generally permanent, you should be confident REIT ownership is your intended endpoint, not a tentative choice, and clear on who should not do a 721 exchange in the first place. The one-way commitment risk is the foundational drawback, underlying the importance of careful consideration. The one-way commitment risk — the generally irreversible nature of the move into REIT ownership (losing 1031 eligibility), which can lock you in even if your circumstances or preferences change — is the most significant risk of a 721 exchange. Understanding this risk underscores the need for certainty before committing. The one-way nature is the defining drawback, making the 721 exchange a decision to approach with full conviction. The irreversibility is the central risk to weigh.

sections.heading: Loss of control
paras: A second key drawback is the loss of control — converting to REIT ownership makes you a passive investor, with the REIT controlling the real estate. As a direct property owner, you control your property: the management, leasing, financing, improvements, and the decisions to hold, sell, or exchange. After a 721 exchange, you hold OP units, and the REIT controls the portfolio — you have no say in the property decisions.

The risk in losing control is that you're now dependent on the REIT's decisions, which may not align with what you'd choose. If the REIT makes decisions you disagree with (acquiring or selling properties, financing choices, distribution levels), you have little recourse — you're a passive unit holder, not a decision-maker. So you've traded control of your own real estate for a passive stake in someone else's decisions.

For owners who value control (making their own real estate decisions), this loss is a significant drawback. For owners ready to step back (wanting passivity), the loss of control is acceptable (even welcome — no more management). So the loss of control is a drawback whose weight depends on how much you value control. Loss of control — becoming a passive investor with the REIT controlling the real estate, so you depend on the REIT's decisions with little recourse — is a key drawback of the 721 exchange. Its weight depends on how much you value controlling your own real estate. Understanding the loss of control helps you assess whether giving up control (for passivity) is acceptable to you. For control-valuing owners, this is a major drawback; for those ready to step back, it's acceptable. The loss of control is a defining trade-off of the 721 exchange.
After a 721 exchange you're a passive unit holder, not a decision-maker — you depend on the REIT's choices about the properties, with little recourse if you disagree.

sections.heading: REIT performance and management risk
paras: A third risk is REIT performance and management risk — your returns and your holding's value depend on the REIT's performance and management, not your own decisions. After a 721 exchange, your economic outcome is tied to the REIT: its portfolio's performance, its management's decisions, its financial health, and its strategy all determine your returns (distributions) and the value of your units/shares. So you're reliant on the REIT doing well.

The risk is that the REIT may underperform or face problems — poor management decisions, a struggling portfolio, financial difficulties, or strategic missteps can hurt your returns and your holding's value. Unlike a direct property owner who controls their outcome, you're dependent on the REIT's performance, which is outside your control. So a poorly-managed or underperforming REIT directly harms you, with little you can do.

This makes evaluating the REIT critical before converting — since you're tying your outcome to the REIT, its quality, management, track record, and financial health matter greatly. A strong, well-managed REIT reduces this risk; a weak one increases it. REIT performance and management risk — your returns and value depending on the REIT's performance and management (outside your control), with the risk that the REIT underperforms or has problems — is a key risk of the 721 exchange. It makes evaluating the REIT's quality essential before converting. Understanding this risk underscores that you're betting on the REIT, so you should choose a strong one. The dependence on the REIT's performance is a significant risk, mitigated by careful REIT selection but never eliminated.

sections.heading: Liquidity and conversion-tax risk
paras: A fourth set of risks involves liquidity and the conversion tax. While the 721 exchange offers a path to liquidity (converting OP units to REIT shares), this liquidity has limitations and costs. First, the conversion-tax risk: converting units to shares triggers the deferred gain (taxable), so accessing liquidity beyond the deferral has a tax cost — you can't access your full value potentially tax-free. This means the liquidity is real but taxed.

Second, liquidity limitations: OP units have a holding period before conversion, and the liquidity of the resulting shares depends on the REIT type — a publicly-traded REIT offers robust share liquidity, but a non-traded REIT offers limited (program-based) liquidity. So if you end up in a non-traded REIT, your liquidity may be more constrained than expected. The liquidity isn't guaranteed to be immediate or robust.

These mean the 721's liquidity, while a benefit, comes with the tax cost (conversion triggers gain) and potential limitations (holding period, non-traded constraints). So you shouldn't assume easy, free liquidity — accessing your wealth has a tax cost and may be constrained. Liquidity and conversion-tax risk — the conversion triggering tax (so liquidity isn't free) and liquidity limitations (the holding period, and limited liquidity for non-traded REITs) — are risks to understand about the 721's liquidity. The liquidity is real but taxed and potentially constrained, not easy and free. Understanding these risks tempers the liquidity benefit with realism: accessing your wealth has costs and limits. The liquidity-and-tax risk means the 721's liquidity should be understood as taxed and potentially constrained, not unlimited free access.

sections.heading: Market, share-price, and valuation risk
paras: A fifth risk is market, share-price, and valuation risk — the value of your holding can fluctuate. For a publicly-traded REIT, the REIT's share price (which your units convert into, and which reflects your units' value) fluctuates with the market — so your holding's value can rise and fall with REIT market conditions, interest rates, and investor sentiment. This share-price volatility is a risk: your holding's value isn't stable.

For a non-traded REIT, there's valuation risk — the shares aren't market-priced, so their value is determined by the REIT's periodic valuations (which may be less transparent or timely than market pricing). So you face uncertainty about the true value of a non-traded REIT holding, and the valuations may not reflect real-time conditions. The valuation risk is a different but real concern for non-traded REITs.

Both forms — share-price volatility (traded) and valuation uncertainty (non-traded) — mean your holding's value is subject to market and valuation risk, not fixed. Combined with the broad real estate market risk (the REIT's properties are exposed to real estate cycles), your holding's value can decline. faq.q: What are the main risks of a 721 exchange?
a: The one-way commitment risk (generally irreversible loss of 1031 eligibility, which can lock you in), loss of control (becoming a passive investor dependent on the REIT), REIT performance and management risk (your returns depend on the REIT), liquidity and conversion-tax risk (accessing liquidity triggers tax and may be limited), market/valuation risk (your holding's value can fluctuate), and fees, complexity, and sponsor risk. None necessarily outweighs the benefits, but you should understand them all before committing to this significant, generally irreversible transaction.

faq.q: What's the biggest risk of a 721 exchange?
a: The one-way commitment risk — the move into REIT ownership is generally irreversible (you lose 1031 eligibility and can't potentially tax-free return to direct real estate), so it can lock you in even if your circumstances or preferences change. This is the most significant risk because it's structural and permanent. If you later wish you'd stayed in direct real estate, you can't get back potentially tax-free. This is why being certain before committing is essential. The irreversibility makes the 721 exchange a decision to approach with full conviction.

faq.q: Do I lose control in a 721 exchange?
a: Yes — converting to REIT ownership makes you a passive investor, with the REIT controlling the real estate (management, leasing, financing, buy/sell decisions). You have no say in the property decisions and little recourse if you disagree with the REIT's choices. So you trade control of your own real estate for a passive stake in the REIT's decisions. For owners who value control, this is a significant drawback; for owners ready to step back (wanting passivity), it's acceptable. The loss of control's weight depends on how much you value controlling your real estate.

faq.q: What if the REIT performs poorly?
a: Your returns and your holding's value depend on the REIT's performance and management, so a poorly-managed or underperforming REIT directly harms you — its poor decisions, struggling portfolio, or financial difficulties hurt your distributions and your units'/shares' value, with little you can do (you're a passive investor). This is the REIT performance and management risk. It makes evaluating the REIT's quality, management, track record, and financial health essential before converting, since you're tying your outcome to the REIT. Choosing a strong REIT mitigates (but doesn't eliminate) this risk.

faq.q: Is the 721's liquidity risky?
a: It has costs and limitations. Converting OP units to shares (to access liquidity) triggers the deferred gain (taxable), so liquidity isn't free. And the liquidity depends on the REIT type — a publicly-traded REIT offers robust share liquidity, but a non-traded REIT offers limited, program-based liquidity (so your liquidity may be more constrained than expected). Plus there's a holding period before conversion. So the 721's liquidity is real but taxed and potentially limited — don't assume easy, free access to your wealth. Understand the tax cost and the REIT type's liquidity.

faq.q: Can my holding lose value after a 721 exchange?
a: Yes — your holding's value is subject to market and valuation risk. For a publicly-traded REIT, the share price (reflecting your holding's value) fluctuates with the market, interest rates, and sentiment, so it can decline. For a non-traded REIT, the valuation (set by periodic appraisals) carries uncertainty. Plus the REIT's properties face broad real estate market risk (cycles, rates). So the 721 exchange doesn't guarantee a stable value — your holding can decline with market and real estate conditions. The conversion doesn't eliminate market risk.

faq.q: Are there fees in a 721 exchange?
a: Yes — the transaction costs and the REIT's ongoing fees and expenses (management fees, etc.) reduce your net returns, as with any managed investment. The fee structure varies by REIT and should be evaluated. The fees are a drag on returns and a drawback to understand. Beyond fees, the 721 exchange's complexity (the partnership contribution, securities, tax mechanics, documentation) requires professional guidance (a cost and effort). So fees and complexity are practical drawbacks accompanying the structural risks. Understand the specific REIT's fees when evaluating a 721 exchange.

faq.q: What is sponsor risk?
a: The risk tied to the REIT's sponsor and management — you're relying on them, so their integrity, competence, and financial health matter to your investment. A problematic sponsor (poor management, conflicts of interest, or financial trouble) is a risk. Evaluating the sponsor's track record, reputation, and financial strength is part of mitigating this risk. Since the 721 exchange ties your outcome to the REIT and its sponsor, the sponsor's quality is a key consideration. Sponsor risk is a real drawback, mitigated by careful evaluation of the sponsor before converting.

faq.q: Do these risks mean I shouldn't do a 721 exchange?
a: Not necessarily — the risks are real but must be weighed against the benefits (deferral, diversification, liquidity, passivity, estate planning). For owners ready to commit to REIT ownership (accepting the one-way nature, loss of control, and REIT dependence), the benefits may well outweigh the risks. For owners who value control and flexibility, the risks may be dealbreakers. So the risks inform the decision, they don't automatically disqualify the 721 exchange. Understanding them ensures you decide with eyes open, weighing the real drawbacks against the benefits for your situation.

faq.q: How can I mitigate the 721 exchange's risks?
a: Be certain before committing (addressing the one-way risk), choose a strong, well-managed REIT with a sound sponsor (mitigating performance and sponsor risk), prefer a publicly-traded REIT if liquidity matters (addressing liquidity risk), understand the fees, plan conversions to manage the tax, and work with professionals (handling the complexity). Diversifying isn't possible within one conversion, but evaluating the REIT's own diversification helps. So careful REIT selection, certainty, and professional guidance mitigate the risks — though they can't eliminate them. Mitigation reduces but doesn't remove the risks.

faq.q: Are non-traded REITs riskier in a 721 exchange?
a: They carry particular risks — more limited liquidity (program-based, not market-traded), valuation uncertainty (periodic appraisals rather than market pricing), and often higher fees. So a non-traded REIT can be riskier on liquidity and valuation than a publicly-traded one. However, non-traded REITs also have potential merits depending on the offering. If liquidity and transparent valuation matter to you, a publicly-traded REIT may be preferable. Understand the specific REIT type's risks — non-traded REITs warrant extra scrutiny on liquidity, valuation, and fees. FINRA has cautioned investors to carefully review non-traded REITs.

faq.q: Should I get professional advice on the risks?
a: Yes — given the 721 exchange's significant, generally irreversible nature and its multiple risks (structural, performance, liquidity, market, fees, sponsor), you should assess the risks with professional guidance: a financial advisor (suitability and risk evaluation), your CPA (the tax risks), and your attorney (the structuring and documentation). The complexity and consequences make professional advice essential for understanding and weighing the risks. Don't evaluate the 721 exchange's risks alone — professional guidance ensures you understand them fully and decide soundly. We help you assess the risks candidly as part of the decision.

faq.q: How do the risks compare to keeping my property?
a: Keeping your property carries its own risks — concentration risk (your wealth in one property), management burden, illiquidity, and exposure to that property's specific fate (a tenant leaving, local decline). The 721 exchange trades these for different risks (REIT dependence, the one-way commitment, market/valuation risk). So it's not risk versus no-risk; it's one risk profile (concentrated, self-managed direct property) versus another (diversified, passively-held REIT ownership). The 721 reduces concentration risk and management burden but adds REIT-dependence and one-way-commitment risk. Weigh which risk profile fits your situation and comfort better.

faq.q: Are the risks different for a publicly-traded vs. non-traded REIT?
a: Yes — a publicly-traded REIT carries share-price volatility (market fluctuations) but offers robust liquidity and transparent pricing. A non-traded REIT carries valuation uncertainty (periodic appraisals rather than market pricing), more limited liquidity (program-based), and often higher fees — but avoids daily market volatility. So the risk profiles differ: traded REITs have market/price risk but liquidity and transparency; non-traded REITs have valuation and liquidity risk but less daily volatility. FINRA has specifically cautioned investors to review non-traded REITs carefully. Consider which risk profile (traded or non-traded) fits your needs when evaluating a 721 exchange.

title: 721 Exchange Risks: REIT Underperformance
lead: A key risk of a 721 exchange is REIT underperformance — because your outcome depends on the REIT, its underperformance directly hurts your returns and your holding's value, and the one-way nature means you can't easily exit. This guide explains the underperformance risk, what drives REIT performance, the impact on you, and how to mitigate the risk.

One of the most important risks to understand before a 721 exchange is REIT underperformance. When you transition into a REIT, your financial outcome — your distributions, your holding's value, and your returns — becomes tied to that REIT's performance. If the REIT underperforms (poor returns, declining value, reduced distributions), you bear the consequences directly. And because the 721 exchange is generally a one-way, largely irreversible move, you can't easily exit if the REIT disappoints (without triggering the deferred gain by converting and selling). So the risk of REIT underperformance is significant and largely unavoidable once you've committed. Understanding this risk — what drives REIT performance, the impact on you, and how to mitigate it (mainly through careful REIT selection) — is essential. This guide explains the 721 exchange risk of REIT underperformance.
takeaways: REIT underperformance is a key risk — your outcome depends on the REIT, so its poor performance hurts your income and value.
Performance is driven by the portfolio, management, financial structure, and broader factors (markets, rates, economy) — all outside your control.
You can't easily exit an underperforming REIT (the one-way nature), so the risk is largely unavoidable once committed.
Mitigate primarily through careful REIT selection upfront, plus the diversification within the REIT (which cushions single-property problems).

sections.heading: The risk of REIT underperformance
paras: The risk of REIT underperformance is that, after a 721 exchange, your outcome depends on the REIT — and if the REIT performs poorly, your returns and your holding's value suffer. Unlike a direct property owner who controls their property's performance (through their management), as a passive REIT investor you're dependent on the REIT's performance, which is outside your control. So if the REIT underperforms, you bear it, with no ability to fix it.

This is a fundamental risk of the 721 exchange — and one of several drawbacks worth weighing — because you've traded control of your own property's outcome for dependence on the REIT's. A well-performing REIT rewards you; an underperforming one hurts you, regardless of your wishes. So the underperformance risk is inherent in the transition into passive REIT ownership.

The risk is heightened by the one-way nature — you can't easily exit if the REIT underperforms, so you're stuck with the underperforming REIT (unless you convert and sell, triggering the tax). So the risk is both significant (your outcome depends on the REIT) and hard to escape (the one-way nature). sections.heading: What drives REIT performance
paras: Understanding what drives REIT performance helps you assess the underperformance risk. REIT performance depends on several factors: the portfolio's performance (the properties' income, occupancy, and value — driven by the real estate markets, the properties' quality, and tenant performance), the management's decisions (acquisitions, dispositions, financing, strategy — good decisions help, poor ones hurt), and the financial structure (leverage, debt costs — excessive debt or rising rates can pressure performance).

Broader factors also drive performance: the real estate market conditions (cycles, supply-demand, the sectors the REIT is in), interest rates (affecting borrowing costs and, for traded REITs, share prices — see our interest-rate guide), and the economy (affecting tenants and demand). So REIT performance reflects the properties, the management, the financial structure, and the broader environment.

Underperformance can result from any of these — weak properties, poor management decisions, excessive leverage, adverse markets, rising rates, or economic downturns. So the drivers of performance are also the potential sources of underperformance. So accept that some underperformance risk comes with the 721 exchange, mitigate it through careful selection, and weigh it against the benefits — it's a real, partly-unavoidable risk to factor into your decision.

faq.q: Would a partial 721 exchange reduce the underperformance risk?
a: It could, somewhat — by transitioning only some of your real estate into the REIT (a partial approach) and keeping some in direct ownership, you'd reduce your concentration in the single REIT (spreading your risk between the REIT and your retained property). So a partial transition limits your exposure to any one REIT's underperformance. However, it also limits the 721's benefits (passivity, diversification) to the contributed portion. So a partial approach is one way to reduce the single-REIT underperformance risk, at the cost of fully realizing the 721's benefits. Whether it's feasible depends on your situation. We help you weigh a full versus partial transition, considering the risk-reduction trade-off.

title: 721 Exchange Tax Benefits: Deferral & Estate Planning
lead: A 721 exchange offers three core benefits that make it a compelling exit from direct real estate: tax deferral (under Section 721), diversification (transforming a single property into a stake in a REIT's portfolio), and estate planning (the step-up at death and easy divisibility among heirs). This guide explains each benefit, plus the bonus benefits of passive income and liquidity, and weighs them against the trade-offs.

Sell a long-held building outright and the combined federal capital gains, state, depreciation-recapture, and NIIT bill can take a third or more of the gain. The 721 exchange defers all of it, and in the same step moves a property owner who is ready to exit direct real estate into a diversified REIT portfolio. In a single tax-deferred transition, it delivers three core benefits: deferral of the capital gains tax, diversification (converting your concentrated single-property holding into a stake in a REIT's broad portfolio), and estate-planning advantages (the step-up in basis at death, plus the ease of dividing REIT units among heirs). It can also provide passive income (distributions on your units, which are not guaranteed) and a potential path to liquidity (converting units to REIT shares, subject to lock-ups and, for non-traded REITs, limited redemption programs). This guide explains the 721 exchange's tax benefits — deferral, diversification, and estate planning — plus the bonus benefits, and weighs them against the trade-offs and risks.
takeaways: The 721 exchange delivers three core benefits in one transition: tax deferral, diversification, and estate planning.
Deferral (Section 721) preserves your full capital by avoiding the four-layer tax a sale would trigger.
Diversification transforms a concentrated single property into an instant stake in the REIT's broad portfolio.
Estate planning — the step-up at death (erasing the gain) and divisible units (easing the transfer) — is often the most compelling benefit; passive income and liquidity are valuable bonuses.

sections.heading: The three core benefits
paras: The 721 exchange's appeal rests on three core benefits that work together. First, tax deferral — under Section 721, contributing your property to a REIT's operating partnership for units defers the capital gains tax, just as a 1031 defers it. You don't lose a portion of your gain to taxes at the transition. Second, diversification — your single property becomes a stake in the REIT's entire portfolio, spreading your risk across many properties, types, and markets. Third, estate planning — the OP units receive a step-up in basis at death (which may reduce or eliminate the deferred gain under current law) and are easily divided among heirs.

These three benefits are interrelated and reinforcing. The deferral preserves your full capital (no tax leakage), which then gets diversified across the REIT's portfolio (reducing risk), and ultimately can pass to heirs tax-efficiently (via the step-up). In a single transition, it combines tax deferral, diversification, and estate benefits — the combination that distinguishes it from other exit options.

Compared to alternatives, this combination stands out. A taxable sale gives diversification and liquidity but loses the tax (no deferral). A 1031 gives deferral but keeps you in direct (concentrated, illiquid) real estate. The 721 gives deferral and diversification (and liquidity and estate benefits) together. The three core benefits — tax deferral, diversification, and estate planning, working together in a single transition — are the foundation of the 721 exchange's appeal. Understanding how these benefits combine (deferral preserving capital, diversification reducing risk, estate planning easing transfer) shows why the 721 exchange is compelling for the right owner. The rest of this guide examines each benefit in depth, plus the bonus benefits and the trade-offs. The three core benefits together define the 721 exchange's value proposition.

sections.heading: Tax deferral
paras: Tax deferral is the foundational benefit of the 721 exchange. Under Section 721, contributing your property to the REIT's operating partnership in exchange for OP units is tax-deferred — you don't recognize the capital gain at the contribution. This matters because a taxable sale of appreciated real estate triggers the four-layer tax (federal capital gains up to 20%, depreciation recapture up to 25%, the 3.8% NIIT, and state tax), which under 2026 federal rates can total a third or more of the gain depending on your income level, state of residence, and individual circumstances. The 721 exchange defers all of this.

The deferral preserves your full capital for reinvestment (in the REIT's portfolio). Instead of losing, say, a third of your gain to taxes and diversifying only the after-tax remainder, you transition your full pre-tax value into the REIT, keeping all of it working. This is the same compounding dynamic behind a 1031 — keeping the full pre-tax amount invested may enhance compounding compared with paying the tax and reinvesting only the remainder, although actual results depend on the REIT's investment performance, which is not guaranteed.

The deferral continues as long as you hold the OP units, and can become permanent through the step-up at death (discussed under estate planning). So the deferral isn't just a one-time benefit; it persists, and can ultimately eliminate the gain entirely. Tax deferral — Section 721 deferring the four-layer tax on contribution, preserving your full capital for diversified reinvestment, continuing while you hold the units and potentially eliminated by the step-up — is the foundational 721 benefit. It keeps your full value working in the REIT's portfolio, the same way a 1031 keeps it working in replacement real estate. Understanding the deferral's value (avoiding the substantial tax a sale would trigger) is the starting point for appreciating the 721 exchange, since the deferral is what enables the other benefits to apply to your full, untaxed capital.
A taxable sale can lose a third or more of your gain to the four-layer tax; the 721 exchange defers all of it, transitioning your full pre-tax value into the REIT's diversified portfolio.

sections.heading: Diversification
paras: Diversification is a benefit the 721 exchange offers that a 1031 into a single property can't match as easily. When you contribute your property for OP units, you transform a concentrated single-property holding into a stake in the REIT's entire portfolio — which typically holds many properties across different types (apartments, retail, industrial, office, etc.) and geographic markets. So your risk, formerly concentrated in one property (one location, one tenant base, one local economy), is spread across the REIT's diversified holdings.

This diversification may reduce concentration risk. A single property is exposed to property-specific risks (a major tenant leaving, local market decline, property damage), which can severely impact a concentrated owner. The REIT's diversified portfolio spreads these risks — one property's problem affects only a small portion of the REIT's value, cushioning the impact. So the 721 exchange may reduce the concentration risk that single-property (or few-property) owners face. Diversification does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market.

The diversification is also instant and comprehensive. Rather than building diversification gradually (acquiring multiple properties over time, as in serial 1031 exchanges), the 721 exchange instantly gives you a stake in the REIT's already-diversified portfolio. And it's professionally managed diversification — the REIT's team manages the portfolio. Diversification — transforming a concentrated single property into an instant, comprehensive, professionally-managed stake in the REIT's diversified portfolio — is a core 721 benefit that reduces the concentration risk single-property owners face. Unlike the gradual diversification of serial 1031 exchanges, the 721 provides instant, broad diversification. Understanding the diversification benefit shows why the 721 exchange appeals to owners concentrated in one property who want to spread their risk without the work of assembling a diversified portfolio themselves. The diversification is a key advantage of the 721 over staying in direct real estate.

sections.heading: Estate planning
paras: Estate planning is often the most compelling 721 benefit for older owners, centering on the step-up in basis and the divisibility of units. The step-up: under current law, if you hold your OP units until death, your heirs may receive a stepped-up basis (reset to fair market value at your death), which can reduce or eliminate the deferred gain. This benefit depends on the operating partnership's tax elections (generally a Section 754 election), the estate's circumstances, and future law, and estate tax may still apply. Subject to those conditions, the gain you deferred through the 721 exchange (and any further appreciation) may pass to your heirs free of the income tax that a sale would have triggered — a wealth-transfer tool that can address decades of deferred gain. Consult your own tax and estate advisors.

The divisibility of OP units is the second estate benefit. A single property is hard to divide among multiple heirs (you can't easily split a building four ways), often forcing a sale or creating co-ownership disputes. OP units, by contrast, are easily divisible — you can leave specific numbers of units to each heir, cleanly dividing your real estate wealth without forcing a sale or creating shared-property complications. So the 721 exchange simplifies estate division.

Together, the step-up (which may eliminate the deferred gain under current law) and the divisibility (easing the division) make the 721 exchange well-suited to estate planning. An owner can defer the gain during life (earning income on the units, though distributions are not guaranteed), pass the units to heirs at death (where the step-up may eliminate the gain, subject to the partnership's tax elections and any applicable estate tax), and have the units divide cleanly among the heirs. Estate planning — the step-up at death that may eliminate the deferred gain, plus the easy divisibility of OP units among heirs — makes the 721 exchange a useful wealth-transfer tool, often the most compelling benefit for older owners. The combination of erasing the gain (step-up) and easing the division (divisible units) addresses two major estate challenges. Understanding the estate benefits shows why the 721 exchange is especially attractive for owners focused on passing real estate wealth to heirs tax-efficiently and cleanly. The estate-planning advantages are a defining strength of the 721 exchange.

sections.heading: Passive income and liquidity
paras: Beyond the three core benefits, the 721 exchange offers passive income and liquidity — important bonus benefits. Passive income: OP units pay distributions (comparable to the REIT's dividends), so you may earn regular income from the REIT's portfolio without any management work. Distributions are not guaranteed and may be reduced or suspended at the REIT's discretion, and may include a return of capital. For an owner exiting active property management, this passive income replaces the active rental income with hands-off distributions — you keep earning real estate income, but without the work of being a landlord.

Liquidity: OP units are convertible into REIT shares, and for publicly-traded REITs those shares can be sold on the market in portions. Conversion is typically subject to lock-up periods and triggers the deferred gain, and most 721/UPREIT programs reached through DSTs involve non-traded REITs, whose liquidity is limited to share-repurchase programs that the board may modify or suspend. Investors should be prepared to hold indefinitely. Where available, this offers more flexibility than direct real estate (illiquid, all-or-nothing): you can convert and sell portions of your holding over time as you need cash, recognizing the gain on what you convert. So a 721 exchange can offer some liquidity that direct real estate can't, though that liquidity is limited and not assured.

These bonus benefits enhance the core three. The passive income suits owners stepping back from management; the liquidity suits owners wanting flexibility to access their wealth over time. Together with the deferral, diversification, and estate benefits, they round out the 721 exchange's value. Passive income and liquidity — hands-off distributions on your units and a path to liquidity via convertible shares — are valuable bonus benefits of the 721 exchange, complementing the three core benefits. The passive income replaces active landlording with hands-off income, and the liquidity provides flexibility direct real estate lacks. Understanding these bonus benefits completes the picture of the 721 exchange's advantages: deferral, diversification, estate planning, passive income, and liquidity, all in one transition. Together they make the 721 exchange a comprehensive solution for the right owner.

sections.heading: Weighing the benefits against trade-offs
paras: The 721 exchange's benefits come with trade-offs that should be weighed honestly. The main trade-off is the loss of control and flexibility — you give up direct ownership control (the REIT manages the portfolio) and the ability to do another 1031 (OP units aren't real property, so the 721 is generally a one-way move). So the benefits come at the cost of becoming a passive REIT investor committed to that path, rather than a direct property owner who can keep trading.

Other considerations include dependence on the REIT's management and performance (your returns depend on the REIT, not your own decisions), the tax triggered when you convert units to shares (the deferral ends on conversion, unless you hold until death), and, for the units' value, exposure to the REIT's share price (for public REITs, market volatility affects your holding's value once converted, and the units' value tracks the REIT). So the benefits aren't free; they come with these trade-offs.

Whether the benefits outweigh the trade-offs depends on your goals. For an owner who wants diversification, liquidity, passivity, and estate benefits, and is ready to give up control and the ability to 1031 (committing to REIT ownership), the benefits clearly outweigh the trade-offs. For an owner who values control and flexibility (wanting to keep trading real estate), the trade-offs may not be worth it. Weighing the benefits against the trade-offs — the deferral, diversification, estate, income, and liquidity benefits versus the loss of control and flexibility, dependence on the REIT, and the conversion tax — is essential to deciding whether the 721 exchange is right for you. The benefits are compelling for owners ready to transition into passive REIT ownership; the trade-offs matter most for those who value direct control. Understanding both sides lets you make an informed decision about whether the 721 exchange's benefits fit your goals. The decision turns on weighing these benefits against the trade-offs for your situation.

title: 721 Exchange Timeline and Closing Process
lead: Unlike a 1031 exchange with its strict 45- and 180-day deadlines, a 721 exchange has no fixed statutory deadlines — its timeline is driven by the parties and the transaction. This guide explains the typical timeline phases: due diligence and valuation, documentation and negotiation, the closing (contribution), and the post-closing holding period before conversion.

Investors familiar with the 1031 exchange's strict deadlines (45 days to identify, 180 to close) often wonder about the 721 exchange's timeline. The good news is that a 721 exchange has no fixed statutory deadlines — because it's a contribution of property to a partnership (under Section 721), not a like-kind exchange, it isn't bound by the 1031's 45/180-day rules. Instead, the 721 exchange's timeline is driven by the parties and the transaction: finding a willing REIT, conducting due diligence, valuing the property, negotiating and documenting the contribution, and closing. After closing, there's typically a holding period before you can convert OP units to shares. This guide walks through each phase: due diligence and valuation, documentation and negotiation, the closing, and the post-closing holding period.
takeaways: A 721 exchange has no fixed statutory deadlines (unlike the 1031's 45/180-day rules) — its timeline is driven by the parties.
Typical phases: finding a willing REIT, due diligence and valuation, documentation and negotiation, closing, then the holding period.
Due diligence and valuation (the REIT evaluating the property, the parties agreeing on value) and documentation (especially tax protection) take significant time.
The closing (the contribution of property for OP units) consummates the exchange; a holding period (often ~1 year) follows before conversion.

sections.heading: No fixed statutory deadlines
paras: A fundamental point about the 721 exchange timeline is that it has no fixed statutory deadlines, unlike the 1031 exchange. The 1031's 45-day identification and 180-day completion deadlines are specific to like-kind exchanges — they govern the deferred exchange of real property for real property. A 721 exchange is different: it's a contribution of property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest (under Section 721), not a like-kind exchange, so the 1031's deadlines don't apply.

This means the 721 exchange isn't bound by the time pressure that makes 1031 exchanges stressful. There's no clock requiring you to identify a target within 45 days or close within 180 days. Instead, the timeline is driven by the parties (you and the REIT) and the transaction's requirements (due diligence, valuation, negotiation, documentation). So the 721 exchange's timeline is more flexible, set by the deal rather than statutory deadlines.

This is generally an advantage: no deadline pressure, so the transaction can proceed at the pace the parties need. (If you reach the 721 via the 1031-then-721 path — a 1031 into a DST first — the 1031 portion carries the deadlines, while the later 721 exit does not.)

sections.heading: The typical timeline phases
paras: While there are no fixed deadlines, a 721 exchange typically proceeds through recognizable phases. The first is identifying a willing REIT and reaching preliminary agreement — finding a REIT that wants your property and agreeing in principle to a contribution. This phase establishes that the transaction is feasible (a willing REIT exists) and sets the framework. It can take time to find the right REIT (or to identify a DST structured for a 721 exit, in the two-step path).

The subsequent phases are due diligence and valuation (the REIT evaluates your property and you agree on its value), documentation and negotiation (drafting and negotiating the contribution agreement, tax protection, and other documents), and the closing (the actual contribution of the property for OP units). After closing comes the holding period (before you can convert units to shares). So the phases run from finding a REIT through closing and into the holding period.

The duration of each phase varies by transaction — there's no set schedule, so the timeline depends on the property, the REIT, the complexity, and the parties' pace. A straightforward transaction might move quickly; a complex one (with negotiation, due diligence, or structuring issues) takes longer.

A 721 exchange moves through phases — finding a willing REIT, due diligence and valuation, documentation and negotiation, closing, then the holding period — but without the fixed statutory clock a 1031 imposes.

sections.heading: Due diligence and valuation phase
paras: The due diligence and valuation phase is a substantial part of the timeline, where the property is evaluated and its value agreed. The REIT conducts due diligence on your property — examining its physical condition, title, financials (income and expenses), leases, environmental status, and other factors — to confirm it wants the property and on what terms. This due diligence is thorough (as the REIT is acquiring the property into its portfolio), so it takes time.

Concurrently, you and the REIT determine the property's value, which sets the number of OP units you'll receive. The valuation is typically negotiated, informed by appraisals and the property's financials. Reaching agreement on value is a key milestone, as it determines the economic terms of your contribution (your units' value for your property). The valuation phase can involve back-and-forth negotiation.
This phase is important because it confirms the transaction (the REIT's due diligence) and sets the economics (the valuation). Both must be completed before proceeding to documentation and closing.

sections.heading: Documentation and negotiation
paras: After due diligence and valuation, the documentation and negotiation phase prepares the legal agreements for the contribution. The key documents include the contribution agreement (effecting the property's contribution to the operating partnership for OP units), the tax protection agreement (if negotiated, protecting your deferred gain from being triggered by a partnership sale for a period), and the partnership agreement terms (governing your rights as a limited partner).

This phase involves negotiating the terms of these documents — the contribution's specifics, the tax protection's scope and duration, and your rights as a unit holder. The negotiation can be significant, especially for the tax protection (an important term for you) and any property-specific or deal-specific provisions. Your attorney and the REIT's counsel draft and negotiate these documents, with your advisors' input.

Getting the documentation right matters, since it establishes your units, rights, and protections for the long term. This phase takes time, but it is essential to a well-structured contribution and warrants your attorney's close attention.

sections.heading: The closing (contribution)
paras: The closing is where the timeline lands: the actual contribution of your property to the operating partnership in exchange for OP units. At the closing, you transfer ownership of your property to the operating partnership, and the partnership issues you the agreed number of OP units. This is the Section 721 transaction — tax-deferred, with the documents (contribution agreement, etc.) executed and the transfer completed.

The closing effects your transition from property owner to OP unit holder. After it, your property is part of the REIT's portfolio (held by the operating partnership), and you hold OP units representing your stake. The deferral is in place (no gain recognized), and you become eligible to receive any distributions the operating partnership declares; distributions are not guaranteed and may be reduced or suspended. So the closing is the moment the 721 exchange is consummated.

The closing itself is typically a defined event (the execution of documents and transfer), the endpoint of the preceding phases (due diligence, valuation, documentation). Once the parties have completed those phases and agreed on terms, the closing finalizes the contribution and you become an OP unit holder.

sections.heading: After closing: the holding period
paras: After the closing, the timeline continues with the holding period before you can convert OP units to REIT shares. As discussed in our liquidity guide, OP units typically have a holding period (often around one year, varying by REIT) before conversion to shares is allowed. So immediately after closing, you hold your units (earning distributions, deferring the gain) but can't yet convert them to shares for liquidity.

This post-closing holding period is part of the overall timeline to consider, especially if you anticipate needing liquidity. During the holding period, you're a passive unit holder enjoying the distributions and deferral, but the conversion-to-shares liquidity isn't yet available. After the holding period, the conversion option opens, and you can convert (triggering tax) as you wish.
Beyond the holding period, your timeline is open-ended: you can hold the units indefinitely (for income and deferral, toward the step-up) or convert (gradually or fully) as your needs dictate.

a: It varies, since there are no fixed deadlines — the timeline is driven by the parties and the transaction. It can take weeks to months for the contribution, depending on finding a willing REIT, the due diligence, the valuation negotiation, and the documentation. A straightforward transaction might move quickly; a complex one (with negotiation or structuring issues) takes longer. After closing, there's a holding period (often ~1 year) before you can convert units to shares. So the active transaction varies in length, and the post-closing holding period adds time before conversion liquidity.

faq.q: What are the phases of a 721 exchange?
a: Identifying a willing REIT (and reaching preliminary agreement), due diligence and valuation (the REIT evaluates your property and you agree on its value), documentation and negotiation (the contribution agreement, tax protection, partnership terms), the closing (the contribution of property for OP units), and the post-closing holding period (before conversion to shares). These phases run from finding a REIT through closing and into the holding period. The durations are flexible (no fixed deadlines), depending on the property, REIT, complexity, and parties' pace.

faq.q: What happens during due diligence?
a: The REIT examines your property — its physical condition, title, financials (income and expenses), leases, environmental status, and other factors — to confirm it wants the property and on what terms. This is thorough (the REIT is acquiring the property into its portfolio), so it takes time. Concurrently, you and the REIT determine the property's value (informed by appraisals and financials), setting the OP units you'll receive. So due diligence confirms the transaction and, with the valuation, establishes its economics. It's a substantial phase where much of the timeline is spent.

faq.q: How is the closing of a 721 exchange handled?
a: At the closing, you transfer ownership of your property to the operating partnership, and the partnership issues you the agreed OP units — the Section 721 transaction, tax-deferred, with the documents (contribution agreement, etc.) executed and the transfer completed. The closing effects your transition from property owner to OP unit holder: afterward, your property is in the REIT's portfolio, and you hold OP units (with the deferral in place, earning distributions). The closing is the culmination of the preceding phases (due diligence, valuation, documentation), finalizing the contribution.

faq.q: Is there a holding period after closing?
a: Yes — OP units typically have a holding period (often around one year, varying by REIT) before you can convert them to REIT shares. So immediately after closing, you hold your units (earning distributions, deferring the gain) but can't yet convert them to shares for liquidity. After the holding period, the conversion option opens. This is important to plan for if you anticipate needing liquidity — the conversion-to-shares liquidity isn't available right after closing. Beyond the holding period, your timeline is open-ended (hold or convert as you choose).

faq.q: Why is the documentation phase important?
a: Because the documents — the contribution agreement (effecting the contribution), the tax protection agreement (protecting your deferred gain), and the partnership terms (your rights as a unit holder) — establish your units, rights, and protections for the long term. Negotiating them carefully (especially the tax protection, an important term for you) protects your interests. Your attorney and the REIT's counsel draft and negotiate these. Getting the documentation right is essential, since it governs your post-721 ownership. So the documentation phase, while it takes time, is critical to a sound contribution.

faq.q: Can the timeline be faster than a 1031?
a: It can be, since there's no deadline pressure — but it can also be slower, depending on the transaction. The 1031's deadlines (45/180 days) impose urgency but also a defined timeline. A 721 exchange has no such clock, so it proceeds at the parties' pace — which could be faster (no deadline-driven scramble) or slower (extended due diligence, negotiation). The key difference is the absence of statutory pressure, making the timeline flexible. So the 721 exchange isn't inherently faster or slower; its timeline depends on the parties and transaction, without the 1031's fixed deadlines.

faq.q: What if I'm doing the 1031-then-721 path?
a: Then the 1031 portion (into the DST) has the standard 45/180-day deadlines (since it's a like-kind exchange), while the later 721 exit (the DST being acquired by the REIT) doesn't have those deadlines. So in the two-step path, you must meet the 1031 deadlines for the DST step (45 days to identify the DST, 180 to close), but the 721 exit's timing is open-ended (governed by the DST/REIT structure, not statutory deadlines). So the deadlines apply to the first step (the 1031 into the DST), not the second (the 721 into the REIT). Plan the 1031 step's deadlines carefully.

faq.q: Does the absence of deadlines make a 721 easier?
a: In one sense yes — the absence of the 1031's deadline pressure removes a major source of stress (no scramble to identify and close within 45/180 days). So the 721 exchange's timeline is less pressured. However, the 721 exchange is more complex in other ways (finding a willing REIT, the securities nature, the negotiation and documentation), so it's not necessarily 'easier' overall — it trades the deadline pressure for other complexities. The absence of deadlines is an advantage on timeline flexibility, but the 721 has its own demands. It's less deadline-pressured but not simpler overall.

faq.q: How do I plan for the 721 exchange timeline?
a: Recognize the absence of fixed deadlines (the timeline is parties-driven), allow time for each phase (finding a REIT, due diligence, valuation, documentation, closing), plan for the post-closing holding period before conversion liquidity, and work with professionals (advisor, CPA, attorney) to manage the process. Set realistic expectations (the timeline varies by transaction), and if liquidity timing matters, account for the holding period. We help you navigate the phases and set realistic timeline expectations, so the 721 exchange proceeds smoothly from finding a REIT through closing and beyond.

faq.q: Can a 721 exchange fall through during the process?
a: Yes — like any negotiated transaction, a 721 exchange can fall through if the parties don't reach agreement (on value, tax protection, or other terms), if the REIT's due diligence reveals problems with the property, or if circumstances change. Unlike a 1031 (where a failed exchange triggers the tax because you've already sold), a standalone 721 contribution that doesn't close generally leaves you still owning your property (you haven't sold). So a 721 exchange that falls through during negotiation typically means you keep your property and pursue other options, without the tax consequences of a failed 1031. Your advisors help navigate any issues.

faq.q: Should I sell my property first or wait for the 721?
a: In a direct 721 exchange, you contribute the property to the REIT (you don't sell it separately first) — the contribution is the transaction. So you don't sell and then do a 721; the 721 contribution replaces a sale. In the 1031-then-721 path, you sell your property and 1031 into a DST (the sale and 1031 are the first step), then later the 721 exit occurs. So whether you 'sell first' depends on the path: a direct 721 contributes the property (no separate sale), while the 1031-then-721 involves selling into the DST first. Your advisors structure the appropriate path.

faq.q: Does the timeline differ for traded vs. non-traded REITs?
a: The transaction timeline (due diligence, valuation, documentation, closing) is broadly similar, but the post-closing liquidity timeline differs. For a publicly-traded REIT, after the holding period you can convert and sell shares relatively quickly (market liquidity). For a non-traded REIT, liquidity is more limited (program-based redemptions on the REIT's schedule), so accessing liquidity after conversion may take longer. So the contribution timeline is similar, but the time to access liquidity afterward depends on the REIT type. If liquidity timing matters, the traded-vs-non-traded distinction affects your post-conversion timeline, which you should factor into your planning.

title: 721 Exchange Valuation: How Your Property Is Priced
lead: In a 721 exchange, your property's value determines how many OP units you receive, so the valuation is economically critical. This guide explains why valuation matters, how your property's value is determined, how the OP unit value is set, how the units received are calculated, negotiating the valuation, and fairness considerations.

The valuation of your property is the economic heart of a 721 exchange — it determines how many OP units you receive in exchange for your property. Get a higher valuation, and you receive more units (more value); a lower valuation, and you receive fewer. So understanding how your property is priced in a 721 exchange, and ensuring a fair valuation, is critical to getting appropriate value for your property. The valuation involves determining your property's value (through appraisal and negotiation) and the OP unit value (tied to the REIT's net asset value or share price), then calculating the units you receive. This guide explains why valuation matters, how property value is determined, how unit value is set, how units received are calculated, negotiating the valuation, and fairness considerations.

title: 721 Exchange vs. 1031 Exchange: Which One Fits?
lead: Both defer your capital gains tax — but in opposite directions. A 1031 keeps you in direct real estate you can exchange again; a 721 trades it for REIT units you generally can't. Here's how to choose.

The 721 exchange and the 1031 exchange are often discussed as if they were two flavors of the same thing, because both let a real estate owner defer capital gains tax. But they pull in opposite directions. A 1031 exchange keeps you in directly owned real estate that you can exchange again and again; a 721 exchange moves you out of direct ownership and into units of a real estate investment trust, usually for good. Understanding that difference — and the one-way door at the heart of it — is the key to knowing which belongs in your plan, and when.
takeaways: A 1031 exchange swaps one investment property for like-kind real estate, preserving direct ownership and the ability to exchange again.
A 721 exchange (an 'UPREIT' transaction) contributes property to a REIT's operating partnership for OP units, deferring tax but ending future 1031s on that equity.
A 721 removes the 45- and 180-day deadlines but trades control and direct ownership for diversification and potential liquidity.
Many investors use them in sequence — 1031 now to stay flexible, 721 later to consolidate into a REIT.

sections.heading: What a 1031 exchange is
paras: A 1031 exchange, named for Section 1031 of the tax code, lets you sell real property held for investment or business and defer the capital gains tax — and depreciation recapture — by reinvesting the proceeds into "like-kind" replacement real estate. You continue to own real estate directly; the gain rides along in your carried-over basis. Crucially, you can repeat the maneuver indefinitely, rolling from property to property across decades, and if you hold the final property until death, your heirs may receive a stepped-up basis that erases the deferred gain.

The cost of that flexibility is work and discipline: you must find and close on replacement property within strict 45-day identification and 180-day completion windows, and you remain a hands-on owner unless you exchange into a passive structure like a DST. The 1031 is the workhorse of real estate tax deferral precisely because it keeps you in the driver's seat.

sections.heading: What a 721 exchange (UPREIT) is
paras: A 721 exchange takes its name from Section 721, which generally makes it potentially tax-free to contribute property to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest. In real estate, this is the UPREIT ("umbrella partnership REIT") structure: you contribute your property — or, more often today, your interest acquired through a DST — into a REIT's operating partnership, and in return you receive operating-partnership (OP) units rather than cash. The contribution defers your gain, and the OP units entitle you to distributions that track the REIT's dividends.

The trade is fundamentally different from a 1031. You are no longer a direct owner of a building; you hold a partnership interest in a diversified REIT. After a holding period, OP units can typically be converted into REIT shares or redeemed for cash — but doing so is a taxable event that triggers the deferred gain. The 721 is less a way to keep exchanging real estate than a way to exit active real estate into a passive, diversified vehicle while deferring tax on the way in.

sections.heading: The decisive difference: a one-way door
paras: If you remember one thing, remember this: a 721 exchange is generally a one-way door. Once your equity is in OP units, you cannot 1031 it back out into real estate — a partnership interest is not like-kind real property. The deferral continues only inside the REIT structure, and your future options narrow to holding the units, converting them (taxably) to shares, or redeeming them (taxably) for cash.

A 1031 exchange, by contrast, leaves every door open. You can exchange again, refinance, sell, or eventually 721 into a REIT if you choose. This asymmetry is why sequencing matters so much: you can always move from 1031-style direct ownership into a 721/REIT position later, but you cannot move back. Treating the 721 as reversible is the most consequential mistake investors make in this area.

sections.heading: Deadlines and mechanics
paras: The two also differ in how they're executed. A 1031 is an exchange run through a qualified intermediary against the clock: 45 days to identify replacement property, 180 days to close, with no routine extensions. Miss a deadline and the exchange fails. A 721, being a contribution rather than a like-kind exchange, doesn't carry those 45- and 180-day deadlines — the timing is governed by the REIT's acquisition process and any negotiated terms instead.

That difference can make a 721 feel simpler, and in pure timing terms it often is. But the simplicity is bought with the loss of optionality described above. The 1031's deadlines are a discipline; the 721's lack of them reflects that you're making a more permanent move.

sections.heading: Control, liquidity, and diversification
paras: On control, the 1031 wins for hands-on investors: you own the asset and make the decisions (unless you've chosen a passive replacement). The 721 hands control to the REIT's management — you become a passive holder with no say over individual properties.

On liquidity and diversification, the 721 generally wins. A single directly owned property is illiquid and concentrated; OP units represent a slice of a diversified REIT portfolio, and after the holding period they can be converted to shares (liquid, if the REIT is publicly traded) or redeemed. The catch is the tax cost of accessing that liquidity, and — for non-traded REITs — that "liquidity" runs through limited redemption programs rather than a public market. So the 721 offers a path to diversification and eventual liquidity that direct ownership lacks, at the price of control and the one-way commitment.

sections.heading: Repeatability and estate planning
paras: Both strategies support the "swap till you drop" estate play, but along different routes. With serial 1031 exchanges, you defer through successive properties and pass them to heirs with a stepped-up basis. With a 721, you defer into OP units and hold those until death; the step-up can likewise eliminate the deferred gain, and OP units carry a practical advantage for estates — they're far easier to divide among multiple heirs than a single building, and heirs can convert to liquid shares as needed.

Where they diverge is flexibility along the way. The 1031 path can be redirected at any sale; the 721 path, once taken, largely commits you to the REIT. For an investor whose estate plan is settled and who values divisibility and eventual liquidity for heirs, the 721 endgame is attractive; for one who wants to keep options open, repeated 1031s preserve more room to maneuver. We cover this in depth in our memo on 721 exchanges and estate planning.

sections.heading: When each one wins
paras: Reduce it to goals. A 1031 exchange wins when you want to stay in direct real estate, retain control, keep the ability to exchange again, or simply aren't ready to make a permanent move — it is the default for active investors and for anyone who wants to preserve optionality. A 721 exchange wins when you're ready to exit active ownership for good, want the diversification of a REIT portfolio, value divisibility and eventual liquidity for your estate, and accept that you're trading away future 1031 flexibility to get there.
Feature 1031 Exchange 721 Exchange
What you end up owning Direct real estate REIT operating-partnership units
Deadlines 45 / 180 days None (contribution)
Control You (or your DST sponsor) REIT management
Repeat / exchange again Yes, indefinitely No — one-way
Liquidity Low; sell the property Higher via conversion (taxable)

sections.heading: Using them in sequence: the two-step path
paras: The cleanest way to get the best of both is often to use them in order. An investor can 1031 into a DST today — staying flexible and deferring tax — and then, when that DST goes full-cycle, use a 721 exchange to roll into the sponsor's affiliated REIT for OP units. This "two-step" sequence lets you keep 1031 optionality for as long as you want it, then transition into a diversified, semi-liquid REIT position when you're genuinely ready to stop exchanging.

The sequence only runs one way, which is exactly the point: you spend your flexibility deliberately, at the moment of your choosing, rather than surrendering it up front. For many investors approaching retirement or simplification, that ordering — flexible now, permanent later — is the whole strategy.

faq.q: What's the main difference between a 721 and a 1031 exchange?
a: A 1031 keeps you in directly owned, like-kind real estate you can exchange again; a 721 contributes property to a REIT's operating partnership for OP units, deferring tax but generally ending future 1031s on that equity.

faq.q: Can I 1031 exchange out of a 721 position later?
a: Generally no. OP units are a partnership interest, not like-kind real property, so you can't 1031 them back into real estate. The 721 is a one-way move — that's why sequencing matters.

faq.q: Does a 721 exchange have 45- and 180-day deadlines?
a: No. Because it's a contribution to a partnership rather than a like-kind exchange, the 721 doesn't carry the 1031's 45- and 180-day deadlines; timing follows the REIT's acquisition process instead.

faq.q: When should I use a 1031 instead of a 721?
a: Use a 1031 when you want to stay in direct real estate, keep control, retain the ability to exchange again, or preserve flexibility. Use a 721 when you're ready to exit active ownership for a diversified REIT position permanently.

faq.q: Can I do both a 1031 and a 721?
a: Yes, often in sequence: 1031 into a DST now to defer and stay flexible, then a 721 into the affiliated REIT at full-cycle to consolidate. The order only runs one way, so you spend your flexibility deliberately.
