title: How to Evaluate a REIT: FFO, AFFO & NAV
lead: Standard net income understates how much a REIT really earns, because real estate depreciation is a large non-cash charge even as properties often appreciate. This guide explains how to evaluate a REIT using the right metrics — why earnings metrics differ for REITs, funds from operations (FFO), adjusted FFO (AFFO), net asset value (NAV), and how to put the metrics together.

Evaluating a REIT is not like evaluating an ordinary company, because the standard earnings measure — GAAP net income — systematically understates a REIT's true earning power. The culprit is depreciation: real estate depreciation is a large, non-cash accounting charge that reduces reported net income, even though real estate often appreciates rather than declines in value. As a result, sophisticated REIT analysis relies on industry-specific metrics that add back this non-cash charge and get closer to the real cash a REIT generates: FFO (funds from operations), AFFO (adjusted FFO), and NAV (net asset value). Understanding these metrics — what each measures, how they are calculated, and what they tell you — is essential to evaluating a REIT's earnings, its capacity to pay distributions, and whether its shares trade at a premium or discount to the value of its properties. This guide explains why earnings metrics differ for REITs, defines FFO, AFFO, and NAV, and shows how to put the metrics together. This is educational information, not investment advice — verify current figures and methodologies in each REIT's filings.
takeaways: GAAP net income understates REIT earnings because large non-cash real estate depreciation depresses it even as properties often appreciate.
FFO (net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales) is the Nareit-standard earnings metric; P/FFO is the REIT P/E equivalent.
AFFO refines FFO by subtracting recurring maintenance capex and straight-line rent adjustments, getting closer to true distributable cash and distribution sustainability.
NAV (per-share value of properties less liabilities) gauges premium or discount; use FFO, AFFO, and NAV together with debt and qualitative factors — no single metric suffices.

sections.heading: Why earnings metrics differ for REITs
paras: Earnings metrics differ for REITs because GAAP net income understates their true earnings, primarily due to depreciation. Under accounting rules, a REIT depreciates its buildings over time, recording a large non-cash depreciation expense that reduces reported net income each year. But real estate often holds or grows its value rather than declining — so the depreciation charge does not reflect a real economic loss in the way it might for a wasting asset like equipment. So GAAP net income is depressed by a non-cash charge that overstates the REIT's economic decline.

Because depreciation is such a large expense for a property-heavy business, GAAP net income can be a poor measure of a REIT's actual cash-generating ability — a REIT can report modest or even negative net income while generating substantial cash from its properties. So relying on net income (or a standard P/E ratio) to evaluate a REIT is misleading. This is why the industry developed metrics that add back real estate depreciation to better reflect the cash the REIT actually produces.

So earnings metrics differ for REITs because the standard net-income measure is distorted by non-cash real estate depreciation, requiring purpose-built metrics (FFO, AFFO) to gauge true earning power. Why earnings metrics differ for REITs — GAAP net income being understated by large non-cash real estate depreciation, even though real estate often appreciates, making net income and standard P/E ratios misleading for property-heavy REITs and prompting industry-specific metrics that add depreciation back — is the foundation of REIT analysis. Depreciation is the key distortion. Understanding it shows why FFO and AFFO exist. GAAP net income understates REIT earnings because large non-cash real estate depreciation depresses it even as properties appreciate — so REITs require purpose-built metrics like FFO and AFFO rather than ordinary net income or P/E.

sections.heading: Funds from operations (FFO)
paras: Funds from operations (FFO) is the foundational REIT earnings metric and the Nareit (National Association of Real Estate Investment Trust s) industry standard. FFO is calculated by taking GAAP net income, adding back real estate depreciation and amortization (the large non-cash charges that distort net income), and subtracting gains on property sales (which are one-time, not recurring operating income). So FFO = net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales (with some additional adjustments per the Nareit definition).

The logic is to strip out the non-cash depreciation distortion and the non-recurring sale gains, leaving a measure that better reflects the recurring cash earnings from the REIT's operating properties. So FFO is a far more meaningful earnings measure for a REIT than net income — it is the metric analysts and the industry use to gauge a REIT's operating performance. The P/FFO ratio (price divided by FFO per share) is the REIT equivalent of a P/E ratio, used to compare valuations; our deeper walkthrough on how to read a REIT's FFO shows where to find it in the filings.

So FFO is the standard, foundational measure of a REIT's recurring earnings, correcting net income's depreciation distortion. Funds from operations (FFO) — the Nareit-standard metric calculated as net income plus real estate depreciation and amortization minus gains on property sales, stripping out the non-cash depreciation distortion and non-recurring sale gains to reflect recurring operating cash earnings, and used via the P/FFO ratio as the REIT equivalent of P/E — is the foundational REIT earnings measure. It corrects net income's central flaw. Understanding it is the first step in REIT analysis. FFO (net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales) is the Nareit-standard REIT earnings metric, correcting net income's depreciation distortion, with P/FFO serving as the REIT's P/E equivalent.
FFO is the REIT world's answer to earnings: it strips out the non-cash depreciation that depresses net income, revealing the recurring cash a REIT's properties actually generate. P/FFO is its P/E.

sections.heading: Adjusted FFO (AFFO)
paras: Adjusted FFO (AFFO) refines FFO to get even closer to the true cash a REIT has available to distribute. While FFO adds back depreciation, it does not account for the real, recurring capital a REIT must spend to maintain its properties, or for certain accounting smoothing of rent. AFFO adjusts for these: it takes FFO and subtracts recurring maintenance capital expenditures (the ongoing capex needed to keep properties competitive) and straight-line rent adjustments (an accounting smoothing of lease income). So AFFO = FFO − recurring/maintenance capex − straight-line rent adjustments (with some variation in how REITs define it).

The result is a measure closer to the actual cash available for distribution to shareholders — because it accounts for the real, ongoing spending FFO ignores. So AFFO is often considered a better gauge of a REIT's sustainable distribution capacity than FFO, since it reflects the cash truly left over after maintaining the properties — a debate we weigh in full in AFFO vs. FFO: which metric matters more. The trade-off is that AFFO definitions vary across REITs (there is no single standardized formula), so comparisons require care.

So AFFO refines FFO by subtracting recurring capex and rent adjustments, yielding a closer estimate of distributable cash. Adjusted FFO (AFFO) — FFO minus recurring/maintenance capital expenditures and straight-line rent adjustments, accounting for the real ongoing spending FFO ignores to better reflect the cash actually available for distribution, though with definitions varying across REITs — is a refinement that gauges sustainable distribution capacity. It is closer to true distributable cash than FFO. Understanding it shows the cash-flow nuance. AFFO (FFO − recurring maintenance capex − straight-line rent adjustments) refines FFO toward true distributable cash, making it a better gauge of sustainable distribution capacity, though definitions vary across REITs.

sections.heading: Net asset value (NAV)
paras: Net asset value (NAV) measures what a REIT is worth from a balance-sheet perspective — the value of its properties net of its debts. NAV is calculated by estimating the current market value of the REIT's real estate (and other assets), subtracting its liabilities (debt and obligations), and dividing by the shares outstanding to get NAV per share. So NAV per share represents the estimated underlying value of the REIT's net assets attributable to each share.

NAV is useful for gauging whether a REIT's shares trade at a premium or a discount to the value of its properties. If a traded REIT's share price is below its NAV per share, the shares trade at a discount (potentially cheap relative to the underlying real estate); if above, at a premium — a dynamic explored further in REIT NAV premiums and discounts explained. For non-traded REITs, the periodic NAV is the basis for the share value and redemption pricing. So NAV provides an asset-based valuation reference distinct from the earnings-based FFO and AFFO.

So NAV estimates the per-share value of a REIT's net assets, helping you judge premium or discount versus the underlying real estate. Net asset value (NAV) — the estimated market value of a REIT's properties less its liabilities, divided by shares outstanding, giving a per-share asset-based value used to judge whether shares trade at a premium or discount (and to price non-traded REIT shares and redemptions) — is the asset-based complement to the earnings-based FFO and AFFO. It gauges value versus the underlying real estate. Understanding it adds the balance-sheet view. NAV (the per-share market value of a REIT's properties less liabilities) is an asset-based valuation gauge for premium or discount to the underlying real estate, complementing the earnings-based FFO and AFFO.

sections.heading: Putting the metrics together
paras: No single metric tells the whole story — sound REIT evaluation uses FFO, AFFO, and NAV together, alongside other factors. Use FFO (via P/FFO) to gauge earnings and compare valuations across REITs (the REIT P/E equivalent). Use AFFO to assess the sustainability of distributions — comparing the distribution per share to AFFO per share gives a payout ratio against true distributable cash (a payout above AFFO is a warning sign that distributions may not be sustainable). Use NAV to judge whether the shares are priced at a premium or discount to the underlying real estate.

Beyond these three, also consider the REIT's debt levels (leverage and maturity profile), property type and quality, occupancy and lease terms, management quality, and growth prospects — the metrics are tools within a broader analysis, not a substitute for it. So combine the earnings view (FFO), the distributable-cash view (AFFO and payout ratio), and the asset view (NAV), with debt and qualitative factors, for a rounded evaluation.

So putting the metrics together — FFO for earnings, AFFO for distribution sustainability, NAV for premium/discount, plus debt and qualitative factors — gives a complete picture no single metric provides. Putting the metrics together — using P/FFO to gauge earnings and valuation, the AFFO payout ratio to assess distribution sustainability, NAV to judge premium or discount, and adding debt levels and qualitative factors (property quality, management, growth) — yields a rounded REIT evaluation that no single metric delivers. The metrics are complementary tools. Understanding how to combine them is the goal. Evaluate a REIT by combining P/FFO (earnings and valuation), the AFFO payout ratio (distribution sustainability), NAV (premium or discount), and debt and qualitative factors — no single metric suffices, so use them together.

sections.heading: Payout ratios and debt levels
paras: Two further checks sharpen a REIT evaluation: the payout ratio against AFFO and the REIT's debt levels. The payout ratio — comparing the distribution per share to AFFO per share — tells you whether distributions are covered by sustainable cash flow. A payout ratio comfortably below 100% of AFFO suggests the distribution is supported by real cash with a cushion; a ratio at or above AFFO is a warning that distributions may not be sustainable and could be cut. So checking the AFFO payout ratio helps you assess distribution safety.

Debt levels — REITs use leverage, so their debt matters. Examine the leverage ratio (debt relative to assets or to a cash-flow measure), the debt-maturity schedule (when debt comes due and whether it must be refinanced in a difficult market), and interest costs. High leverage amplifies both returns and risk, and near-term maturities create refinancing risk. So a REIT's debt profile is a key part of its risk assessment, alongside the earnings and asset metrics.

So payout ratios (against AFFO) and debt levels round out the evaluation by addressing distribution safety and financial risk. Payout ratios and debt levels — the AFFO payout ratio gauging whether distributions are covered by sustainable cash (a ratio at or above AFFO being a warning), and the debt profile (leverage ratio, maturity schedule, interest costs) gauging financial risk and refinancing exposure — sharpen a REIT evaluation beyond the headline metrics. Distribution safety and leverage are central. Understanding them completes the risk view. Check the AFFO payout ratio (distribution sustainability — a ratio at or above AFFO is a warning) and the debt profile (leverage, maturities, interest costs) to assess a REIT's distribution safety and financial risk.

faq.q: Why doesn't net income work for evaluating a REIT?
a: Because GAAP net income systematically understates a REIT's true earnings, primarily due to depreciation. Under accounting rules, a REIT depreciates its buildings over time, recording a large non-cash depreciation expense that reduces reported net income each year. But real estate often holds or grows its value rather than declining — so the depreciation charge does not reflect a real economic loss the way it might for a wasting asset like equipment. Because depreciation is such a large expense for a property-heavy business, net income can be a poor measure of a REIT's actual cash-generating ability — a REIT can report modest or even negative net income while generating substantial cash. So relying on net income (or a standard P/E ratio) to evaluate a REIT is misleading. This is why the industry developed metrics like FFO and AFFO that add back real estate depreciation to better reflect the cash the REIT actually produces. So use the purpose-built REIT metrics, not ordinary net income, to evaluate a REIT's earning power.

faq.q: What is FFO?
a: FFO stands for funds from operations, the foundational REIT earnings metric and the Nareit (National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts) industry standard. FFO is calculated by taking GAAP net income, adding back real estate depreciation and amortization (the large non-cash charges that distort net income), and subtracting gains on property sales (which are one-time, not recurring operating income), with some additional adjustments per the Nareit definition. So FFO = net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales. The logic is to strip out the non-cash depreciation distortion and the non-recurring sale gains, leaving a measure that better reflects the recurring cash earnings from the REIT's operating properties. So FFO is a far more meaningful earnings measure for a REIT than net income — it is the metric analysts and the industry use to gauge operating performance. The P/FFO ratio (price divided by FFO per share) is the REIT equivalent of a P/E ratio, used to compare valuations across REITs. FFO is the first metric to learn for REIT analysis.

faq.q: How is FFO calculated?
a: FFO is calculated by starting with GAAP net income and making two main adjustments: adding back real estate depreciation and amortization, and subtracting gains (or adding back losses) on the sale of properties. The Nareit definition includes some additional adjustments, but the core formula is: FFO = net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales. Adding back depreciation corrects the central distortion (the large non-cash charge that depresses net income even though real estate often appreciates), and removing property-sale gains strips out one-time items that are not recurring operating income. The result better reflects the recurring cash earnings from the REIT's operating properties. REITs report FFO in their filings, and you can compute FFO per share by dividing by shares outstanding. So FFO is net income adjusted to add back depreciation and remove one-time sale gains — a measure of recurring operating earnings. Always check how a specific REIT defines and reconciles its FFO, since there can be minor variations, but the Nareit standard provides the common framework.

faq.q: What is AFFO and how does it differ from FFO?
a: AFFO stands for adjusted FFO, a refinement of FFO that gets closer to the true cash a REIT has available to distribute. While FFO adds back depreciation, it does not account for the real, recurring capital a REIT must spend to maintain its properties, or for certain accounting smoothing of rent. AFFO adjusts for these: it takes FFO and subtracts recurring maintenance capital expenditures (the ongoing capex needed to keep properties competitive) and straight-line rent adjustments (an accounting smoothing of lease income). So AFFO = FFO − recurring/maintenance capex − straight-line rent adjustments, with some variation across REITs. The result is a measure closer to the actual cash available for distribution to shareholders, because it accounts for the real ongoing spending FFO ignores. So AFFO is often considered a better gauge of a REIT's sustainable distribution capacity than FFO. The trade-off is that AFFO definitions vary across REITs (there is no single standardized formula), so comparisons require care. Use AFFO to assess whether distributions are supported by real, sustainable cash flow.

faq.q: What is NAV for a REIT?
a: NAV stands for net asset value — a measure of what a REIT is worth from a balance-sheet perspective, the value of its properties net of its debts. NAV is calculated by estimating the current market value of the REIT's real estate (and other assets), subtracting its liabilities (debt and obligations), and dividing by the shares outstanding to get NAV per share. So NAV per share represents the estimated underlying value of the REIT's net assets attributable to each share. NAV is useful for gauging whether a REIT's shares trade at a premium or a discount to the value of its properties: if a traded REIT's share price is below its NAV per share, the shares trade at a discount (potentially cheap relative to the underlying real estate); if above, at a premium. For non-traded REITs, the periodic NAV is the basis for the share value and redemption pricing. So NAV provides an asset-based valuation reference distinct from the earnings-based FFO and AFFO — a balance-sheet view of value against the underlying real estate. NAV estimates carry some uncertainty, since they rely on appraisals and assumptions.

faq.q: What is the P/FFO ratio?
a: P/FFO is the price-to-FFO ratio — a REIT's share price divided by its FFO per share — and it is the REIT equivalent of the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio used for ordinary stocks. Because FFO is the meaningful earnings measure for a REIT (correcting net income's depreciation distortion), P/FFO is the appropriate valuation multiple for comparing REITs. A lower P/FFO suggests a REIT is priced more cheaply relative to its FFO earnings; a higher P/FFO suggests a richer valuation, which the market may justify by faster growth or higher property quality. So you use P/FFO much as you would use P/E for a stock — to compare valuations across REITs and against historical norms, ideally among REITs of similar property type and quality. Do not use a standard P/E ratio for a REIT, since net income is distorted by depreciation; P/FFO is the correct tool. Combine P/FFO with AFFO-based distribution analysis and NAV (premium/discount) for a fuller valuation picture, since P/FFO alone, like any single multiple, does not capture distribution sustainability, leverage, or asset value.

faq.q: What does it mean if a REIT trades at a discount to NAV?
a: A REIT trading at a discount to NAV means its share price is below the estimated per-share value of its net assets (its properties less liabilities). In principle, this suggests the market is valuing the REIT for less than its underlying real estate would be worth — potentially indicating the shares are cheap relative to the assets. A premium to NAV means the opposite: the share price exceeds the per-share asset value, suggesting the market is paying up (perhaps for growth, quality, or management). However, discounts and premiums should be interpreted carefully: a persistent discount may reflect real concerns (poor management, bad assets, high leverage, or sector headwinds) rather than a bargain, and NAV itself is an estimate based on appraisals and assumptions, so it carries uncertainty. So a discount to NAV is a signal worth investigating, not an automatic buy — examine why the discount exists and whether the NAV estimate is reliable. Use the premium/discount to NAV alongside FFO, AFFO, debt, and qualitative analysis, rather than in isolation, to judge whether a REIT is genuinely undervalued.

faq.q: How do I assess whether a REIT's distribution is sustainable?
a: The key check is the payout ratio against AFFO — comparing the distribution per share to AFFO per share. Because AFFO approximates the true cash available for distribution (after accounting for maintenance capex and rent smoothing that FFO ignores), comparing the distribution to AFFO tells you whether the distribution is covered by sustainable cash flow. A payout ratio comfortably below 100% of AFFO suggests the distribution is supported by real cash with a cushion; a ratio at or above AFFO is a warning that the distribution may not be sustainable and could be cut. You can also look at the FFO payout ratio, but AFFO is the more conservative, cash-focused gauge. Beyond the ratio, consider how the distribution has trended, whether any portion is funded by return of capital or borrowing (less sustainable), and the REIT's growth prospects. So to assess distribution sustainability, focus on the AFFO payout ratio (is the distribution covered by real cash?), the funding sources, and the trend — a high payout near or above AFFO signals risk. A sustainable distribution is covered by AFFO with room to spare.

faq.q: Why do debt levels matter for a REIT?
a: Debt levels matter because REITs use leverage, and leverage amplifies both returns and risk. A REIT borrows to acquire properties, so its debt profile is central to its risk. Key things to examine: the leverage ratio (debt relative to assets or to a cash-flow measure like EBITDA), which shows how much the REIT relies on borrowing; the debt-maturity schedule (when debt comes due and whether it must be refinanced, possibly in a difficult or high-rate market); and interest costs (which reduce cash flow and rise with rates on variable or maturing debt). High leverage magnifies gains in good times but also losses in downturns, and near-term maturities create refinancing risk if credit conditions tighten. So a REIT's debt is a key part of its risk assessment, alongside the earnings (FFO) and asset (NAV) metrics. A REIT with high leverage and looming maturities is riskier than one with moderate, well-laddered debt, even at similar FFO. So always examine the debt profile when evaluating a REIT — it can turn an otherwise attractive REIT into a risky one, or provide reassurance about resilience.

faq.q: Are REITs sensitive to interest rates?
a: Yes — REITs are generally sensitive to interest rates, which matters when you evaluate them. Higher rates can affect REITs in several ways: they raise the REIT's borrowing costs (especially on variable-rate or maturing debt that must be refinanced), reducing FFO and AFFO; they can pressure property values (and thus NAV), since real estate is often valued by capitalizing income at a rate tied to interest rates; and they make a REIT's yield compete with higher yields on bonds and cash, which can weigh on traded REIT share prices. Conversely, falling rates can be supportive. So when evaluating a REIT, consider its interest-rate exposure — the share of variable-rate debt, the debt-maturity schedule (near-term maturities are more exposed to refinancing at higher rates), and the sector's rate sensitivity. This ties back to the debt analysis and to NAV: a REIT with a strong, well-laddered, mostly fixed-rate balance sheet is more resilient to rising rates than one with heavy near-term, variable-rate debt. So factor interest-rate sensitivity into your evaluation alongside FFO, AFFO, NAV, and debt — it is a key part of a REIT's risk profile and can significantly affect both earnings and valuation over time.

faq.q: Can I rely on a single REIT metric?
a: No — no single metric tells the whole story, and relying on one can mislead you. FFO shows recurring earnings but not distribution sustainability or asset value. AFFO is closer to distributable cash but its definition varies across REITs. NAV gauges premium or discount to assets but is an estimate based on appraisals. The yield alone says nothing about whether the distribution is sustainable or how much risk you are taking. So sound REIT evaluation uses the metrics together: P/FFO to gauge earnings and valuation, the AFFO payout ratio to assess distribution sustainability, and NAV to judge premium or discount — plus debt levels and qualitative factors (property type and quality, occupancy, lease terms, management, growth prospects). Each metric covers a different dimension, and combining them gives a rounded picture no single number provides. So treat FFO, AFFO, NAV, payout ratios, and debt as a toolkit, not a single verdict, and add qualitative judgment about the business. A high yield or low P/FFO in isolation can hide real problems that the full set of metrics would reveal.

faq.q: Do REITs report FFO and AFFO themselves?
a: Yes — REITs typically report FFO (and often AFFO) in their financial filings and earnings releases, along with reconciliations to GAAP net income, because these metrics are the industry standard for communicating REIT performance. FFO follows the Nareit definition, which provides a common framework, so reported FFO is reasonably comparable across REITs (though you should still check each REIT's reconciliation for any variations). AFFO is less standardized — REITs may label it AFFO, FAD (funds available for distribution), or CAD (cash available for distribution), and the specific adjustments (which capex counts as recurring, how rent is adjusted) can vary — so AFFO comparisons across REITs require care to ensure you are comparing like with like. NAV is sometimes provided by the REIT (especially non-traded REITs, which report a periodic NAV) and sometimes estimated by analysts. So you can generally find FFO and AFFO in a REIT's reporting, but read the definitions and reconciliations, since the labels and adjustments are not perfectly uniform. So use the REIT's reported figures as a starting point, verify the methodology, and be cautious comparing AFFO across REITs with different definitions.

faq.q: Is a higher FFO always better?
a: Not necessarily — higher FFO is generally good, but FFO must be considered in context. FFO measures the level of recurring earnings, but evaluation also depends on the price you pay (P/FFO valuation), the growth rate of FFO (a REIT with growing FFO is more attractive than one with flat or declining FFO at the same level), the sustainability of distributions (AFFO payout ratio), the asset value (NAV premium or discount), and the risk (debt levels, property quality). So a high FFO at a high price (high P/FFO) may be less attractive than a moderate FFO at a low price. And FFO growth matters as much as the absolute level — a REIT whose FFO per share is rising is creating value, while one whose FFO is shrinking (perhaps from dilution or declining properties) is not, regardless of the current level. So do not look at FFO in isolation or assume higher is always better; consider FFO per share, its growth, the valuation multiple, and the other metrics together. The goal is sustainable, growing FFO per share at a reasonable valuation, with sound distribution coverage and manageable debt — not simply the highest FFO.

faq.q: What qualitative factors should I consider beyond the metrics?
a: Beyond FFO, AFFO, and NAV, several qualitative factors are central to evaluating a REIT. Property type and quality — different sectors (e.g., industrial, residential, retail, office, healthcare, data centers) have different dynamics, and higher-quality, well-located properties tend to be more resilient. Tenant and lease profile — occupancy rates, lease lengths, tenant credit quality, and rent escalators affect income stability. Management quality and track record — experienced, aligned, shareholder-friendly management matters greatly. Growth prospects — the REIT's pipeline, markets, and ability to grow FFO per share. Balance-sheet strength — beyond raw leverage, the cost and structure of debt and access to capital. And the broader sector and economic backdrop — interest-rate sensitivity and demand trends for the property type. So the metrics are tools within a broader analysis, not a substitute for judgment about the business. So combine the quantitative metrics (FFO, AFFO, NAV, payout, debt) with these qualitative factors for a complete evaluation. A REIT with strong metrics but weak assets, management, or sector outlook may be less attractive than the numbers alone suggest.

title: How to Find a 1031 Replacement Property Fast
lead: The 45-day identification window is the tightest deadline in a 1031 exchange, so finding suitable replacement property fast is one of the most important exchange skills. This guide explains why speed matters, how to start before you sell, where to source replacements, why DSTs are the fastest option, how to vet quickly without cutting corners, and how to build a backup list.

The single greatest source of stress in a 1031 exchange is the 45-day identification window. From the day you sell your relinquished property, you have just 45 days to identify your replacement property in writing — and if you can't find suitable replacements in time, the exchange fails and you owe the tax. Forty-five days sounds like enough, but it's a tight window for finding, evaluating, and committing to replacement real estate, especially in a competitive market. The investors who navigate it successfully are the ones who prepare — they start the search before they sell, line up sourcing channels, know that DSTs offer a fast and certain option, vet efficiently, and build a backup list. This guide explains how to find replacement property fast: why speed matters, starting before you sell, sourcing channels, DSTs as the fastest option, vetting quickly, and building backups.
takeaways: The 45-day identification window is unforgiving — speed in finding suitable replacements is essential.
Start the search before you sell — the single most powerful habit, converting the tight window into a confirmation period.
Work multiple sourcing channels (agents, listings, sponsors, network) early and actively.
DSTs are the fastest, most certain option — pre-packaged and fast-closing — ideal as a primary passive choice or a certain backup.

sections.heading: Why speed matters in the 45-day window
paras: The 45-day identification window drives the urgency. From the sale of your relinquished property, the clock runs 45 calendar days (no extensions for weekends or holidays) to identify your replacement property in writing. If you don't make a valid identification by day 45, the exchange fails — you can't acquire replacement property you didn't identify, so the deferral is lost and the tax comes due. The 45-day deadline is unforgiving, which is why speed in finding replacements is essential.

Forty-five days is tighter than it sounds because you're not just finding property — you're finding suitable property you're prepared to commit to. You need to identify replacements you can actually close on within the 180-day window, which means evaluating their quality, price, financing, and fit — and understanding what counts as replacement property in a 1031 exchange in the first place. Rushing to identify property you haven't vetted risks identifying something you can't or shouldn't close on. So the 45 days must accommodate both finding and reasonably evaluating replacements, compressing the timeline further.

The competitive reality adds pressure. In active markets, good replacement properties attract multiple buyers, so finding and securing one within 45 days competes against other buyers without the deadline pressure. This is why preparation — starting early, lining up channels, knowing your options — is so valuable: it lets you move fast when the clock starts. The investors who struggle are those who start the search only after selling, losing precious days. Understanding why speed matters — the unforgiving 45-day deadline, the need to find suitable (not just any) property, and the competitive market — motivates the preparation and strategies that let you find replacement property fast. The 45-day window rewards those who prepare to move quickly, which is the theme of finding replacements fast.

sections.heading: Start before you sell
paras: The most powerful way to find replacement property fast is to start the search before you sell — ideally before you even list the relinquished property. The 45-day clock starts at the sale, but nothing stops you from searching, evaluating, and even lining up replacements beforehand. An investor who has identified candidate replacements before selling can move immediately when the clock starts, or even have replacements ready to identify on day one. Starting early effectively extends your usable search time well beyond 45 days.

Starting before you sell lets you search without deadline pressure, evaluating replacements carefully and waiting for good ones rather than rushing. You can build a list of candidates, monitor the market, line up financing, and engage sponsors for DST options — all before the clock starts. Then, when you sell, you're not starting from scratch under pressure; you're executing on a prepared list. This transforms the 45-day window from a frantic search into a confirmation of choices you've already evaluated.

The practical step is to begin sourcing and evaluating replacements as soon as you decide to sell (or even before), coordinating with your agent, advisor, and sponsors to build a candidate list. Line up your qualified intermediary, understand your financing, and have DST options identified as backups. By the time you sell, you should have a clear sense of your replacement targets and backups, so the 45 days are about confirming and identifying rather than discovering. Starting before you sell is the single most important habit for finding replacement property fast — it converts the tight 45-day window into a manageable confirmation period, because the hard work of finding and evaluating replacements was done beforehand. Investors who prepare this way rarely struggle with the 45-day deadline.
The most powerful way to find replacement property fast is to start the search before you sell — turning the frantic 45-day window into a confirmation of choices you've already evaluated.

sections.heading: Sourcing channels
paras: Multiple channels can source replacement property, and using several increases your odds of finding suitable replacements fast. A 1031-experienced real estate agent or broker is a primary channel — they can identify on-market and off-market properties, leverage their network, and move quickly on your behalf, knowing the exchange deadlines. sections.heading: DSTs: the fastest replacement option
paras: Among all replacement options, DSTs are the fastest and most certain, making them invaluable for finding replacement property fast. Because the property and structure already exist, a DST can close in days, not the weeks or months a direct property purchase takes. This speed makes DSTs the go-to fast replacement.

DSTs are also certain to close, unlike direct deals that can fall through. The DST is available and ready; once you commit and fund, the closing is quick and reliable. For finding replacement property fast, DSTs offer a ready solution: pre-vetted (by the sponsor), available, and fast-closing, requiring you to select and commit rather than find and negotiate a property. But for speed and certainty, DSTs are unmatched. DSTs as the fastest replacement option — pre-packaged, available, and fast-closing — are a key tool for finding replacement property fast, whether as a primary passive choice or a certain backup. The goal is to vet efficiently: doing the essential due diligence quickly without cutting the corners that lead to bad acquisitions. This means having a streamlined evaluation process — knowing your criteria, the key things to check, and how to assess them quickly — so you can evaluate replacements within the tight timeline.

Efficient vetting focuses on the essentials: the property's price and value, income and expenses, condition, location, financing, and fit with your goals. The balance is doing enough due diligence to make a sound decision without taking so long that you miss the deadline. Preparation helps here too — investors who know their criteria, have their team ready, and have pre-evaluated candidates can vet fast because much of the work is done. The risk to avoid is identifying property you haven't vetted (and discovering problems after you've committed) or being so thorough that you run out of time. Vetting quickly without cutting corners — efficient, essentials-focused due diligence enabled by preparation — lets you find and commit to good replacements within the window. sections.heading: Building a backup list
paras: A backup list is essential insurance for finding replacement property fast and ensuring the exchange succeeds. Because direct deals can fall through (a seller walks, financing fails, due diligence reveals problems), a deliberate identification strategy that builds in backups gives you alternatives if your primary replacement doesn't close. The identification rules allow identifying multiple properties (typically up to three under the three-property rule, or more under the 200% rule), so you can identify your primary plus backups — and a replacement-property value calculator helps confirm you're reinvesting enough to fully defer the tax.

The strongest backup is a fast-closing DST. Identifying a DST as a backup means that if your primary direct deal stalls, you can pivot to the DST and close it fast, completing the exchange. This is the standard insurance — a certain-to-close DST backup that prevents the exchange from failing if the primary falls through. So a typical fast-replacement strategy is to identify your primary target(s) plus a DST backup, ensuring you have a certain option.

Building the backup list happens during the identification window (by day 45) but is informed by your earlier sourcing — the candidates and DST options you lined up before and after selling. The list should include your primary target(s) and at least one certain backup (usually a DST), so you're covered if the primary fails. With a backup list, the exchange is far more likely to succeed, because you're not dependent on a single deal closing. Building a backup list — primary targets plus a certain DST backup, identified within the window — is the insurance that makes finding replacement property fast also mean finding it reliably. The backup list ensures that even if your first choice falls through, you have a certain option to complete the exchange, which is the final piece of finding replacements fast and successfully.

title: How to Identify DSTs Within the 45-Day Window
lead: The 45-day identification window is the hardest part of a 1031 exchange. This guide explains why the deadline creates so much pressure, why pre-packaged DSTs can be identified and closed quickly, how to use DSTs as backup identifications, how to apply the identification rules, and how to coordinate with your qualified intermediary.

In a 1031 exchange, the clock is unforgiving. From the day you sell your relinquished property, you have just 45 days to identify your replacement property in writing, and 180 days total to close. The 45-day identification window is widely regarded as the hardest part of the exchange: finding, vetting, and committing to suitable replacement real estate in six weeks — while competing with other buyers and risking that a deal falls through — is a real source of failed exchanges. Delaware Statutory Trusts (DSTs) help solve this problem because they are pre-packaged: the sponsor has already acquired, financed, and offered the property, so a DST can be identified and closed quickly, even late in the window. DSTs also make excellent backup identifications if your primary deal collapses. This guide explains why the 45-day window is so tight, why DSTs identify quickly, how to use them as backups, how to apply the identification rules, and how to coordinate with your qualified intermediary. sections.heading: The 45-Day Pressure Problem
paras: The 45-day identification window is the single tightest constraint in a 1031 exchange, and it is where many exchanges fail. The rule is strict: within 45 calendar days of selling your relinquished property, you must identify your replacement property in writing, delivered to your qualified intermediary. The clock starts on the closing of your sale, runs on calendar days (weekends and holidays included), and cannot be extended for ordinary reasons. Miss it, and your exchange collapses — the proceeds become taxable, and you owe the capital-gains tax you were trying to defer.

The pressure comes from how much must happen in those six weeks. You have to find suitable replacement real estate, perform enough due diligence to commit, negotiate or secure it, and often arrange financing — all while competing with other buyers in the open market. If your first-choice property falls through after you have identified it, you may have little time left to find an alternative. Traditional replacement property is slow: deals can take months to close, and a seller who delays or backs out can blow up your exchange. So the 45-day window forces investors to make a high-stakes commitment quickly, with limited room for error and no margin for a deal that does not come together.

So the 45-day window is a hard, unextendable deadline whose pressure causes failed exchanges when replacement property is slow or falls through. Understanding the problem frames why DSTs help. It leaves little margin for error. Understanding the problem frames why pre-packaged DSTs are valuable. sections.heading: Why DSTs Identify Quickly
paras: DSTs are uniquely suited to the 45-day window because they are pre-packaged. By the time a DST is offered, the sponsor has already acquired the property, arranged the financing (including any non-recourse debt), completed the legal structuring, and prepared the offering documents. There is no negotiation with a seller, no race to lock up a property, and no separate loan application — the work that makes traditional replacement property slow has already been done. You are buying into a finished, available offering rather than assembling a deal yourself.

This means a DST can be identified and closed quickly, even late in the window. Once you decide a DST is suitable, the subscription process is relatively fast: you complete the paperwork, your equity is invested, and the exchange can close well inside the 180-day limit — sometimes in a matter of days. Because the property already exists and is fully structured, there is far less that can go wrong between identification and closing than with an open-market purchase — one of the central trade-offs in choosing a DST over direct property ownership in a 1031 exchange. That reliability is a major reason 1031 investors turn to DSTs when time is short: a DST is available on demand, in known amounts, with known terms. So a DST removes most of the execution risk that makes the 45-day window so stressful.

sections.heading: Using DSTs as Backup Identifications
paras: One of the most valuable ways to use a DST is as a backup in your 1031 identification. The identification rules let you identify more than one replacement property within the 45-day window, and a smart strategy is to identify your primary target — say, an open-market property you are negotiating — alongside one or more DSTs as fallbacks. If your primary deal closes, you simply proceed with it. If it falls through, you already have a suitable, pre-packaged DST identified and ready to close, so your exchange is protected rather than lost.

This backup approach directly addresses the biggest risk of the 45-day window: that your chosen property collapses after you have identified it, leaving you no time to find an alternative. Because a DST is available on demand and closes quickly, it is the ideal safety net — you can pivot to it late in the process and still close within the 180-day window. Many experienced 1031 investors and advisors build this redundancy in deliberately, treating an identified DST as insurance against execution risk. The key is to identify the DST within the 45-day window (you cannot add it later) and to respect the identification rules that limit how many properties you can name. So a DST backup turns a fragile exchange into a resilient one.

sections.heading: Applying the Identification Rules
paras: When you identify replacement property — including DSTs — you must follow one of three identification rules, and choosing the right one shapes how many properties you can name. The three-property rule lets you identify up to three properties of any value, regardless of their total price; this is the most common choice and is usually sufficient when you are naming a primary property plus a DST or two as backups. The 200% rule lets you identify any number of properties, as long as their combined value does not exceed 200% of the value of your relinquished property — useful when you want to diversify across several DSTs.

The third option, the 95% rule, lets you identify any number of properties of any value but requires you to actually acquire at least 95% of the total value you identified — a high bar that is rarely used and risky if any identified property fails to close. For most 1031 investors using DSTs, the three-property rule or the 200% rule is the practical choice. Identifications must be unambiguous and in writing, signed and delivered to your qualified intermediary by midnight of the 45th day. For a DST, the identification should clearly describe the specific offering. So applying the right identification rule lets you name your primary property and your DST backups correctly without violating the limits.

sections.heading: Coordinating With Your QI
paras: Your qualified intermediary (QI) is central to a valid identification, and coordinating with them early is essential. The QI holds your sale proceeds (you cannot touch them without disqualifying the exchange) and is the party to whom your written identification must be delivered. The identification must be signed and received by the QI by midnight of the 45th day — not postmarked, but actually delivered — so you need to know your QI's process, deadlines, and accepted delivery methods well before the clock runs out. A late or improperly delivered identification can invalidate the entire exchange.

Good coordination means engaging your QI before you even sell, so the exchange is set up correctly from the start, and then working with them to prepare your identification document as the 45-day deadline approaches. If you are identifying DSTs, the QI needs the specific offering details to record the identification properly. Because DSTs close quickly, your QI can also help orchestrate the timing so that funds move smoothly from the trust account to the DST subscription within the 180-day window. So coordinating with your QI ensures your written identification is delivered correctly and on time and that funds move properly into your DSTs within the deadlines. Understanding the QI's role completes the picture. Coordinating with your QI — engaging the qualified intermediary before the sale, understanding their process and delivery deadlines, delivering a signed, unambiguous written identification (including specific DST details) by midnight of the 45th day, and orchestrating the smooth movement of funds into the DST subscription within 180 days — is essential to a valid exchange. The QI is both fund custodian and identification recipient. Understanding the QI's role completes the picture. Coordinate early with your QI, who holds your proceeds and must receive your signed written identification by the 45th day, to keep your DST identifications valid and your exchange compliant.
The identification only counts if your qualified intermediary actually has it in writing by midnight of day 45 — so know your QI's process before the clock starts, not after.

sections.heading: Putting a 45-Day DST Plan Together
paras: Bringing the pieces together produces a practical playbook for using DSTs to survive the 45-day window. Before you sell, engage a qualified intermediary and start lining up potential DST offerings, so you are not starting from zero when the clock begins. As soon as your relinquished property closes, the 45-day clock starts, so move quickly: shortlist suitable DSTs — often through a 1031 exchange marketplace for finding DST and NNN deals — complete your due diligence and suitability review, and decide which identification rule you will use.

Then identify deliberately. If you have a primary open-market property, name it and add one or more DSTs as backups under the three-property or 200% rule; if you are going all-in on DSTs, identify the specific offerings you intend to acquire (potentially diversifying across several). Deliver the signed, written identification to your QI before the 45th day. If your primary deal holds, close it; if it falls through, pivot to your identified DST and close it inside the 180-day window. Because DST interests are securities, you will work through a broker-dealer and complete a suitability review before subscribing. So a disciplined plan — QI engaged early, DSTs pre-shortlisted, identification made correctly, backups in place — turns the 45-day window from a threat into a manageable process.

So putting a 45-day DST plan together means engaging your QI early, shortlisting DSTs, identifying primary and backup properties under the right rule, and closing on time. Our role is to help you use DSTs to meet the 45-day deadline and complete a compliant, suitable exchange.

faq.q: What is the 45-day identification window in a 1031 exchange?
a: The 45-day identification window is the period during which you must identify your replacement property in a 1031 exchange. From the day you close on the sale of your relinquished property, you have exactly 45 calendar days to identify, in writing, the replacement property (or properties) you intend to acquire, with that identification delivered to your qualified intermediary. The clock runs on calendar days — weekends and holidays included — and the deadline is strict and unextendable for ordinary reasons. If you fail to identify suitable replacement property within 45 days, your exchange fails, your sale proceeds become taxable, and you owe the capital-gains tax you were trying to defer. The 45-day window is widely regarded as the hardest part of a 1031 exchange because finding and committing to suitable replacement real estate in just six weeks is genuinely difficult. So the 45-day window is the tightest, most consequential deadline in the exchange — and the reason many investors turn to pre-packaged DSTs, which can be identified and closed quickly when time is short.

faq.q: Why is the 45-day window so difficult?
a: The 45-day window is difficult because a great deal must happen in a short, unextendable period. Within six weeks of selling your property, you have to find suitable replacement real estate, perform enough due diligence to commit, negotiate or secure it, and often arrange financing — all while competing with other buyers in the open market. The clock runs on calendar days and cannot be extended for ordinary reasons, so there is no margin if a deal moves slowly. Worse, if your first-choice property falls through after you have identified it, you may have little or no time left to find an alternative, and a seller who delays or backs out can blow up your entire exchange. Traditional replacement property is slow — deals can take months to close — which clashes with the tight deadline. So the 45-day window forces high-stakes commitments quickly, with limited room for error. This is precisely why DSTs, which are pre-packaged and close fast, are so valuable for investors racing against the clock.

faq.q: Why can DSTs be identified and closed so quickly?
a: DSTs can be identified and closed quickly because they are pre-packaged. By the time a DST is offered to investors, the sponsor has already acquired the property, arranged the financing (including any non-recourse debt), completed the legal structuring, and prepared the offering documents. There is no negotiation with a seller, no race to lock up a property, and no separate loan application — the slow, uncertain work of assembling a real estate deal is already done. You are buying into a finished, available offering rather than building a transaction yourself. Once you decide a DST is suitable and complete the subscription paperwork, your equity is invested and the exchange can close in a matter of days, well inside the 180-day limit. Because the property already exists and is fully structured, there is far less that can go wrong between identification and closing than with an open-market purchase. So DSTs are available on demand, in known amounts and with known terms — which is exactly why they are reliable when the 45-day clock is running down.

faq.q: Can I use a DST as a backup if my primary deal falls through?
a: Yes — using a DST as a backup identification is one of the smartest ways to protect a 1031 exchange. The identification rules let you identify more than one replacement property within the 45-day window, so you can name your primary target (say, an open-market property you are negotiating) alongside one or more DSTs as fallbacks. If your primary deal closes, you proceed with it. If it falls through, you already have a suitable, pre-packaged DST identified and ready to close, so your exchange is protected rather than lost. This directly addresses the biggest 45-day risk: a chosen property collapsing after identification with no time to find an alternative. Because a DST is available on demand and closes quickly, you can pivot to it late in the process and still close within the 180-day window. The key is to identify the DST within the 45-day window — you cannot add it later — and to respect the identification rules limiting how many properties you can name. So an identified DST acts as insurance against execution risk, turning a fragile exchange into a resilient one.

faq.q: What are the three identification rules?
a: The three identification rules govern how many replacement properties you can identify in a 1031 exchange. The three-property rule lets you identify up to three properties of any value, regardless of their total price — this is the most common choice and usually sufficient when naming a primary property plus a DST or two as backups. The 200% rule lets you identify any number of properties, as long as their combined value does not exceed 200% of the value of your relinquished property — useful when you want to diversify across several DSTs. The 95% rule lets you identify any number of properties of any value, but requires you to actually acquire at least 95% of the total value you identified — a high bar that is rarely used and risky if any identified property fails to close. For most 1031 investors using DSTs, the three-property rule or the 200% rule is the practical choice. Whichever you use, the identification must be unambiguous, in writing, signed, and delivered to your qualified intermediary by the 45th day. So pick the rule that fits how many properties you need to name.

faq.q: Which identification rule should I use with DSTs?
a: For most investors using DSTs, the three-property rule or the 200% rule is the practical choice. The three-property rule — letting you identify up to three properties of any value — is usually sufficient when you are naming a primary open-market property plus one or two DSTs as backups, or when you want to acquire just a few DSTs. If you intend to diversify your exchange across several DSTs (more than three), the 200% rule is better, because it lets you identify any number of properties as long as their combined value stays within 200% of your relinquished property's value. The 95% rule is rarely used with DSTs because it requires acquiring 95% of everything you identify, which is unnecessarily risky. The right rule depends on your strategy: a few targets with backups suits the three-property rule, while broader diversification across many DSTs suits the 200% rule. So choose based on how many DSTs (and other properties) you want to identify, and confirm the values stay within the chosen rule's limits. Your qualified intermediary and advisor can help you structure the identification correctly.

faq.q: What is the role of the qualified intermediary in identification?
a: The qualified intermediary (QI) is central to a valid identification. The QI holds your sale proceeds — you cannot take possession of them without disqualifying the exchange — and is the party to whom your written identification must be delivered. The identification has to be signed and actually received by the QI by midnight of the 45th day; it is not enough to postmark it or decide internally, it must be in the QI's hands. A late or improperly delivered identification can invalidate the entire exchange. Beyond receiving the identification, the QI helps orchestrate the movement of funds from the trust account into your replacement property — including a DST subscription — within the 180-day window. This is why coordinating with your QI early matters: you need to know their process, deadlines, and accepted delivery methods before the clock runs out, and you should engage them before you even sell so the exchange is set up correctly. So the QI is both the custodian of your funds and the recipient of your identification, making close coordination essential to a compliant exchange.

faq.q: When does the 45-day clock start?
a: The 45-day clock starts on the day you close the sale of your relinquished property — that is, the date the transfer of your old property is completed. From that date, you have exactly 45 calendar days to deliver your written identification of replacement property to your qualified intermediary. The count includes weekends and holidays; there is no pausing for non-business days. Importantly, the 180-day window for actually closing on your replacement property runs concurrently from the same starting date, not from the end of the 45-day period — so the 45-day and 180-day clocks both begin when you sell. This means you do not get 45 days plus another 180; you get 45 days to identify and 180 days total to close, both measured from the sale. The deadlines are strict and generally cannot be extended except in narrow circumstances like federally declared disasters. So know your exact sale-closing date, mark day 45 and day 180 on the calendar immediately, and work backward to ensure your identification and closing both happen in time. DSTs help because they close fast within these windows.

faq.q: What happens if I miss the 45-day deadline?
a: If you miss the 45-day identification deadline, your 1031 exchange fails. Without a valid, timely written identification delivered to your qualified intermediary, you cannot acquire replacement property within the exchange, so the sale of your relinquished property is treated as a fully taxable sale. The proceeds the QI is holding are released to you, and you owe the capital-gains tax (and any depreciation recapture) that you were trying to defer. There is generally no grace period or extension for ordinary reasons — the deadline is strict and runs on calendar days. The only common exceptions are narrow, such as relief granted after a federally declared disaster. This is exactly why the 45-day window is so high-stakes and why investors build in protection: identifying a pre-packaged DST as a backup ensures you have a suitable, ready-to-close property identified before the deadline, so a primary deal falling through does not cost you the exchange. So missing the deadline means losing your deferral entirely — making careful planning, early QI coordination, and DST backups essential safeguards against a costly failure.

faq.q: Can I identify multiple DSTs in one exchange?
a: Yes — you can identify multiple DSTs in a single 1031 exchange, subject to the identification rules. Under the three-property rule, you can identify up to three properties of any value, which could be three DSTs (or a mix of DSTs and other property). If you want to identify more than three DSTs — to diversify across asset classes, geographies, or sponsors — you would use the 200% rule, which lets you identify any number of properties as long as their combined value does not exceed 200% of your relinquished property's value. Identifying multiple DSTs is a common diversification strategy: because DST minimums are relatively low, you can split one exchange across several DSTs to spread your risk rather than concentrating in a single replacement property. Each DST must be clearly and unambiguously described in your written identification to the qualified intermediary, delivered by the 45th day. So yes, multiple DSTs are allowed and often advisable for diversification — just choose the identification rule that accommodates how many you want to name and keep within its limits.

faq.q: How quickly can a DST actually close?
a: A DST can close very quickly — often within days of your decision to invest, and almost always well inside the 180-day window. Because the DST is pre-packaged, with the property already acquired, financed, and structured, there is no lengthy escrow, seller negotiation, or loan underwriting to complete. Once you have decided a DST is suitable, performed your due diligence, and the suitability review is done, the closing essentially involves completing the subscription paperwork and having your qualified intermediary transfer your exchange funds to the DST. This can happen in a matter of days, which is why DSTs are so valuable when the 45-day clock has run down or a primary deal has just collapsed. By contrast, an open-market property purchase can take weeks or months to close, with many points of potential failure. The speed and reliability of a DST closing is one of its biggest practical advantages in a time-pressured exchange. So if you need to close fast — especially late in the exchange timeline — a DST is typically the most dependable option. Confirm the specific subscription process with your advisor.

faq.q: Do I still need due diligence if a DST closes quickly?
a: Yes — speed of closing does not replace the need for due diligence. Even though a DST is pre-packaged and can close fast, you should still evaluate the offering carefully: the sponsor's track record, the property and its market, the lease structure, the debt terms, the fees, the projected (not guaranteed) distributions, and the risks. The convenience of a quick close is about execution, not about skipping analysis. Because DST interests are securities, you will also go through a suitability review with your broker-dealer, which assesses whether the offering fits your financial situation, goals, and risk tolerance. The good news is that DST due diligence can be performed efficiently, because the offering documents are already prepared and the property is already acquired — so you can do thorough analysis within the 45-day window. The key is to start early: shortlist suitable DSTs before or right after your sale, so you have time to evaluate them properly. So always do your due diligence, even on a fast-closing DST — just plan to do it efficiently within the exchange timeline. Quick closing is a benefit, not a license to skip diligence.

faq.q: Can the 45-day or 180-day deadlines ever be extended?
a: The 45-day and 180-day deadlines are strict and generally cannot be extended for ordinary reasons — not for a deal falling through, financing trouble, or simply needing more time. They run on calendar days from your sale closing and are firm. The principal exception is relief granted by the IRS in connection with a federally declared disaster: when the IRS issues disaster relief, it may postpone 1031 deadlines for affected taxpayers in the designated area, sometimes by a meaningful number of days. These extensions are not automatic for every situation — they apply only when the IRS specifically grants relief and you qualify under its terms. Outside of such relief, you should plan as if the deadlines are immovable, because they almost always are. This is why building in protection — early QI coordination, pre-shortlisted DSTs, and DST backup identifications — matters so much: you cannot rely on getting more time. So treat the 45-day and 180-day deadlines as fixed, verify the current rules with your tax advisor, and structure your exchange to comply without depending on an extension.

faq.q: How should I prepare for the 45-day window before I sell?
a: The best preparation for the 45-day window happens before you sell. First, engage a qualified intermediary and set up the exchange correctly, since you cannot take possession of the sale proceeds without disqualifying it. Second, start lining up potential replacement property in advance — including shortlisting suitable DST offerings — so you are not starting from zero when the clock begins. Third, understand the identification rules (three-property, 200%, and 95%) and decide roughly how you will identify: a primary property with DST backups, or a set of DSTs directly. Fourth, get your financial and accreditation information ready, since DSTs require a suitability review. Doing this groundwork before the sale means that when the 45-day clock starts, you can move quickly to evaluate, identify, and close. Because DSTs are pre-packaged and close fast, having a few suitable ones shortlisted gives you a reliable path to completing the exchange even if an open-market deal falls through. So preparation — QI engaged, DSTs shortlisted, rules understood, paperwork ready — is what turns the 45-day window from a threat into a manageable process. Start before you sell.
