title: How to Invest in a Private REIT: Minimums, Yield & Liquidity
lead: Private REITs offer diversified, income-focused real estate for accredited investors — at the cost of liquidity. Here's who can invest, what to expect, and what to check first.

A private REIT can be an appealing way to own a diversified slice of institutional real estate and collect regular income, without managing anything or riding the daily swings of the public market. But it's a private, illiquid security with real constraints, and investing in one well means understanding the requirements, the economics, and the terms that govern getting your money back. This memo walks through who can invest, what you'll typically commit, what to expect on yield and liquidity, and the due diligence that separates a sound private REIT from a weak one.
takeaways: Private REITs are generally limited to accredited investors and sold through Regulation D private placements, with status verified at subscription.
Minimums usually run higher than public or non-traded REITs, often tens of thousands of dollars, so the position should sit inside a diversified portfolio.
Distributions are a target, not a guarantee, can move with the portfolio, and may include return of capital that reduces your basis rather than true income.
Liquidity is conditional. You exit through a redemption program with lock-ups, periodic windows, caps, and the sponsor's discretion to slow or suspend buybacks.
The fee load and how net asset value is set deserve as much scrutiny as the yield, because both quietly shape what you actually keep.
The private placement memorandum is the document that governs the deal. Read it in full, and weigh the sponsor's track record before you fund.
If you are still mapping out the landscape, our complete guide to private and non-traded REITs frames where this vehicle fits before you commit capital to one.

sections.heading: What a private REIT actually is
paras: A private REIT is a real estate investment trust that does not register its shares for public sale and does not list on any exchange. Like every REIT, it owns income-producing property and must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income to shareholders each year, which lets it avoid corporate-level tax and pass the income through to you. What sets the private version apart is the sales channel and the audience. Shares are offered under Regulation D, the same private-placement framework used for DSTs and many funds, and sold to accredited and institutional investors rather than the general public. That single structural choice drives the higher minimums, the limited liquidity, and the lighter public-reporting profile that define the rest of this memo.

It helps to place the private REIT against its cousins. A publicly traded REIT lists on an exchange, trades daily at a market price, and is open to anyone with a brokerage account. A non-traded REIT is SEC-registered but not listed, priced at periodic net asset value and sold through advisors. A private REIT is the least liquid and least public of the three, available only to accredited investors and built for a multi-year hold. If you are weighing the family as a whole, our private vs. public vs. non-traded comparison sets all three side by side; this memo assumes you have decided the private version is worth a serious look and want to know how to do it well.

sections.heading: Who can invest: the accredited standard
paras: Because a private REIT is sold under Regulation D and not registered for public sale, it is generally available only to accredited investors. The federal definition gives you a few ways to qualify. On income, you need more than $200,000 individually, or $300,000 jointly with a spouse, in each of the two most recent years, with a reasonable expectation of the same in the current year. On net worth, you need more than $1 million excluding the value of your primary residence. Since 2020 there are also credential-based paths: holding a Series 7, 65, or 82 license in good standing qualifies you regardless of income or net worth. Our guide to accredited-investor requirements walks through each test in detail.

You do not simply check a box. As part of subscribing, your status is verified, typically through tax documents, brokerage and account statements, a letter from your CPA or attorney, or a third-party verification service. The sponsor and the broker-dealer placing the offering are obligated to confirm you qualify before accepting your money. Investors who are not accredited but want REIT exposure are not shut out of real estate; they generally use public or non-traded REITs instead, which carry no accreditation requirement. The accredited gate exists because a private placement carries less mandated disclosure than a registered offering, and the rule presumes a qualifying investor can absorb the risk and evaluate the deal.

sections.heading: Typical minimum investment
paras: Private REIT minimums sit at the high end of the REIT spectrum. Where a public REIT can be bought one share at a time and a non-traded REIT often starts in the low thousands, a private REIT frequently asks for a minimum in the tens of thousands of dollars, and some institutional-style offerings ask for more. The higher floor reflects both the private nature of the offering and the sophistication the structure presumes of its accredited participants. It also reflects the economics of a private placement, which is not built to process thousands of small tickets.

The size of the commitment carries a planning consequence. Because the position is both sizable and illiquid, a private REIT should generally be one holding within a diversified portfolio, not a concentrated bet, and the dollars you commit should be money you can leave invested for years without touching. A useful gut check: if losing access to this capital for five years or more would strain your plan, the amount is too large or the vehicle is the wrong fit. Sizing the position so that an extended lock-up is an inconvenience rather than a crisis is the single most important decision an investor makes before reading a word of the offering.

sections.heading: Distributions and yield expectations
paras: Private REITs are typically income-oriented, aiming to pay regular distributions funded by the rental income of the portfolio. The headline yield varies widely with the strategy, the leverage, and the property type, and like any real-estate return it is a target, not a guarantee. A distribution can be cut if occupancy slips, financing costs rise, or a sale environment softens. Treat any quoted yield as a projection that depends on the business plan working, not as a coupon.

Two cautions carry over from how we evaluate DSTs. First, be skeptical of a distribution that appears to exceed the portfolio's actual cash flow, because the gap may be funded by return of capital, which hands you back part of your own investment rather than income the properties earned. Return of capital is not free yield; it lowers your cost basis and defers tax, and a distribution propped up by it can mask a portfolio that is not covering its payout. Second, evaluate yield net of fees, since a gross number means little once the fee load comes out. A transparent sponsor will show you what is funding the distribution and what the coverage looks like; the absence of that clarity is itself a piece of information. Our memo on how private REIT dividends are taxed explains how a single distribution can split into ordinary income, capital gain, and return of capital at tax time.

sections.heading: Liquidity, redemptions, and lock-ups
paras: The defining constraint of a private REIT is illiquidity, and understanding exactly how it works is the heart of investing in one well. There is no public market, so you cannot sell your shares to another investor. Instead you access your capital through the sponsor's redemption program, and those programs come with conditions. Most include an initial lock-up, often a year or more, during which you cannot redeem at all. After that, redemptions happen on periodic windows, monthly or quarterly, and are usually capped at a small share of net assets per period. When more investors want out than the cap allows, requests are prorated, and the sponsor typically retains discretion to limit or suspend the program entirely, most often in exactly the stressed markets when investors most want their money.

The practical lesson is that the ability to exit is real but conditional, and least reliable precisely when it matters most. Read the redemption terms as carefully as the return projections, because they determine whether a label like "semi-liquid" means anything when you need it to. Specifically, confirm the length of the lock-up, the redemption frequency, the per-period cap, whether early redemptions carry a discount to NAV, and the exact language on the sponsor's right to gate. A program that looks generous on paper can still leave you waiting several quarters to fully exit if a wave of redemptions hits the cap. Plan to hold to the sponsor's full-cycle event, and treat the redemption program as a relief valve, not a checking account.

sections.heading: Fees and how NAV is set
paras: Fees are where a private REIT's economics quietly diverge from a low-cost public one, and they deserve direct attention. Depending on the offering you may encounter an upfront selling commission or dealer-manager fee, an ongoing asset-management fee, acquisition and disposition fees on properties, financing fees, and in some structures a performance or promote that pays the sponsor a share of profits above a hurdle. None of these is automatically disqualifying, since active management and deal sourcing cost money, but the all-in load is what erodes your return, and you should add the layers up rather than judge any one in isolation.

Just as important is how net asset value is determined, because NAV is both your entry price and the basis for redemptions. Ask how often NAV is recalculated, who performs the appraisals, and what methodology and assumptions sit behind it. An NAV that is updated infrequently or set with optimistic assumptions can overstate what your shares are really worth, which matters most on the way out. A sponsor that explains its valuation process plainly, and uses independent third-party appraisals, is showing the transparency a private, illiquid vehicle demands.
The table below lays out the terms that most shape a private REIT investment, and the question each one should prompt before you commit.

sections.heading: Term What it covers What to ask
paras: Minimum investment The smallest amount accepted Can I size this as one position, not a concentration?
Lock-up Initial period with no redemptions How long before I can request any exit?
Redemption cap Limit on buybacks per period What share of NAV per quarter, and is there proration?
Gating rights Sponsor's right to slow or suspend Under what conditions can redemptions be halted?
Fee load Upfront and ongoing charges What is my projected return net of all fees?
NAV process How shares are priced How often, by whom, and on what assumptions?
Distribution coverage What funds the payout Is the distribution covered by cash flow, or return of capital?

sections.heading: The subscription process, step by step
paras: Investing in a private REIT runs through a structured subscription, usually with a broker-dealer or adviser involved because the offering requires suitability review. The sequence is straightforward once you know the pieces.
Confirm suitability and accredited status, and that the illiquidity genuinely fits your timeline and your need for the capital.
Review the offering materials, the strategy, the portfolio, the leverage, the fees, and the redemption terms, before any paperwork.
Read the private placement memorandum (PPM) in full, since it holds the complete risk and fee disclosure that the marketing summary does not.
Complete the subscription agreement and verify accreditation, typically with supporting documents or a verification letter.
Fund the investment, then hold and monitor, collecting distributions, reviewing statements, and tracking NAV updates and any redemption-program changes.

Because private REITs are sold through financial professionals who conduct suitability review and often rely on third-party due-diligence reports, an adviser is usually part of the process. Understand how that adviser is compensated, whether through a commission embedded in the offering or a separate fee, because compensation can shape what gets recommended. The same point applies across private real estate; we make it in our how to invest in a DST memo, and it is worth asking directly.

sections.heading: Where a private REIT fits in a portfolio
paras: A private REIT is a tool, not a default, and it earns its place for a specific kind of investor. It suits someone who wants diversified, professionally managed real-estate income, can meet the accredited standard, and genuinely does not need the committed capital for years. The diversification is part of the appeal: rather than owning one building through a single-asset deal, you own a fractional slice of a portfolio that spreads tenant, property, and sometimes geographic risk across many holdings. For an investor who has sold an active rental and wants to stay in real estate without managing anything, that pooled exposure can be a clean fit.

It is a poor fit for money you might need on short notice, for an investor who is not comfortable holding through a multi-year lock-up, or for anyone who would have to concentrate to meet the minimum. It also differs from a Delaware Statutory Trust in a way that matters for 1031 investors: a private REIT is not 1031 replacement property, so you cannot exchange a real-estate gain directly into one. If deferring a gain is the goal, a DST is the direct route, and a private REIT may enter the picture later through a 721 roll-up. Our private REIT vs. syndication vs. DST memo compares these passive structures side by side, and the right choice turns on your goal, your horizon, and whether tax deferral is in play.

sections.heading: A due-diligence checklist
paras: Before committing, make sure you can answer a short list of questions in concrete terms, not generalities. What is the sponsor's track record, and how have prior offerings actually performed through a full cycle, including any that disappointed? What does the portfolio hold, and how diversified and how leveraged is it, since leverage amplifies both returns and losses? What is the full fee load, and what is your projected return net of it? Is the distribution supported by real cash flow, or partly by return of capital? And, most important for a private vehicle, what exactly are the redemption terms and lock-up, and how and how often is NAV determined?

A sponsor who answers these clearly is demonstrating the transparency that a private, illiquid vehicle demands. Evasiveness on any single one is a reason to slow down, not a detail to wave past. It is also worth confirming the basics that are easy to skip: who custodies the assets, how often you will receive reporting, what the tax documents will look like, and what happens at the end of the fund's life. Our companion piece, are private REITs safe, walks through the risk factors behind these questions. As always, review the specifics with your own financial, tax, and legal advisors before you invest, because the right answer depends on your facts, not on any single offering's pitch.

faq.q: Do I have to be accredited to invest in a private REIT?
a: Generally yes. Private REITs are sold under Regulation D and limited to accredited investors, and your status is verified when you subscribe. You can qualify by income (over $200,000 individually or $300,000 jointly for two years), by net worth (over $1 million excluding your primary residence), or by holding a Series 7, 65, or 82 license. Non-accredited investors typically use public or non-traded REITs.

faq.q: How much do I need to invest in a private REIT?
a: Minimums are typically higher than public or non-traded REITs, often in the tens of thousands of dollars and sometimes more for institutional offerings. Because the position is sizable and illiquid, treat it as one holding in a diversified portfolio rather than a place to concentrate.

faq.q: What yield do private REITs pay?
a: It varies by strategy, leverage, and property type, and it is a target rather than a guarantee that can be cut if the portfolio underperforms. Evaluate yield net of fees, and be wary of distributions that exceed cash flow, which may be funded partly by return of capital rather than income.

faq.q: How do I get my money out of a private REIT?
a: Through the sponsor's redemption program, which typically has an initial lock-up, periodic windows, caps on how much can be redeemed per period, and the sponsor's discretion to limit or suspend redemptions in stressed markets. Liquidity is real but conditional, so read those terms before investing and plan to hold to the full-cycle event.

faq.q: What fees should I expect?
a: Depending on the offering, you may see an upfront selling commission, an ongoing asset-management fee, acquisition and disposition fees, financing fees, and in some cases a performance promote. None is automatically disqualifying, but add the layers up and judge your projected return net of the all-in load, not on the gross yield.

faq.q: How is the share price set if it does not trade?
a: By net asset value, an appraisal-based per-share value of the portfolio net of debt, recalculated on a schedule. NAV is both your entry price and the basis for redemptions, so ask how often it is updated, who performs the appraisals, and what assumptions underlie it. An infrequent or optimistic NAV can overstate what your shares are really worth.

faq.q: What should I check before investing in a private REIT?
a: The sponsor's track record through a full cycle, the portfolio's diversification and leverage, the full fee load and net return, whether distributions are supported by cash flow, and the redemption, lock-up, and NAV terms. Clear answers signal transparency; evasiveness on any of them is a reason to step back. Review the specifics with your own advisors.

title: How to Read a DST Offering: Fees, Debt, and Distributions
lead: Every DST private placement memorandum tells its story in three numbers: the fee load, the debt, and the distribution. Here is how to find them, weigh them, and read the risk factors that surround them.

A DST offering is sold by a document, not a pitch. The private placement memorandum runs a few hundred pages, and most of it is boilerplate, but the deal lives in three numbers: what you pay to get in, how much debt sits on the property, and what the trust expects to distribute. Find those three, weigh them against each other, and read the risk factors that frame them, and you can tell a strong offering from a weak one in an afternoon. This guide walks the PPM the way a practitioner reads it, in the order the numbers actually matter, and points out where the durability of a deal hides behind a headline rate.
takeaways: The whole offering is in the PPM. Read the fee table, the loan terms, the projected distribution, the rent roll, and the risk factors before anything else.
The fee load is the spread between what you pay and what the trust pays for the real estate. A high load can be justified by a hard asset to acquire, but it has to be earned back.
Debt is non-recourse at the trust level. Leverage lifts the distribution rate, and it lifts the risk of a wipe-out if values fall. Read the LTV and the loan maturity together.
The distribution rate is not the return, and it is not a yield you are owed. Test it against the rent roll and the lease expirations to see whether it can last.
The sponsor's full-cycle record is the single best predictor. Count how many programs they have taken full cycle and whether those met their projections.
The seven deadly sins constraints freeze the trustee. They cannot raise new money, refinance, or make major new investments, so the PPM has to plan for trouble in advance through reserves.

sections.heading: What a PPM is and how it is organized
paras: A Delaware Statutory Trust is offered to accredited investors through a private placement memorandum, the PPM, under Regulation D. It is the governing document of the deal and the only place the real terms live. A broker's flyer will give you a headline distribution rate and a glossy photo; the PPM gives you the fee table, the loan agreement summary, the projected cash flows, the rent roll, the sponsor's track record, and forty-plus pages of risk factors. If a fact is not in the PPM, it is not part of the deal.

The document follows a predictable order. It opens with a summary of terms, then the offering and the use of proceeds, then a description of the property and its leases, then the sponsor and its affiliates, then the projected financial results, then federal income tax consequences, and finally the risk factors and the trust agreement as exhibits. You do not read it front to back. You skip to the use-of-proceeds table to find the load, the loan summary to find the debt, and the projections to find the distribution, then you anchor each of those against the property description and the risk factors. The PPM review checklist lays out that order as a worksheet.

One structural fact shapes everything that follows. A DST is passive by design and frozen by law. The Internal Revenue Service requires the trust to be passive for investors to qualify for 1031 treatment, which means the trustee cannot do most of the things an active owner would do to save a struggling property. That constraint, often called the seven deadly sins, is the reason the PPM spends so much ink on reserves and loan terms. The deal has to be built to run on autopilot, because once it closes nobody can change the plan.

sections.heading: The fee load: what you pay versus what the trust buys
paras: The first number to find is the load. Go to the use-of-proceeds or estimated-use-of-proceeds table near the front of the PPM. It shows the total offering amount, then itemizes how much goes to the real estate and how much goes to fees and costs. The gap between the two is the load. If a trust raises $50 million and $42.5 million goes into the property and reserves, the load is roughly 15 percent. That spread is real money you are paying above the value of the underlying real estate on day one.
The load is built from several fees, and they fall into three buckets by when they hit.

sections.heading: Fee type When it is charged What to watch
paras: Acquisition / load Up front, out of the raise Selling commissions, dealer-manager fee, acquisition fee, organization and offering costs. Typically the largest bucket.
Asset management Annually, while you hold An ongoing fee, often a percentage of assets or gross revenue. It comes out of cash flow before your distribution.
Disposition At the full-cycle sale A fee on the sale price, sometimes with a promote or carried interest above a return hurdle.

A high load is not automatically a bad deal. Some of it pays for things that protect you: a real acquisition team, an arranged non-recourse loan, funded reserves, and the cost of registering and distributing the offering. The question is not whether the load is low but whether the property and the business plan can earn it back. A 12 percent load on a credit-tenant property with a 15-year lease is different from a 12 percent load on a half-empty building that needs a lease-up. The first has a clear path to recover the spread through years of contracted rent; the second is asking you to pay a premium for a turnaround that may or may not happen. Our breakdown of DST returns and fees goes deeper on how the load drags on net return over a typical hold.

Two checks keep you honest. First, compare the load to the property, not to other deals; a self-storage portfolio and a single net-lease pharmacy carry different fair loads. Second, read whether affiliates of the sponsor are on both sides of any fee. Acquisition fees paid to a sponsor affiliate, property management kept in-house, a disposition fee plus a promote, all are common and all are disclosed, but they stack, and you want to see the full stack before you judge the rate.

sections.heading: The debt and LTV: leverage cuts both ways
paras: The second number is the debt. Find the loan summary in the offering section. It gives you the loan amount, the loan-to-value ratio, the interest rate, whether the rate is fixed or floating, the term, and the maturity date. In a DST the debt is non-recourse at the trust level, which is one of the structure's real advantages: you are not personally on the hook for the mortgage, and your credit and your other assets are not pledged. The lender's recourse is to the property, not to you.

Loan-to-value is where you read how aggressive the deal is. A trust at 40 to 50 percent LTV is conservatively financed; a trust at 60 to 70 percent is using more debt to lift the distribution rate. Leverage is a multiplier in both directions. Borrow at a fixed rate below the property's cash yield and the spread flows to investors, raising the distribution. But the same debt that lifts the rate magnifies a decline: if the property value falls below the loan balance, the equity, your investment, is what absorbs the loss first. The higher the LTV, the thinner the cushion between a soft market and a wipe-out.

Read the LTV next to the loan maturity, because the two interact. A DST with a 5-to-7-year business plan and a 10-year fixed-rate loan is matched; the sponsor can sell before the loan comes due. A DST with a 5-year loan and a 7-year plan has a refinancing problem built in, and refinancing is one of the things the trustee is largely barred from doing. Floating-rate debt adds another layer: if rates rise, the interest expense rises with them, and the distribution gets squeezed from the top. A fixed-rate, long-dated, non-recourse loan at a moderate LTV is the quiet sign of a carefully structured deal.

One structural note. Many leveraged DSTs use a master lease: the trust leases the entire property to a master tenant affiliated with the sponsor, which then handles operations and subleasing. This exists to satisfy the passivity rules while still allowing the property to be actively managed. A master-lease structure is normal and not a red flag, but read who the master tenant is, how the rent to the trust is set, and what happens if the master tenant underperforms. In a direct-ownership DST without a master lease, the trust holds the leases itself, which is simpler but limits how the property can be operated.

sections.heading: The distribution rate versus its durability
paras: The third number is the one the flyer leads with: the projected distribution rate, often quoted as an annualized percentage of your invested capital, paid monthly. Start by separating three things that get blurred together. The distribution is the cash the trust expects to pay out. The yield is that cash as a percentage of what you put in. The total return is the distributions plus whatever gain or loss you realize when the property sells. A 6 percent distribution tells you nothing about total return, and it is not a coupon you are owed; it is a projection the sponsor can cut at any time if cash flow falls short.

The real question is durability. Read the distribution rate against the rent roll and the lease expiration schedule, both in the property section. A distribution backed by a single credit tenant on a 15-year absolute-net lease with contractual rent bumps is about as durable as DST cash flow gets; the rent is contracted, the tenant is investment-grade, and the escalations are written into the lease. A distribution backed by a multi-tenant building where 40 percent of the leases roll in the next three years is a different animal, because that cash flow depends on re-leasing space at rents nobody can promise.

Two patterns deserve special suspicion. First, a distribution rate that is higher than the property's actual in-place cash yield. That gap is usually filled either by leverage, which you have already sized, or by a return of capital, where the trust pays you partly with your own money or with funded reserves. A return of capital is disclosed and is not always bad, but a rate propped up by it is not the same as a rate covered by rent. Second, a near-term lease-up story, where the projected distribution rises over the hold as vacant space gets filled. That can work, but it is a forecast, not a contract, and you are paying today for cash flow that does not yet exist. Weigh the headline rate against how much of it is contracted versus hoped for.

sections.heading: The sponsor's full-cycle track record
paras: The single best predictor of how a DST performs is the firm running it. The PPM includes a prior-performance section and a description of the sponsor and its affiliates; that is where you do the work. The number that matters most is how many programs the sponsor has taken full cycle, meaning bought, held, and sold, returning capital to investors. A sponsor with thirty full-cycle programs has a record you can read. A sponsor with one offering and a deck has a promise.

For the full-cycle deals, ask two questions. Did they return investor capital, and did the realized results land near the projections the sponsors originally published. A sponsor that consistently hit or beat its underwriting across multiple market cycles has earned credibility; one whose deals routinely cut distributions or returned less than projected has told you something the current PPM will not. Prior performance is not a guarantee of future results, and the PPM says so, but a long, honest, full-cycle record is the closest thing to evidence you get in this market. Our guide to DST sponsor due diligence lists the specific questions to put to a sponsor, and how DSTs go full cycle explains what a clean exit looks like.

Read the affiliate web too. DST sponsors operate through layers of related entities, the sponsor, the trustee, the master tenant, the property manager, and the dealer-manager, and many of those collect fees. None of that is improper, and all of it is disclosed, but it tells you how the sponsor makes money and where their incentives sit. A sponsor that earns a large up-front load and little on the back end is paid to raise money; a sponsor with a meaningful disposition promote tied to a return hurdle is paid to perform. You want as much of the sponsor's compensation as possible tied to outcomes you share.

sections.heading: Property and lease quality
paras: Behind every distribution is a building and a tenant. The property section of the PPM describes the asset, its market, its physical condition, and its leases, and this is where you judge whether the cash flow has a solid foundation. Four things carry most of the weight. Tenant credit tells you how likely the rent is to be paid; an investment-grade national tenant is a different risk than a regional operator with no public rating. WALT, the weighted average lease term, tells you how long the contracted rent runs before it has to be renewed at unknown market rates. Market tells you whether the location can re-lease at all if a tenant leaves. And asset class, whether it is multifamily, industrial, net-lease retail, self-storage, or medical office, sets the baseline for how cyclical and how management-intensive the cash flow will be.

Match the asset to the structure. A long-WALT, single-tenant, credit-backed net-lease property pairs naturally with a master-lease DST and a long fixed-rate loan, because the cash flow is contracted and predictable. A multifamily or self-storage property with hundreds of short leases is more management-intensive and more sensitive to the local market, which raises the importance of the sponsor's operating skill and the reserves behind the distribution. Neither is better in the abstract. The point is that the property's risk profile should match the debt and the distribution promise stacked on top of it; a stabilized net-lease asset can carry a steadier, lower rate, while a value-add multifamily deal should be priced and underwritten for the lease-up risk it carries.

sections.heading: The seven deadly sins and why they matter to a PPM reader
paras: To preserve 1031 eligibility, the IRS requires a DST to be passive, and Revenue Ruling 2004-86 lists the things the trustee cannot do. Practitioners call them the seven deadly sins. The trustee cannot raise new capital from investors once the offering closes. It cannot renegotiate or refinance the existing loan, nor borrow new money. It cannot make major new investments or reinvest sale proceeds. It cannot do more than minor, non-structural improvements, and it cannot meaningfully renegotiate the leases or change the master lease terms outside narrow limits.

For a reader of the PPM, this list is not trivia; it is the reason the rest of the document is structured the way it is. Because the trustee cannot raise new money or refinance, a DST that hits a cash crunch has no easy rescue. An active owner with a struggling property can put in more equity, restructure the loan, or sell a piece. The DST trustee can do none of that. So the deal has to anticipate trouble before it closes, which is why a careful sponsor over-funds reserves and locks in long, fixed-rate debt. When you read a PPM, every constraint should send you back to two questions: are the reserves deep enough to survive a vacancy or a capital expense, and is the loan structured so it will not come due while the trust is unable to refinance. If a sponsor offers a master-lease workaround or a planned conversion to an LLC to regain flexibility, read exactly when and how that can happen and what it does to your 1031 status.

sections.heading: The risk factors: where diligence begins
paras: Most investors skip the risk-factors section because it reads like a wall of disclaimers, and that is a mistake. The risk factors are where real diligence begins. Yes, much of it is generic boilerplate that appears in every PPM, but the specific risks, the ones written for this property, this loan, this tenant, this market, are a map of what the sponsor's own lawyers think could go wrong. Read them with a highlighter.

Look for the risks that are specific rather than generic. A single-tenant deal will disclose tenant-concentration risk; if that tenant leaves, the income goes to zero. A leveraged deal will disclose the consequences of a loan default, including that the lender can foreclose and the investors can lose the entire investment. A floating-rate deal will disclose interest-rate risk in plain terms. A deal with near-term lease rollover will disclose re-leasing risk. The risk factors also restate the structural limits: the illiquidity, since there is no secondary market and you may not be able to sell your interest; the lack of control, since you cannot vote on or direct the property; and the dependence on the sponsor. None of these makes a deal bad. They tell you what you are accepting, and they let you check whether the sponsor's headline rate is honestly priced for the risks the lawyers felt obligated to spell out.

sections.heading: Reserves and lender requirements
paras: Because the trustee cannot raise more money, reserves are the deal's only shock absorber, and a PPM reader should treat them as a headline number, not a footnote. The offering will disclose how much of the raise is set aside as initial reserves and, often, how much ongoing cash flow is swept into reserves before distributions are paid. Deep reserves cost you a little distribution today and buy you durability tomorrow; a thin reserve raises the current rate and leaves the trust exposed to the first unexpected vacancy or roof replacement.

Lenders impose their own discipline, and the loan summary will show it. Many commercial loans require a lockbox or cash management arrangement, where rent flows to the lender first and is released to the trust only after debt service and reserve requirements are met. Loans often carry covenants, a minimum debt-service-coverage ratio for example, that can trap cash if the property underperforms, meaning distributions pause while the lender holds the money. These mechanics are disclosed, and they are not necessarily bad; they protect the loan, which protects the equity. But they tell you how a distribution can stop even when the property is occupied, so read the cash-management and covenant terms next to the distribution projection, not separately from it.

sections.heading: How the DST exits
paras: A DST is not a perpetual holding; it has a planned end. Most programs target a full-cycle sale in roughly five to ten years, when the sponsor sells the property and returns capital plus any gain to investors. The PPM will lay out the expected hold period and the business plan that drives the timing. Read it against the loan maturity you already found; a sponsor planning a 7-year hold on a 10-year loan has room, while one planning a long hold on short debt is relying on a refinance the trustee may not be able to execute.

At the exit you generally have three choices, and a good PPM and sponsor will frame them. You can take the cash and pay the deferred tax. You can 1031 again into another DST or another property, continuing the deferral, since a full-cycle sale is itself a taxable event you can roll forward. Or, in some programs structured for it, you can do a 721 exchange into the operating partnership of a REIT, trading your DST interest for OP units and moving from a single property into a diversified, professionally managed portfolio. The 721 route ends the chain of 1031 exchanges and changes your liquidity and tax profile, so it is a decision to make with your CPA, not a default. The point at the PPM stage is simpler: know the planned hold, confirm the debt is matched to it, and understand which exits the structure actually permits before you commit capital you cannot easily get back. For the full picture of the structure, start with the DST guide.

faq.q: What is the most important number in a DST PPM?
a: There are three, and they have to be read together: the fee load, the debt and loan-to-value, and the projected distribution. The load tells you what you pay above the real estate, the debt tells you how aggressive the deal is, and the distribution tells you what cash to expect, but only the rent roll behind it tells you whether that distribution can last.

faq.q: What is a typical DST load and is a high load bad?
a: Loads commonly run in the low double digits as a percentage of the raise, covering selling commissions, acquisition costs, and organization and offering expenses. A high load is not automatically bad. The question is whether the property and business plan can earn it back, which a credit-tenant property on a long lease can do more reliably than a building that needs a speculative lease-up.

faq.q: Is the projected distribution rate guaranteed?
a: No. The distribution rate is a projection, not a coupon you are owed. The sponsor can reduce or suspend distributions if cash flow falls short, if a tenant leaves, or if a loan covenant traps cash. Distributions are also not the same as total return, which depends on the eventual sale price.

faq.q: Why does loan-to-value matter so much in a DST?
a: The debt is non-recourse at the trust level, so you are not personally liable, but leverage still cuts both ways. Higher LTV lifts the distribution rate when times are good and thins the equity cushion when values fall. Because the trustee generally cannot refinance, the loan maturity should also be matched to the planned hold period.

faq.q: What is the sponsor's full-cycle track record and why check it?
a: Full cycle means a program the sponsor has bought, held, and sold, returning capital to investors. The number of full-cycle programs, and whether those met their original projections, is the best available evidence of how a sponsor performs across market conditions. A long, honest record carries more weight than any single deal's headline rate.

faq.q: What are the seven deadly sins in a DST?
a: They are the actions the IRS bars a DST trustee from taking so the trust stays passive and 1031-eligible: raising new capital, refinancing or borrowing, making new investments or reinvesting sale proceeds, and doing more than minor improvements or lease changes. They matter because a frozen trustee cannot rescue a struggling property, so the deal must rely on reserves and well-matched debt set up before closing.

faq.q: How and when does a DST end?
a: Most DSTs target a full-cycle sale in about five to ten years. At the sale you can take cash and pay the deferred tax, do another 1031 exchange to keep deferring, or, in programs structured for it, do a 721 exchange into a REIT for OP units. The planned hold should be matched to the loan maturity, which you can confirm in the PPM.

faq.q: Why read the risk-factors section if it is mostly boilerplate?
a: Because the deal-specific risks are buried in the boilerplate, and they are a map of what the sponsor's own lawyers think could go wrong. Tenant concentration, loan-default consequences, interest-rate risk on floating debt, and re-leasing risk are written for this property. They also restate the structural realities: illiquidity, no secondary market, and no investor control.

title: How to Read a REIT's FFO
lead: FFO — Funds From Operations — is the metric REIT investors use instead of GAAP net income. This guide explains why net income misleads for REITs, what FFO adds back, how to calculate and find FFO, how to use FFO per share and growth, and FFO's limitations.

If you try to evaluate a REIT using its GAAP net income, you'll often be misled — and that's not your fault. Real estate accounting includes a huge non-cash depreciation charge that distorts a REIT's reported earnings, making profitable, growing REITs look far less profitable than they are. To get around this, the REIT industry uses a standardized metric called Funds From Operations (FFO), defined by Nareit, which adds back real estate depreciation and removes one-time gains and losses on property sales to better reflect a REIT's recurring operating performance. Understanding how to read FFO — where to find it, how it's calculated, how to use FFO per share and its growth, and what FFO can't tell you — is essential to evaluating any REIT. This guide explains why net income misleads, what FFO adds back, how to calculate and find FFO, how to use FFO per share and growth, and FFO's limitations. This is educational information, not investment advice — verify current details and a REIT's own definitions before relying on them.
FFO is reported by listed and unlisted REITs alike, and our 2026 REIT investing guide shows where each type discloses its operating metrics.
takeaways: GAAP net income misleads for REITs because non-cash real estate depreciation understates earning power and property-sale gains distort earnings.
FFO = net income + real estate depreciation and amortization − gains on property sales (+ losses), per the Nareit standard.
Find FFO already reconciled in the REIT's earnings release and supplemental financial package, then use FFO per share and its growth.
FFO's limits: it doesn't subtract recurring maintenance capex (AFFO does), 'core' definitions vary by company, and it isn't a perfect cash measure.

sections.heading: Why Net Income Misleads for REITs
paras: GAAP net income — the standard bottom-line profit measure for most companies — is misleading for REITs, primarily because of how real estate depreciation works. Under GAAP, a company depreciates its buildings over time, recording a large non-cash expense that reduces reported net income each year. For an ordinary company with depreciating equipment, this roughly reflects economic reality. But real estate often holds or gains value over time rather than wearing out, so the depreciation charge overstates the economic 'cost' and understates the REIT's true earning power.

Because a REIT's assets are mostly real estate, this depreciation charge is enormous — often large enough to make a profitable, cash-generating REIT show low or even negative GAAP net income, even as it collects steady rents and grows. A second distortion comes from gains and losses on property sales: when a REIT sells a building, GAAP net income spikes (or drops) with the one-time gain or loss, making earnings lumpy and hard to compare from period to period. So net income, dragged down by non-cash depreciation and jolted by one-time sale gains, paints a distorted picture of a REIT's recurring operating performance. That's the core problem FFO was created to solve.

So GAAP net income misleads for REITs because non-cash real estate depreciation overstates costs (real estate often holds value) and one-time property-sale gains and losses distort earnings. So this is why FFO exists. Why net income misleads for REITs — GAAP depreciating buildings as a huge non-cash expense even though real estate often holds or gains value (understating true earning power), and one-time gains and losses on property sales jolting reported earnings — means net income can make a profitable, growing REIT look unprofitable and lumpy. The depreciation charge is the central distortion. Understanding this explains why the industry turned to FFO. GAAP net income misleads for REITs because non-cash real estate depreciation understates earning power and one-time property-sale gains distort earnings — the reason FFO was created.

sections.heading: What FFO Adds Back
paras: FFO — Funds From Operations — is the REIT industry's standard measure of operating performance, defined by Nareit to correct the distortions in net income. The core idea is simple: start with GAAP net income, then add back the non-cash real estate depreciation and amortization (the charge that doesn't reflect a real cash cost for value-holding real estate), and remove the one-time gains on property sales (and add back losses), so that what remains reflects the REIT's recurring, real-estate operating performance rather than accounting artifacts.

So the FFO formula is: net income, plus real estate depreciation and amortization, minus gains on property sales (plus losses on sales). By adding back depreciation, FFO reverses the largest non-cash distortion in REIT accounting; by stripping out property-sale gains and losses, it removes the lumpy, one-time items that have nothing to do with recurring operations. The result is a measure that's far more representative of the cash a REIT generates from running its real estate, and one that's comparable across REITs because Nareit standardizes the definition. So FFO adds back depreciation and removes sale gains to reveal recurring operating performance that net income obscures.

So what FFO adds back — real estate depreciation and amortization — and what it removes — gains (and losses) on property sales — transforms distorted net income into a measure of recurring operating performance. So this adjustment is the heart of FFO. What FFO adds back — starting from net income, adding back non-cash real estate depreciation and amortization (reversing the largest distortion) and removing one-time gains on property sales (adding back losses) per the Nareit standard — produces a measure of a REIT's recurring real-estate operating performance that's comparable across REITs. The depreciation add-back is the key correction. Understanding the adjustment is the heart of reading FFO. FFO starts from net income, adds back real estate depreciation and amortization, and removes gains on property sales (adds back losses), turning distorted net income into a measure of recurring operating performance.

The whole point of FFO is one big correction: add back the depreciation that GAAP subtracts but real estate doesn't actually lose, and you turn a distorted net income into a usable measure of operating performance.

sections.heading: Calculating and Finding FFO
paras: Calculating FFO follows the Nareit formula directly: take net income (per GAAP), add back real estate depreciation and amortization, and subtract gains on the sale of property (adding back any losses). Some adjustments also remove impairment write-downs of real estate, since those, like depreciation, are non-cash charges on value-holding assets. The arithmetic is straightforward once you have the inputs; the work is mainly in locating the right figures.

You'll find FFO in a REIT's quarterly and annual reporting — specifically in its earnings release and, most usefully, its supplemental financial package (often just called the 'supplemental'), which most REITs publish alongside earnings. sections.heading: FFO Per Share & Growth
paras: To make FFO useful for evaluating a REIT, look at it on a per-share basis and track its growth. FFO per share — total FFO divided by shares outstanding — is the REIT equivalent of earnings per share, and it's what matters to you as a shareholder, because a REIT that grows total FFO only by issuing lots of new shares isn't necessarily creating value per share. Watching FFO per share keeps the focus on the value accruing to each existing share rather than on headline totals.

FFO-per-share growth — its trend over multiple quarters and years — is one of the most important indicators of a REIT's operating health. Steady, rising FFO per share suggests a REIT is growing its recurring real-estate income on a per-share basis, which can support a growing dividend; flat or declining FFO per share is a warning sign. FFO per share also anchors valuation: the price-to-FFO (P/FFO) multiple — share price divided by FFO per share — is the REIT analog of the price-to-earnings ratio, used to compare a REIT's valuation to its peers and its own history, and one of the three pillars when you evaluate a REIT using FFO, AFFO, and NAV together. So FFO per share and its growth are the practical lenses for judging a REIT's performance and value.

sections.heading: Using FFO to Compare REITs
paras: One of FFO's biggest strengths is comparability, which makes it the workhorse metric for comparing REITs. Because Nareit standardizes the FFO definition, two different REITs' reported FFO are calculated on a broadly consistent basis, so you can line up their FFO-per-share growth and their price-to-FFO multiples and make meaningful comparisons — something you can't reliably do with GAAP net income, which is distorted differently depending on each REIT's depreciation schedule and sale activity.

In practice, you use FFO to compare REITs along a few dimensions: which REIT is growing FFO per share faster, which trades at a higher or lower P/FFO multiple (and whether that gap is justified by growth, quality, or sector), and how each REIT's FFO covers its dividend. Comparing P/FFO across REITs in the same sector helps you gauge relative valuation, while comparing FFO-per-share growth helps you gauge relative momentum. The key is to compare like with like — REITs in the same sector with similar risk and growth profiles — since a data-center REIT and a net-lease REIT naturally trade at different multiples. So FFO's standardization is what makes cross-REIT comparison possible and meaningful.

So using FFO to compare REITs leverages its standardization to line up growth and valuation across REITs — best done within a sector, like with like. So comparability is FFO's defining advantage. Using FFO to compare REITs — relying on Nareit's standardized definition to line up FFO-per-share growth, price-to-FFO multiples, and dividend coverage across REITs (best within the same sector, comparing like with like) — leverages FFO's comparability, the advantage net income lacks. sections.heading: Limitations of FFO
paras: For all its usefulness, FFO has real limitations you should keep in mind. The most important is that FFO does not subtract recurring maintenance capital expenditures — the ongoing capital a REIT must spend to keep its properties competitive and leased (roofs, HVAC, tenant improvements, leasing commissions). Because these are real, recurring cash costs, FFO overstates the cash truly available to fund dividends. This is exactly the gap that AFFO (Adjusted FFO) is designed to close, by subtracting maintenance capex and other normalizations from FFO — which raises the question of whether AFFO or FFO matters more.

A second limitation is definitional drift: while Nareit's FFO is standardized, many REITs report 'adjusted,' 'core,' or 'normalized' FFO with company-specific adjustments (adding back acquisition costs, one-time items, or non-cash charges of their choosing), and these varying definitions aren't directly comparable across REITs. You have to check whether you're looking at Nareit FFO or a company-defined version. A third limitation is that FFO isn't a perfect cash-flow measure — it's an accounting-based proxy that still includes some non-cash items (like straight-line rent) and excludes others. So FFO is a powerful tool but not a complete one; it must be read alongside AFFO, the payout ratio, and a careful read of the REIT's balance sheet.

So FFO's limitations — it ignores recurring maintenance capex (AFFO addresses this), 'core' definitions vary and aren't comparable, and it isn't a perfect cash measure — mean it should be used with care and alongside other metrics. faq.q: What is FFO?
a: FFO stands for Funds From Operations, the REIT industry's standard measure of operating performance. It exists because GAAP net income is misleading for REITs, mainly due to the large non-cash real estate depreciation charge that understates a REIT's true earning power (real estate often holds or gains value rather than wearing out). FFO, defined by Nareit, corrects this: it starts with net income, adds back real estate depreciation and amortization, and removes one-time gains on property sales (adding back losses), so the result reflects a REIT's recurring real-estate operating performance rather than accounting artifacts. FFO is far more representative than net income of the cash a REIT generates from running its properties, and because Nareit standardizes the definition, FFO is comparable across REITs. You'll find it in a REIT's earnings release and supplemental financial package. So FFO is the metric REIT investors use instead of net income — a standardized measure of recurring operating cash flow that adds back depreciation and strips out one-time sale gains, giving a clearer picture of how a REIT is actually performing.

faq.q: Why is net income misleading for REITs?
a: Net income misleads for REITs mainly because of how real estate depreciation works under GAAP. Companies depreciate their buildings over time, recording a large non-cash expense that reduces reported net income each year. For ordinary equipment that wears out, this roughly reflects reality — but real estate often holds or gains value rather than declining, so the depreciation charge overstates the economic cost and understates a REIT's true earning power. Because a REIT's assets are mostly real estate, this depreciation charge is enormous, often large enough to make a profitable, cash-generating REIT show low or even negative GAAP net income even as it collects steady rents and grows. A second distortion comes from gains and losses on property sales: when a REIT sells a building, net income spikes or drops with the one-time gain or loss, making earnings lumpy and hard to compare across periods. So net income, dragged down by non-cash depreciation and jolted by one-time sale gains, paints a distorted picture of a REIT's recurring operating performance — which is exactly why the industry created FFO to provide a clearer measure.

faq.q: How do you calculate FFO?
a: You calculate FFO using the Nareit formula: start with GAAP net income, add back real estate depreciation and amortization, and subtract gains on the sale of property (adding back any losses on sales). Some calculations also add back impairment write-downs of real estate, since those, like depreciation, are non-cash charges on value-holding assets. The logic is to reverse the two main distortions in REIT net income — the large non-cash depreciation charge and the lumpy, one-time gains or losses from selling properties — so what remains reflects recurring operating performance. The arithmetic is straightforward once you have the inputs; the work is mostly in locating the right figures, which you'll find in the REIT's financial statements. In practice, you rarely have to compute FFO from scratch, because REITs report it themselves and show a reconciliation from net income to FFO in their earnings release and supplemental package. So FFO equals net income plus real estate depreciation and amortization minus property-sale gains (plus losses) — a simple formula whose purpose is to strip out the accounting items that make net income unrepresentative for a REIT.

faq.q: Where do I find a REIT's FFO?
a: You'll find a REIT's FFO in its quarterly and annual reporting — specifically in the earnings release and, most usefully, the supplemental financial package (often just called the 'supplemental') that most REITs publish alongside earnings. The supplemental typically presents a reconciliation that starts with GAAP net income and walks down to FFO, showing each add-back (real estate depreciation and amortization) and subtraction (gains on property sales), so you can see exactly how the REIT arrived at the figure. REITs report FFO because investors and analysts expect it, so you rarely have to compute it from scratch. The supplemental usually also reports FFO per share and often AFFO, along with property-level operating detail, debt schedules, and other useful data. Checking the reconciliation is worthwhile because it shows you precisely what's included — and whether the REIT is presenting Nareit FFO or a company-defined 'core' or 'adjusted' version. So look first to the earnings release and supplemental, find the net-income-to-FFO reconciliation, and confirm which definition of FFO you're reading before relying on the number for analysis or comparison.

faq.q: What is the difference between FFO and net income?
a: FFO and net income measure profitability differently, and for REITs the gap is large and important. Net income is the GAAP bottom line, which for a REIT is dragged down by a huge non-cash real estate depreciation charge and jolted by one-time gains or losses on property sales — so it tends to understate a REIT's recurring earning power and make results lumpy. FFO corrects these distortions: it starts with net income, adds back real estate depreciation and amortization (since real estate often holds value rather than wearing out), and removes the one-time property-sale gains (and adds back losses), leaving a measure of recurring real-estate operating performance. The practical result is that FFO is usually substantially higher than net income for a REIT, and far more representative of the cash the REIT generates from operations. Because Nareit standardizes FFO, it's also comparable across REITs in a way net income isn't. So the key difference is that net income reflects distorted GAAP accounting while FFO reflects recurring operating performance — which is why REIT investors rely on FFO, not net income, to evaluate a REIT's results.

faq.q: What is FFO per share?
a: FFO per share is a REIT's total Funds From Operations divided by its shares outstanding — the REIT equivalent of earnings per share (EPS). It matters because, as a shareholder, you care about the operating performance accruing to each share you own, not just the headline total. A REIT can grow its total FFO simply by issuing lots of new shares to buy more properties, but if FFO per share doesn't grow, existing shareholders aren't necessarily better off. Watching FFO per share keeps the focus on per-share value creation. FFO-per-share growth — its trend over multiple quarters and years — is one of the most important indicators of a REIT's operating health: steady, rising FFO per share suggests growing recurring income on a per-share basis, which can support a growing dividend, while flat or declining FFO per share is a warning sign. FFO per share also anchors valuation through the price-to-FFO (P/FFO) multiple, the REIT analog of the P/E ratio. So FFO per share is the practical figure for judging a REIT's performance and value — always prefer it to headline total FFO.

faq.q: What is P/FFO?
a: P/FFO is the price-to-FFO multiple — a REIT's share price divided by its FFO per share — and it's the REIT analog of the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. Because net income is distorted for REITs, the familiar P/E ratio isn't very useful for valuing a REIT, so investors use P/FFO instead, dividing the share price by FFO per share to gauge how much they're paying for each dollar of the REIT's recurring operating performance. P/FFO is used to compare a REIT's valuation to its peers and to its own history: a higher multiple may reflect stronger expected growth, higher quality, or a premium sector, while a lower multiple may reflect slower growth, higher risk, or being out of favor. As with any valuation multiple, the key is to compare like with like — REITs in the same sector with similar growth and risk profiles — since different sectors (for example, data centers versus net-lease) naturally command different multiples. So P/FFO is the standard REIT valuation multiple, and reading it well means comparing it across similar REITs and against a REIT's own historical range, while accounting for differences in growth, quality, and sector.

faq.q: Do all REITs report FFO the same way?
a: Mostly yes for the headline figure, but with important caveats. Nareit defines FFO, so the great majority of REITs report a Nareit-compliant FFO calculated on a broadly consistent basis — net income, plus real estate depreciation and amortization, minus gains on property sales (plus losses) — which is what makes FFO comparable across REITs. So when you're looking at the standard 'FFO' line, you can generally trust that two REITs computed it similarly. The caveat is that many REITs also report a 'core,' 'adjusted,' 'normalized,' or 'recurring' FFO alongside the Nareit figure, adding back items of their own choosing — acquisition costs, one-time charges, certain non-cash items, or other company-specific adjustments. These company-defined versions aren't standardized and aren't directly comparable across REITs, so you have to check which line you're reading. Some REITs also differ in how they treat impairments or particular non-recurring items even within their Nareit FFO. So the practical rule is to confirm you're comparing Nareit FFO to Nareit FFO when you compare REITs, and to read the reconciliation to understand any company-specific adjustments before relying on a 'core' or 'adjusted' figure. Standardization applies to the base FFO, not to every variant a REIT may present.

faq.q: Why is FFO better than net income for REITs?
a: FFO is better than net income for evaluating REITs because it corrects two distortions that make net income unrepresentative. First, it adds back real estate depreciation and amortization — the large non-cash charge that GAAP requires but that doesn't reflect economic reality for real estate that often holds or gains value. This add-back reverses the single biggest reason a profitable REIT can show low or negative net income. Second, FFO removes one-time gains and losses on property sales, which otherwise make net income lumpy and hard to compare from period to period. The result is a measure of a REIT's recurring real-estate operating performance — far closer to the cash the REIT actually generates from running its properties. On top of that, because Nareit standardizes the FFO definition, FFO is comparable across REITs, while net income is distorted differently for each REIT depending on its depreciation schedule and sale activity. So FFO is better because it strips out non-cash depreciation and one-time sale gains to reveal recurring performance, and because its standardization enables meaningful comparison — two things net income can't do for a REIT.

faq.q: Does FFO measure cash flow exactly?
a: No — FFO is a useful proxy for a REIT's operating cash flow, but it isn't a perfect or exact cash-flow measure. FFO is an accounting-based metric: it starts from GAAP net income and makes specific adjustments (adding back real estate depreciation and amortization, removing property-sale gains and losses), but it still includes some non-cash items and excludes others. For example, FFO doesn't subtract recurring maintenance capital expenditures — the real, ongoing cash a REIT must spend to keep its properties competitive and leased — so it overstates the cash truly available to fund dividends. It also typically includes straight-line rent adjustments, which are non-cash. These gaps are exactly why analysts also use AFFO (Adjusted FFO), which subtracts maintenance capex and straight-line rent to better approximate distributable cash. So FFO should be understood as a standardized measure of recurring operating performance, not as exact cash flow. It's the right starting point for evaluating a REIT, but for questions about cash and dividend coverage you should look to AFFO and the actual cash-flow statement alongside it. Use FFO knowing what it does and doesn't capture.

faq.q: What are the limitations of FFO?
a: FFO has several limitations to keep in mind. The most important is that it does not subtract recurring maintenance capital expenditures — the ongoing capital a REIT must spend to keep properties competitive and leased (roofs, HVAC, tenant improvements, leasing commissions). Because these are real, recurring cash costs, FFO overstates the cash truly available to fund dividends; AFFO (Adjusted FFO) is designed to close this gap. A second limitation is definitional drift: while Nareit's FFO is standardized, many REITs also report 'adjusted,' 'core,' or 'normalized' FFO with company-specific adjustments that aren't directly comparable across REITs, so you must check which version you're reading. A third limitation is that FFO isn't a perfect cash-flow measure — it's an accounting proxy that still includes some non-cash items (like straight-line rent) and excludes others. So while FFO is the right primary metric for a REIT's operating performance, it's powerful but incomplete: read it alongside AFFO (for distributable cash and dividend coverage), the payout ratio, and the balance sheet. Knowing FFO's limits keeps you from over-relying on a single number when evaluating a REIT.

faq.q: What is the difference between FFO and AFFO?
a: FFO and AFFO are related REIT metrics, with AFFO building on FFO to better approximate distributable cash. FFO (Funds From Operations) starts with net income, adds back real estate depreciation and amortization, and removes property-sale gains, giving a standardized measure of recurring operating performance. AFFO (Adjusted FFO) takes FFO and goes further, subtracting recurring maintenance capital expenditures and straight-line rent adjustments (and sometimes other normalizations), so it more closely reflects the actual cash available to fund the dividend. The key trade-off is standardization versus accuracy: FFO is more standardized (Nareit defines it) and therefore more comparable across REITs, while AFFO is more economically accurate as a cash measure but less standardized, since companies define their maintenance-capex and other adjustments differently. In practice, investors use both — FFO for comparability and valuation (P/FFO), and AFFO for assessing dividend sustainability via the AFFO payout ratio. So the difference is that FFO measures recurring operating performance in a comparable way, while AFFO refines FFO into a closer estimate of distributable cash — and reading both gives a fuller picture of a REIT than either alone.

faq.q: Should I rely only on FFO to evaluate a REIT?
a: No — FFO is an essential metric, but you shouldn't rely on it alone. FFO is the right primary measure of a REIT's recurring operating performance and the basis for the P/FFO valuation multiple, but it has limitations: it ignores recurring maintenance capex (so it overstates distributable cash), 'core' versions vary by company, and it isn't a perfect cash measure. A sound REIT analysis uses FFO alongside several other tools. AFFO refines FFO into a closer estimate of distributable cash and supports the dividend-coverage analysis (the AFFO payout ratio). The balance sheet — leverage, debt maturities, and interest coverage — reveals financial risk that FFO doesn't capture. NAV (net asset value) estimates the underlying real estate value per share. And property-level metrics like occupancy, same-store NOI growth, and lease expirations show operational health. So treat FFO as the starting point and the key per-share growth and valuation gauge, but combine it with AFFO, the payout ratio, the balance sheet, NAV, and operating fundamentals for a complete view. Relying on any single metric — even one as useful as FFO — risks missing important parts of the picture.

faq.q: Is higher FFO always better?
a: Not necessarily — higher FFO is generally good, but the figure needs context to be meaningful. First, focus on FFO per share rather than total FFO: a REIT can grow total FFO simply by issuing new shares to buy properties, but if FFO per share doesn't grow, existing shareholders aren't better off, so per-share growth is what matters. Second, consider how the FFO was achieved — sustainable, recurring growth from rising rents and good operations is more valuable than a one-time bump, and FFO supported by excessive leverage carries more risk. Third, remember FFO overstates distributable cash because it ignores maintenance capex, so a high FFO doesn't automatically mean a well-covered dividend; check AFFO and the payout ratio for that. Fourth, valuation matters — a REIT with strong FFO growth may already trade at a high P/FFO multiple that prices it in. So higher FFO per share, grown sustainably and at a reasonable valuation, is what to look for, not simply a bigger headline number. Context — per-share basis, quality and sustainability of growth, leverage, dividend coverage, and valuation — determines whether higher FFO is actually better.
