faq.q: What is a REIT's net asset value (NAV)?
a: A REIT's net asset value (NAV) is an estimate of what its underlying real estate is worth, net of its debts, on a per-share basis. You take the estimated market value of all the REIT's properties, subtract its liabilities (mortgages and other debt), and divide by the shares outstanding to get a per-share figure. The hardest part is valuing the properties, since real estate isn't continuously quoted; analysts usually estimate value with a cap-rate approach — dividing a property's net operating income (NOI) by an assumed market cap rate. Because that assumed cap rate drives the result, NAV is sensitive to the assumption and is genuinely an estimate, not a fixed fact. So NAV represents the estimated per-share, private-market value of a REIT's real estate after subtracting its liabilities. It's a useful anchor for what the underlying assets are worth — and the reference point against which a traded REIT's market price is compared to find a premium or discount.

faq.q: What does it mean for a REIT to trade at a premium to NAV?
a: A REIT trades at a premium to NAV when its market share price is higher than its estimated net asset value per share. In other words, the market is willing to pay more than the appraised private-market value of the REIT's properties net of debt. A premium usually reflects optimism — the market may expect growth in rents and net operating income, value the quality of the management team or the portfolio, or anticipate value creation through development and acquisitions. A modest premium for a high-quality, growing REIT can be reasonable. But an unusually large premium raises the question of whether the market has gotten ahead of itself and the shares have become overvalued relative to the underlying real estate. So a premium signals that the market values the REIT above its estimated NAV — often for good reasons like growth and quality, but sometimes a sign of overvaluation. Judge a premium against the REIT's growth prospects, quality, and its own history.

faq.q: What does a discount to NAV mean?
a: A REIT trades at a discount to NAV when its market share price is lower than its estimated net asset value per share — the market is paying less than the appraised private-market value of the REIT's properties net of debt. A discount can mean different things. Sometimes it signals genuine concern: the market may doubt the carrying values, worry about a stretched balance sheet or near-term debt maturities, question management or strategy, or have soured on the whole sector. Other times, a discount can signal a potential value opportunity — sound real estate and cash flows whose shares were dragged down by broad pessimism, rate fears, or sector rotation rather than by anything wrong with the company. So a discount is a starting point for analysis, not a conclusion. You have to investigate why the discount exists before deciding whether it reflects real risk or a mispriced bargain. The cause determines the meaning.

faq.q: Why does a traded REIT's price differ from its NAV?
a: A traded REIT's price differs from its NAV because the two are produced by completely different mechanisms. NAV is an appraisal-style, private-market estimate — analysts value the properties (often by applying an assumed cap rate to net operating income) and subtract liabilities. The share price, by contrast, is set continuously by the public market, reflecting investor sentiment, interest-rate expectations, growth assumptions, liquidity preferences, and broad market swings, not just the appraised value of the buildings. So the market price can run ahead of NAV (a premium) when optimism is high or fall below it (a discount) when pessimism dominates — even though both supposedly describe the same underlying real estate. Private-market and public-market values genuinely diverge, sometimes for long stretches. So the gap between price and NAV isn't an error; it's the difference between how the market prices a REIT today and how appraisal-based methods estimate its real estate is worth. That gap is itself a piece of information.

faq.q: How is NAV calculated for a REIT?
a: NAV is calculated by estimating the market value of a REIT's real estate, subtracting its liabilities, and dividing by shares outstanding. The challenging step is valuing the properties. Analysts most often use a capitalization-rate (cap-rate) approach: for each property (or the portfolio), they take the net operating income (NOI) and divide it by an assumed market cap rate to estimate value — a lower cap rate implies a higher value, and vice versa. They sum those property values, add any other assets, then subtract debt and other liabilities from the balance sheet. Dividing the resulting net value by the shares outstanding gives NAV per share. Because the cap-rate assumption drives the property values, the NAV is highly sensitive to it — different reasonable assumptions yield different NAVs. So NAV calculation combines a cap-rate-based property valuation with balance-sheet liabilities to reach a per-share figure. Understanding the cap-rate step explains why NAV is an estimate, and a range, rather than a single precise number.

faq.q: Is a REIT trading below NAV always a good buy?
a: No — a REIT trading below NAV (at a discount) is not automatically a good buy. A discount can mean the market has correctly identified problems the appraisal-based NAV doesn't fully capture: a stretched balance sheet, looming debt maturities, declining occupancy or rents, weak or conflicted management, or a structurally challenged sector. In those cases, the 'cheap' price reflects real risk, and the NAV itself may be overstated. A discount can also reflect a genuine opportunity — sound real estate mispriced by broad pessimism — but you can't tell which case you're in without investigating the cause. So treat a discount as a question, not an answer. Look at FFO/AFFO trends, dividend coverage, leverage and maturities, sector conditions, and why the discount exists. So a below-NAV price can be a bargain or a value trap; only analysis of the underlying business and balance sheet reveals which. Don't buy a REIT simply because it trades below NAV.

faq.q: How should I use NAV alongside FFO and AFFO?
a: NAV and the cash-flow metrics FFO and AFFO answer different questions, and they're strongest together. NAV estimates what the REIT's real estate is worth (an asset-value view), while funds from operations (FFO) and adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) measure the recurring cash the REIT generates and can distribute (an earnings/cash-flow view). A discount to NAV is far more attractive when paired with solid, growing FFO/AFFO and a well-covered dividend — you'd be buying sound cash flow at less than estimated asset value. The same discount is a warning if FFO/AFFO is shrinking and the dividend is stretched. Conversely, a premium to NAV may be justified by strong FFO/AFFO growth. So use NAV to gauge asset value and FFO/AFFO to gauge cash-flow quality and dividend safety, then read the premium or discount in light of both. Combining the asset view (NAV) with the cash-flow view (FFO/AFFO) and the balance sheet gives a far more complete picture than any single metric alone.

faq.q: Do non-traded REITs have NAV premiums or discounts?
a: Non-traded REITs are priced differently, so the premium/discount concept works differently for them. A publicly traded REIT has a market price set continuously by an exchange, which can diverge from its appraisal-based NAV — producing the premiums and discounts this article describes. A non-traded REIT, by contrast, isn't exchange-listed; it's typically sold and redeemed at a periodically published NAV. So there generally isn't a continuous market price diverging from NAV the way there is for a traded REIT — the NAV essentially is the transaction price, updated periodically. That said, the NAV of a non-traded REIT is still an estimate sensitive to assumptions and can lag actual market conditions, and the price at which you could actually exit (subject to capped, sometimes-suspended redemptions) may differ from headline NAV. So premiums and discounts to NAV are mainly a traded-REIT phenomenon, while non-traded REITs transact at periodic NAV — but in both cases NAV remains an estimate to scrutinize, not a guaranteed value.

faq.q: Why is NAV considered an estimate rather than a fact?
a: NAV is an estimate because its largest component — the value of the REIT's real estate — can't be observed directly the way a stock price can. Real estate doesn't trade continuously, so analysts estimate property value, most often by applying an assumed capitalization rate to net operating income. That cap-rate assumption drives the result: reasonable analysts can choose different cap rates and arrive at materially different property values, and therefore different NAVs, for the same REIT. NAV is also a snapshot in time — values change with rates, demand, and conditions, and appraisal-based estimates are updated periodically, so they can lag the market. Add in judgment calls about which assets and liabilities to include and how to value them, and you get a figure that is genuinely a range of plausible values rather than one precise number. So NAV should be treated as an informed estimate, useful for context and comparison, not as a hard fact or a guaranteed price. Always check the assumptions behind a published NAV.

faq.q: Can NAV become stale or outdated?
a: Yes — NAV can become stale, and this is one of its key limitations. Real estate values move continuously with interest rates, capital-market conditions, supply and demand, and tenant health, but appraisal-based NAV estimates are produced periodically rather than continuously. So a published NAV reflects the assumptions and conditions as of when it was prepared, which can lag the current market — sometimes meaningfully, especially in a fast-moving rate environment where cap rates and property values are shifting quickly. In such periods, a REIT's true private-market value may have changed before the NAV is updated, so the stated NAV may overstate or understate reality. This staleness is part of why a traded REIT's market price (which updates in real time) can diverge from its NAV: the market may already be pricing in changes the NAV hasn't yet captured. So always consider how recent an NAV estimate is and whether conditions have shifted since. A stale NAV can give a false sense of precision, so weight it accordingly in your analysis.

faq.q: How do interest rates affect REIT NAV and premiums or discounts?
a: Interest rates affect both NAV and the premium or discount in important ways. On NAV: rising rates tend to push cap rates higher, and a higher cap rate applied to the same net operating income produces a lower estimated property value — so rising rates generally pressure NAV downward (and falling rates can lift it). On the premium/discount: REIT share prices are sensitive to rates and often react faster than appraisal-based NAVs update, so when rates rise, traded REITs frequently fall to discounts as the market prices in higher cap rates before NAVs are revised; when rates fall, REITs may swing to premiums. This timing mismatch is a common reason discounts widen in rising-rate environments and narrow when rates ease. So interest rates influence the appraised value (through cap rates) and the market's pricing (often faster), which is why rate moves drive much of the variation in REIT premiums and discounts. Understanding the rate sensitivity helps you interpret whether a discount reflects rates, fundamentals, or both.

faq.q: What's the difference between NAV and book value for a REIT?
a: NAV and book value are different measures, and the distinction matters for REITs. Book value (or shareholders' equity) comes from the balance sheet under accounting rules, where real estate is generally carried at historical cost less accumulated depreciation. Because real estate often appreciates over time while accounting depreciation steadily reduces its carrying value, a REIT's book value can sit well below the actual market value of its properties — making book value a poor proxy for what the real estate is worth. NAV addresses this by re-estimating the properties at current market value (typically via a cap-rate approach) rather than depreciated cost, then subtracting liabilities. So NAV aims to reflect today's private-market value of the assets, whereas book value reflects depreciated historical cost. For REITs, NAV is generally the more meaningful asset-value gauge precisely because depreciation distorts book value. So when valuing a REIT's assets, lean on NAV rather than book value — but remember NAV is still an estimate dependent on assumptions.

faq.q: Should I compare a REIT's discount to its peers?
a: Yes — comparing a REIT's premium or discount to its sector peers (and to its own history) is one of the most useful ways to use NAV. An NAV gap in isolation tells you little; in context, it tells you a lot. If a REIT trades at a much wider discount than similar REITs in the same sector, that gap warrants investigation — it may flag specific concerns about that REIT's balance sheet, management, or assets, or it may flag an opportunity if the discount looks unjustified. If most REITs in a sector trade at discounts, the issue may be sector-wide (rates, sentiment, structural headwinds) rather than company-specific. Comparing to the REIT's own historical premium/discount range adds another reference point: a REIT trading far below its typical level invites a closer look at what changed. So use peer and historical comparison to turn a raw premium or discount into a relative signal. Context — versus comparable REITs and versus the REIT's own history — is what makes NAV analysis actionable rather than abstract.

faq.q: Does a premium to NAV mean a REIT is overvalued?
a: Not necessarily — a premium to NAV doesn't automatically mean a REIT is overvalued. A premium means the market is paying more than the estimated appraisal value of the properties net of debt, and that can be entirely rational. High-quality REITs with strong, growing funds from operations, durable competitive advantages, skilled management, and development pipelines often trade at premiums because the market is paying for future growth and value creation that a static, asset-based NAV doesn't capture. In those cases, the premium reflects expected earnings growth, not overvaluation. That said, an unusually large premium — well above the REIT's history or its peers — does raise the question of whether the market has gotten ahead of itself, pricing in growth that may not materialize. So a modest, justified premium can coexist with a fairly or even attractively valued REIT, while an extreme premium warrants caution. So judge a premium against the REIT's growth, quality, and historical range rather than assuming any premium signals overvaluation. NAV is one input, not the whole verdict.

title: REIT Payout Ratios Explained
lead: How do you tell whether a REIT's dividend is well-covered or stretched? This guide explains what a payout ratio measures, why the AFFO payout ratio is more meaningful than the FFO version, how to distinguish a healthy ratio from a stretched one, how to spot dividend risk, and how to compare ratios across REITs.

For an income investor, a REIT's dividend is the main event — and the payout ratio is one of the clearest ways to judge whether that dividend is sustainable. A payout ratio measures how much of a REIT's cash flow it pays out as dividends: dividends divided by funds from operations (FFO), or, more usefully, dividends divided by adjusted funds from operations (AFFO). The lower the ratio, the more cushion the REIT keeps; the closer it runs to 100% — or above it — the more stretched the dividend becomes, and the higher the risk of a cut. But payout ratios aren't read in a vacuum: sector norms vary, AFFO is more meaningful than FFO, and a rising payout ratio or distributions funded by debt or return of capital can warn of trouble before a cut happens. This guide explains what a payout ratio measures, the FFO-versus-AFFO distinction, healthy versus stretched levels, how to spot dividend risk, and how to compare across REITs. Verify current figures with the REIT's own reporting — this is educational information, not investment advice.
Payout ratios behave differently depending on whether a REIT is publicly traded or privately held, a distinction our complete guide to private and non-traded REITs covers.
takeaways: A payout ratio is dividends divided by cash flow (FFO or AFFO) — it shows how much of a REIT's distributable cash goes out as dividends.
The AFFO payout ratio is more meaningful than the FFO version, because AFFO subtracts recurring capex and best approximates distributable cash.
A healthy payout sits comfortably below 100% of AFFO (cushion for capex and downturns); near or above 100% is stretched and risky.
Spot dividend risk through an AFFO payout over 100%, declining coverage, and distributions funded by return of capital or debt — and compare within a sector.

sections.heading: What a Payout Ratio Measures
paras: A REIT's payout ratio measures the share of its cash flow that it distributes to shareholders as dividends. In its simplest form, the payout ratio is dividends divided by a measure of cash flow — most commonly funds from operations (FFO) or adjusted funds from operations (AFFO). If a REIT pays out 80 cents in dividends for every dollar of cash flow, its payout ratio is 80%. The ratio tells you, at a glance, how much room the REIT has between what it earns and what it pays.

Why not just use net income, as you would for an ordinary stock? Because REIT net income is distorted by large non-cash depreciation charges on real estate, which make earnings look far lower than the actual cash the REIT generates. A REIT can easily pay dividends well in excess of net income while still covering them comfortably from cash flow. That's exactly why REIT-specific cash-flow measures — FFO and especially AFFO — are used in the denominator instead of net income, so the payout ratio reflects real distributable cash rather than an accounting figure depressed by depreciation.

So a payout ratio measures dividends as a share of a REIT's cash flow (FFO or AFFO), revealing how much cushion sits between earnings and the dividend. What a payout ratio measures — dividends divided by a cash-flow measure (FFO or, more meaningfully, AFFO), expressed as a percentage that shows how much of the REIT's distributable cash is being paid out — is the foundation of judging dividend sustainability. It uses cash-flow measures rather than net income because depreciation distorts REIT earnings. A lower ratio means more cushion. Understanding what the payout ratio measures frames everything that follows about dividend safety. A payout ratio is dividends ÷ cash flow (FFO or AFFO) — it shows how much of a REIT's distributable cash goes out as dividends, and how much cushion remains.

sections.heading: FFO vs. AFFO Payout Ratios
paras: There are two common versions of the payout ratio, and the difference between them matters. The FFO payout ratio divides dividends by funds from operations — net income with real estate depreciation and amortization added back and gains on property sales removed. FFO is a big improvement over net income for REITs, but it still doesn't account for the recurring capital a REIT must spend to keep its properties competitive, nor for non-cash rent timing.

The AFFO payout ratio divides dividends by adjusted funds from operations — FFO further reduced by recurring maintenance capital expenditures (the money spent to maintain existing properties) and adjusted for items like straight-line rent. Because AFFO subtracts the real, recurring cash a REIT must reinvest just to sustain its portfolio, it more closely approximates the cash actually available to pay dividends. As a result, the AFFO payout ratio is the more meaningful and conservative measure: it's typically higher than the FFO payout ratio for the same REIT (because the denominator is smaller), and it gives a truer picture of dividend coverage.

So while both ratios are used, the AFFO payout ratio is the more meaningful gauge of dividend safety because AFFO best approximates distributable cash. FFO vs. AFFO payout ratios — the FFO version dividing dividends by funds from operations (net income plus real estate depreciation, minus property gains) and the AFFO version dividing dividends by adjusted FFO (FFO minus recurring maintenance capex and straight-line-rent adjustments) — differ because AFFO subtracts the recurring cash needed to sustain the portfolio. AFFO better approximates distributable cash, so its payout ratio is more meaningful (and usually higher). Understanding the FFO/AFFO distinction tells you which ratio to trust. The AFFO payout ratio is more meaningful than the FFO version because AFFO subtracts recurring capex and approximates the cash truly available for dividends.

Net income misleads on REITs and even FFO flatters them — only AFFO subtracts the recurring capital a REIT must spend just to keep its buildings competitive, which is why the AFFO payout ratio is the honest one.

sections.heading: Healthy vs. Stretched Ratios
paras: What counts as a healthy payout ratio? There's no single magic number, but the logic is straightforward: a moderate AFFO payout ratio leaves a cushion — retained cash the REIT can use for capital expenditures, debt paydown, acquisitions, or simply to absorb a downturn without cutting the dividend. A payout ratio comfortably below 100% of AFFO signals that the dividend is covered by distributable cash with room to spare, which is generally the sign of a sustainable distribution.

A stretched ratio is one that runs near or above 100% of AFFO. At that level, the REIT is paying out essentially all (or more than all) of its distributable cash, leaving little or no margin for error. If AFFO dips — because of rising costs, falling occupancy, higher interest expense, or a weak market — a payout already at or above 100% can't be sustained from cash flow, which raises the prospect of a dividend cut or of funding the gap with debt or asset sales. So the gap between the payout ratio and 100% is, in effect, the dividend's margin of safety: the smaller that gap, the more stretched and vulnerable the dividend.

So a healthy payout ratio sits comfortably below 100% of AFFO (leaving cushion), while a stretched one runs near or above 100% (leaving little margin and raising cut risk). Healthy vs. stretched ratios — a moderate AFFO payout leaving a cushion for capex, debt, acquisitions, and downturns versus a payout near or above 100% of AFFO that leaves no margin and signals risk — turn the payout ratio into a read on dividend durability. The distance below 100% is the margin of safety. A stretched ratio can't absorb a dip in AFFO. Understanding healthy versus stretched levels lets you judge whether a yield is built on solid ground. A healthy payout sits well below 100% of AFFO with cushion; a stretched one runs near or above 100%, leaving little margin and raising the risk of a cut.

sections.heading: Spotting Dividend Risk
paras: The payout ratio is a powerful early-warning tool for dividend risk, but the most telling signals come from watching it over time and looking at how the dividend is funded. The clearest red flag is a payout ratio above 100% of AFFO — the REIT is paying out more than its distributable cash, which can't continue indefinitely. Almost as important is the trend: a payout ratio that's steadily rising (declining coverage) suggests the dividend is growing faster than cash flow, or that cash flow is eroding, even if the ratio isn't yet above 100%.

Another warning sign is how the distribution is being funded. If a REIT is covering its dividend by classifying much of it as return of capital, by selling assets, or by borrowing, rather than from operating cash flow, the dividend may be unsustainable even if the headline ratio looks acceptable. Persistent return-of-capital-heavy distributions, in particular, can mean the REIT is effectively returning your own money rather than paying you out of earnings. So the combination of a high or rising AFFO payout ratio, deteriorating coverage, and distributions funded by debt or return of capital is the classic profile of a dividend at risk of being cut.

So dividend risk shows up as a payout ratio above 100% of AFFO, declining coverage over time, and distributions funded by debt or return of capital rather than operating cash. Spotting dividend risk — watching for an AFFO payout above 100%, a rising payout ratio (declining coverage), and distributions funded by return of capital, asset sales, or borrowing rather than operating cash flow — lets you anticipate a dividend cut before it happens. The trend matters as much as the level. Funding source reveals sustainability. Understanding these warning signs helps you avoid yields that are about to be reduced. Dividend risk appears as an AFFO payout over 100%, deteriorating coverage, and distributions funded by debt or return of capital — warning signs a cut may be coming.

A dividend cut rarely arrives without warning: a payout ratio creeping past 100% of AFFO, coverage that's slipping year over year, and distributions quietly funded by debt or return of capital usually flag it first.

sections.heading: Comparing Across REITs
paras: Payout ratios are most informative when compared the right way — within a sector, against peers and history, not across the entire REIT universe. That's because sector norms differ. Net-lease REITs, with long leases and minimal operating responsibilities, often run higher payout ratios because their cash flows are stable and predictable, so a 'normal' net-lease payout might look stretched for another sector. Growth-oriented sectors, by contrast, tend to retain more cash to fund expansion and so carry lower payout ratios. Comparing a net-lease REIT's payout to a high-growth REIT's would be misleading.

The right comparison is therefore relative: how does a REIT's AFFO payout ratio compare to similar REITs in the same sector, and to its own history? A REIT whose payout ratio is markedly higher than its sector peers, or that has been climbing relative to its own past, deserves a closer look — it may simply operate a more stable model, or it may have a dividend that's growing ahead of its cash flow. Pairing the payout ratio with the dividend yield is also useful: a high yield is reassuring only if the payout ratio shows the dividend is well-covered, and worrying if the payout ratio is stretched.

So compare payout ratios within a sector and against a REIT's own history, using AFFO and pairing the ratio with yield — not by comparing unlike REITs. Comparing across REITs — judging a REIT's AFFO payout ratio against peers in the same sector (net-lease running higher, growth sectors lower) and against its own history, and pairing it with the dividend yield to confirm coverage — turns the payout ratio into a relative measure of dividend safety. Sector norms vary, so context is essential. A payout far above peers warrants scrutiny. Understanding how to compare across REITs prevents false alarms and catches real outliers. Compare AFFO payout ratios within a sector and against a REIT's own history, and pair them with yield — sector norms differ, so context determines what's stretched.

sections.heading: Payout Ratios and Dividend Growth
paras: The payout ratio doesn't just tell you whether a dividend is safe today — it also says a lot about a REIT's capacity to grow that dividend tomorrow. A REIT with a moderate AFFO payout ratio retains a meaningful share of its distributable cash, and that retained cash, combined with growth in funds from operations, gives the REIT room to raise the dividend over time without stretching its coverage. So a lower payout ratio is often the fuel behind a reliable dividend-growth track record.

A REIT that already pays out nearly all of its AFFO has little such room: with no cushion, it can only grow the dividend as fast as AFFO itself grows, and any stumble in cash flow puts the existing payout at risk before growth is even on the table. This is why income investors who care about a rising income stream — not just a high current yield — pay attention to the payout ratio as a forward-looking indicator. A well-covered payout supports both stability and future increases; a stretched one constrains both. The interplay between the payout ratio and AFFO growth is, in effect, the engine of sustainable dividend growth.

So the payout ratio is a forward-looking signal too: a moderate, well-covered ratio leaves room to grow the dividend, while a stretched one constrains future increases. Payout ratios and dividend growth — a moderate AFFO payout retaining cash that, alongside FFO/AFFO growth, gives a REIT room to raise its dividend sustainably, versus a near-100% payout that leaves no cushion and caps growth at the pace of AFFO itself — show the payout ratio as a forward-looking indicator, not just a snapshot of current safety. Retained cash fuels future raises. A stretched payout constrains them. Understanding the link between payout and growth completes the picture of dividend quality. A moderate, well-covered payout ratio leaves room for sustainable dividend growth, while a stretched ratio constrains future increases — so the ratio signals both current safety and growth capacity.

faq.q: What is a REIT payout ratio?
a: A REIT payout ratio measures how much of the REIT's cash flow it distributes to shareholders as dividends. In its simplest form, it's dividends divided by a cash-flow measure — most commonly funds from operations (FFO) or, more usefully, adjusted funds from operations (AFFO). If a REIT pays 80 cents in dividends for every dollar of cash flow, its payout ratio is 80%. The ratio shows, at a glance, how much room sits between what the REIT generates and what it pays out. REITs use FFO or AFFO in the denominator rather than net income because large non-cash real estate depreciation charges distort REIT earnings, making net income a poor measure of distributable cash. So the payout ratio expresses dividends as a percentage of a REIT's cash flow, and the lower it is, the more cushion the REIT retains. It's one of the clearest tools for judging whether a REIT's dividend is sustainable — the foundation of dividend-safety analysis for income-oriented REIT investors.

faq.q: Why use FFO or AFFO instead of net income for a REIT payout ratio?
a: You use FFO or AFFO instead of net income because net income badly understates a REIT's true cash generation. Real estate accounting requires large non-cash depreciation charges, which steadily reduce reported earnings even though the buildings often hold or gain value and the REIT keeps collecting rent. As a result, a REIT can pay dividends far in excess of net income while still covering them comfortably from actual cash flow — so a net-income-based payout ratio for a REIT would often look alarming (well over 100%) even for a perfectly healthy company. Funds from operations (FFO) corrects this by adding depreciation back and removing one-time property gains; adjusted FFO (AFFO) goes further by subtracting recurring capital expenditures, giving an even better picture of distributable cash. So FFO and AFFO reflect the real cash a REIT can pay out, while net income is distorted by depreciation. That's why REIT payout ratios are built on FFO or AFFO — they measure dividend coverage against cash, not accounting earnings.

faq.q: What's the difference between the FFO and AFFO payout ratios?
a: The two ratios differ in their denominator, and the difference matters. The FFO payout ratio divides dividends by funds from operations — net income with real estate depreciation and amortization added back and property-sale gains removed. The AFFO payout ratio divides dividends by adjusted funds from operations — FFO further reduced by recurring maintenance capital expenditures (money spent to keep existing properties competitive) and adjusted for items like straight-line rent. Because AFFO subtracts the real, recurring cash a REIT must reinvest just to sustain its portfolio, it more closely approximates the cash actually available for dividends. So the AFFO payout ratio is the more conservative and meaningful measure — and, because its denominator is smaller, it's usually higher than the FFO payout ratio for the same REIT. So if FFO payout looks comfortable but AFFO payout is near 100%, the dividend is more stretched than the FFO figure suggests. For dividend-safety analysis, the AFFO payout ratio is the one to trust.

faq.q: Why is the AFFO payout ratio more meaningful?
a: The AFFO payout ratio is more meaningful because AFFO best approximates the cash a REIT can actually distribute. Funds from operations (FFO) improves on net income by removing distorting depreciation and property-sale gains, but it still ignores a real, recurring cost: the maintenance capital expenditures a REIT must spend to keep its buildings leasable and competitive (roofs, HVAC, tenant improvements, leasing costs). AFFO subtracts those recurring capital costs (and adjusts for non-cash items like straight-line rent), so it reflects the cash genuinely left over for dividends. Because the dividend is paid from real cash — not from FFO that hasn't yet accounted for required reinvestment — measuring the payout against AFFO gives a truer read on whether the dividend is covered. So the AFFO payout ratio captures dividend safety more honestly than the FFO version, which can make coverage look better than it is. So when assessing whether a REIT's dividend is sustainable, weight the AFFO payout ratio most heavily, while recognizing AFFO involves some estimation.

faq.q: What is a healthy REIT payout ratio?
a: There's no single magic number, but the logic is clear: a healthy payout ratio sits comfortably below 100% of AFFO, leaving a cushion of retained cash. That cushion can fund capital expenditures, debt paydown, or acquisitions, and — crucially — lets the REIT absorb a downturn (rising costs, falling occupancy, higher interest expense) without cutting the dividend. A payout ratio well under 100% of AFFO generally signals a dividend covered by distributable cash with room to spare. What counts as 'comfortably below' varies by sector: stable net-lease REITs can sustain higher payouts than growth-oriented REITs, which retain more cash to fund expansion. So rather than fixating on a universal threshold, judge the payout ratio against the REIT's sector norms and its own history, and look for a meaningful gap below 100% of AFFO. So a healthy payout ratio is one that leaves a clear margin of safety — enough cushion that a normal dip in cash flow won't put the dividend at risk. The bigger the gap below 100% of AFFO, the safer the dividend.

faq.q: What does a payout ratio over 100% mean?
a: A payout ratio over 100% means a REIT is paying out more in dividends than its cash flow supports — and that's a warning sign, especially when measured against AFFO. If the AFFO payout ratio exceeds 100%, the REIT is distributing more than its adjusted funds from operations, so the dividend isn't fully covered by distributable cash. That gap has to be filled somehow: by drawing down cash, selling assets, borrowing, or classifying part of the distribution as return of capital (returning investors' own money). None of those can continue indefinitely, so a payout sustainably above 100% of AFFO raises a real risk that the dividend will eventually be cut. There are nuances — a temporary spike above 100% due to a one-off (an acquisition timing issue, a short-term capex surge) may be manageable — but a persistent or rising payout above 100% is a classic red flag. So treat a payout ratio over 100% of AFFO as a signal to investigate why, how the gap is being funded, and whether the dividend is likely to hold. It often precedes a cut.

faq.q: How can a payout ratio help me spot dividend risk?
a: The payout ratio is one of the best early-warning tools for dividend risk, especially when you watch it over time and check how distributions are funded. The clearest red flag is an AFFO payout ratio above 100% — the REIT is paying out more than its distributable cash. Nearly as important is the trend: a payout ratio that's steadily climbing signals declining coverage, meaning the dividend is outgrowing cash flow (or cash flow is eroding) even if the ratio isn't yet above 100%. A third warning sign is the funding source: if a REIT covers its dividend largely through return of capital, asset sales, or borrowing rather than operating cash flow, the distribution may be unsustainable even when the headline ratio looks acceptable. So the combination of a high or rising AFFO payout, deteriorating coverage, and debt- or return-of-capital-funded distributions is the classic profile of a dividend at risk. So use the payout ratio's level, its trend, and the way the dividend is funded together to anticipate a cut before it's announced.

faq.q: Do payout ratios vary by REIT sector?
a: Yes — payout ratios vary meaningfully by sector, which is why they should be compared within a sector rather than across the whole REIT market. Net-lease REITs, which sign long leases and push most operating responsibilities (taxes, insurance, maintenance) onto tenants, tend to have very stable, predictable cash flows and lower recurring capital needs, so they often sustain higher payout ratios — a level that might look stretched elsewhere can be normal for net-lease. Growth-oriented sectors (like certain industrial, data center, or development-heavy REITs) typically retain more cash to fund expansion, so they carry lower payout ratios by design. Sectors with heavier recurring capital needs (some office and retail) may also run lower AFFO payouts to fund reinvestment. So a 'high' or 'low' payout ratio only has meaning relative to the sector's norms. So when you evaluate a payout ratio, compare it to similar REITs in the same sector and to the REIT's own history — a ratio that's normal for one sector can be a warning sign in another.

faq.q: What is return of capital in a REIT distribution?
a: Return of capital (ROC) is the portion of a REIT distribution that isn't paid out of current earnings or profits but instead represents a return of your own invested capital. For tax purposes, ROC generally isn't currently taxed; instead, it reduces your cost basis in the shares, deferring tax until you sell. A degree of ROC is common and often benign for REITs — it can result from the gap between cash flow and taxable income created by depreciation. But ROC matters for dividend-safety analysis: if a large and growing share of a REIT's distribution is classified as return of capital, it can be a sign that the REIT isn't fully covering its dividend from operating cash flow and is effectively returning investors' own money to sustain the payout. So a little ROC is normal; a lot, especially when rising, can be a warning sign worth pairing with the AFFO payout ratio. So watch the ROC component alongside coverage. Baker 1031 doesn't provide tax advice — confirm how ROC affects your basis and taxes with your tax advisor, since the treatment can be technical.

faq.q: Can a high-yielding REIT still have a safe dividend?
a: Yes — a high yield and a safe dividend aren't mutually exclusive, but you have to verify safety through the payout ratio rather than assume it. A high dividend yield can reflect a genuinely generous, well-covered distribution (common in stable, higher-payout sectors like net-lease or among mortgage REITs), or it can be a warning that the market has marked the price down because it expects a cut. The payout ratio — ideally the AFFO payout ratio — is how you tell the difference. If a high-yielding REIT shows an AFFO payout comfortably below 100%, stable or improving coverage, and distributions funded from operating cash flow, the high yield may well be sustainable. If the same yield comes with an AFFO payout near or above 100%, declining coverage, or heavy return-of-capital funding, the dividend is at risk despite (or because of) the high yield. So judge a high-yielding REIT's dividend by its payout ratio and coverage, not by the yield alone. A high yield is safe only when the underlying coverage confirms it.

faq.q: How do I find a REIT's payout ratio?
a: You can find or calculate a REIT's payout ratio from its financial reporting. REITs report funds from operations (FFO) and, increasingly, adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) in their quarterly and annual results, supplemental packages, and earnings materials, and they report the dividends they pay. The payout ratio is simply dividends divided by FFO (for the FFO payout ratio) or by AFFO (for the more meaningful AFFO payout ratio), usually expressed per share or in aggregate. Many financial data providers and REIT research services also publish these ratios. One caution: AFFO isn't standardized — different REITs (and analysts) may define recurring capital expenditures and adjustments slightly differently — so when comparing REITs, try to use a consistent definition and check the REIT's stated methodology. So look to the REIT's own supplemental reporting for FFO, AFFO, and dividends, then compute the ratio, or use a research source while noting its definitions. So always verify the figures and how AFFO was calculated, since the inputs involve some judgment and can affect the ratio.

faq.q: What does a rising payout ratio signal?
a: A rising payout ratio signals declining dividend coverage — and it's one of the most useful trends to watch. When a REIT's payout ratio climbs over time, it means the dividend is consuming a larger share of cash flow, which can happen for two reasons: the dividend is growing faster than cash flow, or cash flow (FFO/AFFO) is eroding while the dividend holds steady. Either way, the cushion between the distribution and the REIT's distributable cash is shrinking. A payout ratio that's been steadily rising toward 100% of AFFO is a warning even before it crosses that line, because it shows the margin of safety thinning. The trend can flag trouble — weakening occupancy, rising interest expense, higher capital needs — that a single snapshot of the ratio might miss. So a rising payout ratio is an early signal that a dividend may become unsustainable if the trend continues. So don't just look at the current payout ratio; look at its direction over several periods. A clearly rising trajectory deserves investigation into what's driving it and whether the dividend can hold.

faq.q: How should I compare payout ratios across REITs?
a: Compare payout ratios within a sector and against each REIT's own history — not across unlike REITs. Sector norms differ: net-lease REITs, with stable cash flows and low recurring capital needs, often run higher payout ratios that would look stretched for a growth-oriented REIT, while growth sectors retain more cash and carry lower ratios by design. So comparing a net-lease REIT's payout to a high-growth REIT's is misleading. The useful question is relative: how does a REIT's AFFO payout ratio compare to similar REITs in the same sector, and to its own past? A REIT whose payout is markedly higher than its sector peers, or that's been climbing relative to its history, warrants a closer look — it may simply run a more stable model, or it may have a dividend outgrowing its cash flow. Pairing the payout ratio with the dividend yield helps too: a high yield is reassuring only if the payout ratio confirms coverage. So use sector-relative and historical comparison, with AFFO, to make payout ratios a reliable measure of dividend safety rather than a source of false alarms.

faq.q: Does a low payout ratio mean a REIT is a better investment?
a: Not by itself — a low payout ratio is generally a positive for dividend safety, but it isn't the whole story. A low AFFO payout ratio means the REIT retains more cash, giving it a strong cushion to maintain (and potentially grow) the dividend, fund capital expenditures, pay down debt, or make acquisitions without raising outside capital. That retained cash can support future growth. But a low payout ratio can also mean the REIT is simply paying a smaller dividend relative to its cash flow — which may suit a growth investor but offer less current income than a higher-payout peer. And a low payout ratio doesn't guarantee a good investment if the underlying real estate, balance sheet, or growth prospects are weak. So a low payout ratio is reassuring for dividend sustainability and growth potential, but you still have to weigh yield, growth, leverage, sector, and valuation. So treat a low payout ratio as one favorable input — a sign of a well-covered, potentially growing dividend — within a broader analysis, not as a standalone verdict on whether a REIT is the better investment.

title: REIT Risks Every Investor Should Know
lead: REITs can offer attractive income and diversification, but they aren't risk-free. This honest guide walks through the key REIT risks every investor should know — interest-rate risk, sector and tenant concentration, leverage and refinancing risk, management and conflict risk, and market and liquidity risk — and how to mitigate them.

REITs are often presented in terms of their benefits — high dividends, diversification, passive real estate exposure — but a clear-eyed investor needs to understand the risks just as well. A REIT is a real investment in real estate that can lose value, cut its distribution, or underperform, and several distinct risks drive those outcomes. Rising interest rates can pressure REIT prices and, for some REITs, their earnings. Concentration in a single sector or tenant can magnify a downturn. Heavy leverage and looming debt maturities can force costly refinancing. Weak or conflicted management can erode returns. And market volatility (for traded REITs) and illiquidity (for non-traded REITs) add their own risks. The point isn't to scare you away from REITs — it's to help you invest with realistic expectations and to mitigate what you can. This guide walks through interest-rate risk, sector and tenant concentration, leverage and refinancing risk, management and conflict risk, and market and liquidity risk, then explains how to mitigate them. Note that past performance does not guarantee future results, and Baker 1031 does not provide tax or legal advice — verify current details before investing.
Before drilling into each risk, it helps to understand how the asset class works overall, which our comprehensive REIT primer lays out across traded and non-traded structures.
takeaways: Interest-rate risk is fundamental: rising rates can pressure REIT prices, valuations, and borrowing costs, and compress mortgage REITs' earning spreads.
Concentration risk — over-reliance on one sector, a few tenants, or one region — magnifies losses; diversification across sectors, tenants, and markets dampens it.
Leverage and refinancing risk make the balance sheet central: too much debt or near-term maturities in a high-rate environment can squeeze distributions or force asset sales.
Mitigate REIT risks through diversification (across REITs and sectors), quality (strong management, sound balance sheets), due diligence, and appropriate position sizing.

sections.heading: Interest-Rate Risk
paras: Interest-rate risk is one of the most significant risks REIT investors face, because REITs are sensitive to changes in interest rates in several ways. When rates rise, REIT share prices often fall. Part of the reason is competition for income: as bonds and other fixed-income investments offer higher yields, income-seeking investors may rotate out of REITs, pressuring their prices. Part of it is valuation: higher rates raise the discount rate applied to future cash flows, lowering present values, including for income-producing real estate.

Rising rates also raise REITs' borrowing costs, since most REITs use debt — when a REIT must refinance maturing debt at higher rates, its interest expense climbs, pressuring cash flow and distributions. Mortgage REITs are especially rate-sensitive: they earn the spread between what their mortgage assets pay and their cost of borrowing, so shifts in rates or the yield curve can compress that spread and the distribution directly. So interest-rate risk affects REITs through prices, valuations, borrowing costs, and (for mortgage REITs) earning spreads. It's important to note that the relationship isn't perfectly mechanical — quality REITs with growing rents can offset some rate pressure — but rate sensitivity is a defining REIT risk.

So interest-rate risk pressures REIT prices, valuations, borrowing costs, and mortgage-REIT spreads, making it a defining risk to understand. So rate sensitivity is the first risk on the list. Interest-rate risk — rising rates pressuring REIT share prices (as competing yields rise and valuations fall), raising borrowing costs that squeeze cash flow when debt is refinanced, and compressing the interest-rate spreads mortgage REITs earn — is one of the most significant REIT risks. The relationship isn't perfectly mechanical, but rate sensitivity is fundamental. Understanding it frames the other risks. Interest-rate risk is a defining REIT risk: rising rates can pressure share prices and valuations, raise borrowing costs that squeeze distributions, and compress mortgage REITs' earning spreads — though quality REITs with growing rents can offset some of the pressure.

sections.heading: Sector & Tenant Concentration
paras: Concentration risk — over-reliance on a single sector or a few tenants — can magnify losses when something goes wrong. A REIT concentrated in one property sector is exposed to that sector's specific fortunes: an office REIT faces the structural challenges of remote work, a retail REIT faces e-commerce pressure, a hotel REIT faces travel downturns. When a sector falls out of favor or faces secular decline, a REIT concentrated there can suffer sharp, prolonged underperformance that a diversified REIT would feel less acutely.

Tenant concentration is the related risk at the property level. A REIT that depends on a few large tenants for much of its rent is vulnerable to those tenants' financial health — if a major tenant defaults, declares bankruptcy, or doesn't renew its lease, the REIT can lose a large chunk of income at once, threatening its distribution and value. Net-lease REITs, while prized for durable leases, can carry meaningful single-tenant exposure on individual properties. Geographic concentration adds another layer: a REIT focused on one city or region is exposed to that area's local economy, regulation, and conditions. So concentration — by sector, tenant, or geography — amplifies the impact of adverse events.

So sector and tenant concentration magnify the effect of a downturn in a sector, a tenant's failure, or a regional shock — diversification dampens it. So concentration is a core REIT risk. Sector and tenant concentration risk — a REIT over-reliant on one property sector being exposed to that sector's secular and cyclical fortunes (office, retail, hotels each facing distinct pressures), a REIT dependent on a few large tenants being vulnerable to their default or non-renewal, and geographic concentration adding local-economy exposure — amplifies the impact of adverse events. Diversification across sectors, tenants, and markets dampens it. Understanding concentration is essential. Concentration risk — over-reliance on one sector, a few tenants, or one region — magnifies losses when a sector declines, a major tenant fails, or a local economy weakens; diversification across sectors, tenants, and geographies reduces it.
Concentration cuts both ways: a focused REIT can outperform when its sector thrives, but when that single sector or a major tenant turns, there's nowhere for the damage to hide.

sections.heading: Leverage and Refinancing Risk
paras: Leverage — the use of debt — amplifies both returns and risk, making it a central REIT risk. Real estate is a leveraged business, and most REITs borrow to acquire properties, which can boost returns when things go well. But debt also magnifies losses when property values or income fall: a heavily leveraged REIT has less cushion to absorb a downturn, and in severe cases excessive leverage can threaten a REIT's solvency. So the level of leverage a REIT carries directly affects how much risk you're taking.

Refinancing risk is the timing dimension of leverage, and it's especially acute in a high-rate environment. When a REIT's debt matures, it must repay or refinance — and if it refinances at higher rates, its interest costs rise, pressuring distributions; if credit markets are tight, it may struggle to refinance at all, potentially forcing asset sales at unfavorable prices. A REIT with large debt maturities concentrated in the near term faces significant refinancing risk, while one that staggers its maturities and locks in fixed-rate debt is more resilient. So both the amount of debt and the schedule of when it comes due matter. Floating-rate debt adds direct exposure to rising rates.

So leverage and refinancing risk — too much debt, or debt maturing at the wrong time in a high-rate environment — can pressure distributions and, in severe cases, solvency. So the balance sheet is a core risk. Leverage and refinancing risk — debt amplifying both returns and losses (a heavily leveraged REIT having less cushion in a downturn), and refinancing risk arising when maturing debt must be refinanced at higher rates or in tight credit markets (concentrated near-term maturities being most dangerous, especially with floating-rate debt) — make the balance sheet a central REIT risk. Both the level and timing of debt matter. Understanding leverage is essential. Leverage and refinancing risk make a REIT's balance sheet central: too much debt amplifies losses, and debt maturing at the wrong time — in a high-rate or tight-credit environment — can squeeze distributions or force asset sales, with concentrated near-term and floating-rate maturities most dangerous.

sections.heading: Management & Conflict Risk
paras: Management and conflict risk reflects the reality that a REIT is run by people whose decisions and incentives shape your outcome. Weak management can allocate capital poorly — overpaying for properties, mistiming the cycle, taking on too much debt, or failing to manage the portfolio well — eroding returns even when the underlying real estate market is healthy. A REIT's leadership matters, and a history of poor decisions or a lack of relevant experience is a genuine risk.

Conflict risk is most acute in externally-managed and non-traded REITs. When a separate management company runs the REIT for fees, its incentives may not fully align with shareholders: a manager paid acquisition fees may grow the REIT's asset base (and its own fees) even when growth isn't in shareholders' best interest, and related-party transactions — buying from or selling to affiliates — may not be at arm's length. High fees themselves are a drag on returns, and conflicts can lead to decisions that benefit the manager more than the investor. So with externally-managed and non-traded REITs especially, the alignment of management's incentives, the fee structure, and the handling of conflicts are real risks to assess. Strong governance and aligned incentives mitigate this; weak governance amplifies it.

So management and conflict risk — poor capital allocation, misaligned incentives, high fees, and related-party conflicts (especially in externally-managed and non-traded REITs) — can erode returns regardless of the real estate. So who runs the REIT matters. Management and conflict risk — weak management allocating capital poorly (overpaying, mistiming, overleveraging), and conflicts in externally-managed and non-traded REITs where fee-driven incentives, high fees, and related-party transactions may not align with shareholders — can erode returns even in a healthy market. Governance and alignment determine the severity. Understanding this risk matters because people run REITs. Management and conflict risk arises because people run REITs: weak management can allocate capital poorly, and externally-managed or non-traded REITs can carry misaligned fee-driven incentives and related-party conflicts — strong governance and aligned incentives mitigate it, weak governance amplifies it.
In an externally-managed REIT, the most important risk often isn't the real estate at all — it's whether the manager is paid to grow your wealth or simply to grow the size of the fund.

sections.heading: Market & Liquidity Risk
paras: Market and liquidity risk takes different forms depending on whether a REIT is publicly traded or non-traded. A publicly traded REIT's shares move continuously with the market, so they carry market-price volatility: the price can fall sharply during a broad sell-off — driven by investor sentiment, rate expectations, or economic fears — even when the underlying properties and rents are stable. This volatility is the price of the daily liquidity traded REITs offer, and it can be uncomfortable for investors who watch (or react to) short-term swings.

A non-traded REIT carries the opposite risk: illiquidity. Because its shares aren't exchange-listed, you generally can't sell on demand — your main avenue for liquidity is the redemption program, which is typically capped (commonly around 5% per year) and can be reduced or suspended at the REIT's discretion, especially during stress when many investors want out at once. So a non-traded REIT ties up your capital, and you may be unable to exit when you'd like. Both structures also face the broader economic and real estate cycle risk — recessions, falling occupancy, and declining rents can reduce income and value regardless of structure. So traded REITs carry volatility, non-traded REITs carry illiquidity, and both carry cycle risk.

So market and liquidity risk means volatility for traded REITs, illiquidity for non-traded REITs, and economic-cycle risk for both. So this risk depends on the structure you choose. Market and liquidity risk — publicly traded REITs carrying market-price volatility (sharp swings driven by sentiment and rates, even when properties are stable), non-traded REITs carrying illiquidity (capped, suspendable redemptions that can trap capital), and both exposed to the broader economic and real estate cycle — varies with the structure you choose. Volatility is the cost of traded liquidity; illiquidity is the cost of smoother non-traded pricing. Understanding this completes the risk picture. Market and liquidity risk depends on structure: traded REITs carry price volatility (sharp swings even when properties are stable), non-traded REITs carry illiquidity (capped, suspendable redemptions), and both face economic and real estate cycle risk that can reduce income and value.

sections.heading: Mitigating REIT Risks
paras: While REIT risks can't be eliminated, they can be managed through a few sound practices. The first is diversification: rather than concentrating in a single REIT, spread your exposure across multiple REITs, sectors, and geographies — a REIT fund or ETF does this automatically, and holding several REITs reduces the impact of any one sector's downturn or any single REIT's troubles. Diversification doesn't prevent losses, but it dampens the effect of concentration risk and the failure of any single investment.

The second practice is quality: favor REITs with strong, aligned management, sound balance sheets (conservative leverage, well-staggered debt maturities), high-quality and well-leased properties, and sustainable, covered distributions. Quality REITs are better positioned to weather rate increases, downturns, and stress than overleveraged, poorly-managed, or richly-yielding-but-fragile ones. The third is due diligence — actually examining the management, balance sheet, portfolio, distribution coverage, and fees before investing, as covered in a thorough REIT checklist. The fourth is appropriate position sizing: keep any single REIT, and your overall REIT allocation, sized so that a bad outcome won't derail your plan. So diversification, quality, due diligence, and sizing together form a sensible risk-management approach.

So mitigating REIT risks means diversifying, favoring quality, doing due diligence, and sizing positions appropriately — managing rather than eliminating risk. So a disciplined approach makes REITs investable. Mitigating REIT risks — diversifying across REITs, sectors, and geographies (reducing concentration risk), favoring quality (strong management, sound balance sheets, well-leased properties, covered distributions), conducting genuine due diligence before investing, and sizing positions appropriately so a bad outcome won't derail your plan — manages the risks even though it can't eliminate them. A disciplined approach makes REITs a sound, if risky, investment. Understanding mitigation completes the picture. Mitigate REIT risks by diversifying across REITs and sectors, favoring quality (strong management, sound balance sheets, covered distributions), doing real due diligence, and sizing positions appropriately — these manage the risks without eliminating them.
